letters.re: Re: Master Theodore Nwosu-Kilbride, aged 11, headaches
body: I am writing to set out my findings for Theodore, seen today with four months of headaches, and to ask you to review him, particularly if they change in character.

The headaches are frontal and band-like, occur about five days a week and worsen through the day. They are absent on waking, have never woken him, and are not associated with vomiting or straining. They ease with rest, paracetamol and stopping tablet use.

Vision is 6/5 in each eye and he needs no glasses on today's results, but accommodation is borderline low, so I will repeat it with a cycloplegic refraction. Dilated examination shows normal optic discs with spontaneous venous pulsation, excluding papilloedema. The pattern suggests tension-type headache.

Contributing factors include seven hours' daily screen use, about six and a half hours' sleep and low fluid intake. I have advised screen breaks, no screens before bed, more sleep and a water bottle. His father is keeping a six-week headache diary.

His paracetamol use, about 16 days a month, meets the threshold for medication-overuse headache and needs review. His father will see you promptly if headaches occur on waking or with vomiting. I will review him in six weeks.

commentary.selection: The headache features that argue against raised pressure, the normal discs with venous pulsation, the borderline accommodation, the paracetamol frequency and the modifiable factors are kept. Individual measurements such as pressures and convergence are summarised, as the GP needs the conclusion, not the figures.
commentary.organisation: Purpose, then headache history, then examination and conclusion, then contributing factors and advice, then medication, red flags and follow-up.
commentary.tone: Reassuring but careful and professional, showing the GP that a thorough examination was done.

letters.re: Re: Miss Beatrice Okonkwo-Wharton, aged 24, presumed microbial keratitis, left eye
body: Following my call to your corneal fellow at 09:15, I am writing to request urgent assessment, corneal scrape and treatment of Miss Okonkwo-Wharton's left eye for presumed contact lens related microbial keratitis. She should arrive by 10:15.

She woke at four this morning with severe pain, photophobia and blurred vision, after two days of mild irritation. Vision is 6/36, previously 6/6. There is a white stromal infiltrate approximately 2.2 mm across, slightly inferior and nasal to the visual axis, with an overlying epithelial defect and stromal haze. Anterior chamber cells were 2+, with no hypopyon at 09:20.

She sleeps in monthly silicone hydrogel lenses most nights, has worn the current pair for seven weeks, has never replaced her case, tops up her solution, and showers and swims in her lenses, so Acanthamoeba should be considered.
No antibiotic or steroid has been given. Her lens, case and solution are enclosed for culture. She takes a combined oral contraceptive only and has no known allergies.
She will not wear lenses or drive; her flatmate is bringing her, and will telephone your fellow if they cannot arrive by 10:15, so that antibiotic can start without delay.

letters.re: Re: Mr Daniel Brooks, aged 26, stable keratoconus, transfer for lens refit
body: I am writing to transfer the ongoing keratoconus management of Mr Brooks, a postgraduate student, to your service, and to request a rigid gas-permeable refit, considering scleral lenses.

He has keratoconus in both eyes and had cross-linking in March 2021 on the right and June 2021 on the left. He has since been stable: maximum keratometry is 52.4 D right and 54.1 D left, within 0.3 D of the 2023 readings, and thinnest pachymetry is 452 microns right and 438 microns left, unchanged. There is no apical scarring.

His current lenses are four years old, with deposits and edge fretting, and the right shows excessive apical bearing. Wearing time has fallen to about six hours because of discomfort. Acuity is 6/9 right and 6/12 left in lenses, but only 6/24 and 6/36 in spectacles, so he depends entirely on lenses for study and driving.
He has atopic eczema and a long history of eye rubbing, the single modifiable risk; his eczema control should be optimised. Annual topography should continue to detect any late progression.
He would prefer to avoid visits next May because of his final-year examinations. Copies of his last three topography maps are enclosed.

letters.re: Re: Mr Kevin O'Sullivan, aged 38, healed right corneal abrasion
body: I am writing to inform you that Mr O'Sullivan, a self-employed carpenter, has made a full recovery from a right corneal abrasion and was discharged from optometric care today. No action is needed.

He attended on 24 August 2026 with pain and a foreign body sensation after cutting timber without safety glasses. Examination showed a small inferior abrasion of approximately 2 mm, with no embedded foreign body, infiltrate or anterior chamber reaction, and right vision of 6/9. He was treated with chloramphenicol ointment four times daily for five days, together with preservative-free lubricants.

Today his symptoms have fully resolved, the cornea is clear with no staining or haze, vision is 6/6 in each eye, and dilated fundus examination is normal. He completed the ointment course and needs no further treatment.

He has been advised to return immediately if pain, redness, discharge or blurred vision recur, as recurrent erosion can follow this type of injury, sometimes months later. As wood is vegetable matter, he will also return the same day with any new pain, redness or discharge in the coming weeks. Workplace eye protection has been reinforced in writing, and he has ordered impact-rated safety glasses.

The telephone check, tear film, appendicectomy, ankle fracture, darts, fishing, family and insurance questions are left out as irrelevant to the GP’s record.

letters.re: Re: Miss Priya Nair, aged 41, suspected macula-on right retinal detachment
body: Thank you for accepting Miss Nair for emergency review today, following my telephone call at 11.40 am. I would be grateful for urgent assessment and repair of a suspected rhegmatogenous retinal detachment in her right eye while the macula remains attached.
She reports two days of new right floaters and temporal flashes and, since waking, a dark curtain rising from below, now covering the lower third of her field, without pain or trauma.

Right vision is 6/12, without pinhole improvement, compared with 6/6 in March 2025, and there is inferior field loss to confrontation. Dilated examination shows a superior bullous detachment with a horseshoe tear at the eleven o'clock position and pigment cells in the anterior vitreous. The macula appears attached, with the detachment edge approximately one and a half disc diameters superior to the fovea. She is highly myopic, at minus 8.50 DS right and minus 8.00 DS left.
Please also document the left temporal lattice degeneration, which has no breaks.

She takes no medication and has no known allergies. She has been advised to rest, avoid exertion, not drive and remain nil by mouth until assessed; her partner is bringing her directly. Widefield photographs are enclosed.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Carol Stevens, aged 58, severe dry eye disease; possible Sjögren's syndrome
body: I am writing to advise you that Mrs Stevens has severe dry eye disease with meibomian gland dysfunction, and to ask you to consider screening for Sjögren's syndrome, including autoantibodies, as she also reports a dry mouth and joint aching.

She has a six-month history of gritty, burning eyes, worse with screens and air-conditioning, with a symptom score of 38, in the severe range. Non-invasive break-up time is four seconds right and three seconds left, with reduced tear meniscus height, moderate inferior corneal staining and conjunctival lissamine green staining. The meibomian glands are blocked, with thickened secretion and dropout, and there is anterior blepharitis. There is no infection.

She also describes a persistently dry mouth, needing water to swallow dry food, aching in the hands and knees for around a year, and two new dental fillings this year. She takes levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily, and her occasional antihistamine may be contributing to the dryness.

I have started warm compresses with lid massage, lid hygiene, preservative-free lubricants four times daily and a night-time gel, with screen advice. I will review her in eight weeks, and she is happy for any results to be shared with this practice.

letters.re: Re: Mr Raymond Whitfield, aged 58, newly detected diabetic retinopathy
body: I am writing to inform you that Mr Whitfield, who has type 2 diabetes, has newly detected non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes, and to request a review of his glycaemic and blood pressure control. I would also be grateful if you could confirm his enrolment in the diabetic eye screening programme.

Dilated examination today showed dot haemorrhages, microaneurysms and a few hard exudates temporal to each macula, with no new vessels and no exudate within one disc diameter of either fovea. Undilated views in March 2024 showed no retinopathy. Best corrected vision is 6/9 in each eye. As optical coherence tomography is unavailable here, subclinical macular oedema cannot be excluded.

His last HbA1c, as he reports it, was around 69 mmol/mol (8.5 per cent) six months ago, and he has not seen the practice nurse since. He takes metformin 1 g twice daily and atorvastatin 20 mg at night, with no antihypertensive. He smokes ten cigarettes daily, and cessation has been advised.

He has missed his last two screening appointments, possibly because invitations went to his old address after he moved in 2025. His early-morning shifts make daytime appointments difficult. I will review him in six months.

letters.re: Re: Mr Gerald Hutchinson, aged 59, suspected primary open-angle glaucoma
body: I am writing to inform you that Mr Hutchinson has findings suggestive of primary open-angle glaucoma, and that I referred him electronically to the hospital eye service under the glaucoma pathway on 28 August 2026. Please note the suspected diagnosis in his record.

He is asymptomatic. Goldmann pressures were 28 mmHg right and 30 mmHg left, and 27 and 29 mmHg on repeat, having been 24 and 25 mmHg on non-contact testing in 2024. Cup-disc ratios are 0.7 right and 0.75 left, with inferior rim thinning, more marked on the left. Visual fields show a reproducible early superior arcuate defect on the left and a borderline right field. The angles are open. Pachymetry is pending and will be forwarded.
His mother had glaucoma. Importantly, he has asthma and uses a salbutamol inhaler, so topical beta-blockers should be avoided. He has no known allergies.

He was anxious because of his mother's history, and understands that field loss is irreversible and that treatment aims to prevent further loss. He has been advised that first-degree relatives over forty should have regular sight tests, and will contact us if he has not heard from the hospital within a few weeks.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Helen Archer, aged 61, possible left Horner's syndrome
body: I am writing to inform you that Mrs Archer has been referred today as a same-day emergency to the emergency department. Her new left ptosis and small left pupil suggest a Horner's syndrome, which, with neck pain on the same side, must be treated as a possible carotid artery dissection because of the stroke risk.

The left lid has drooped over three weeks, and she has had aching on the left side of her neck for about a month. Margin-to-reflex distance is 4.0 mm right and 2.5 mm left, with normal levator function. Anisocoria is 1.0 mm in bright light and 2.0 mm in dim light, localising it to the smaller left pupil. Vision, motility and fundi are normal; old photographs show equal lids and pupils.

The department has accepted her for CT or MR angiography of the head and neck, with imaging of the chest apex because of her thirty pack-year smoking history. She has hypertension, takes amlodipine 5 mg daily and has no known allergies.
She has been told to call 999 if she develops weakness, speech disturbance or severe headache before being seen. Her partner is driving her, and she understands why she must attend today.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Edith Caldwell, aged 78, suspected neovascular AMD, right eye
body: I would be grateful if you could see Mrs Caldwell urgently under the fast-track macular pathway, ideally within a week, for assessment of suspected neovascular age-related macular degeneration in her right eye and consideration of anti-VEGF treatment.

She reports five days of distorted central vision in the right eye and a central grey patch, first noticed three days ago and enlarging. Right vision has fallen to 6/24 from 6/9 in July 2025, with near vision N18 and no pinhole improvement. Amsler testing shows metamorphopsia and a small scotoma just above fixation. Dilated examination shows macular subretinal fluid with a small subretinal haemorrhage inferotemporal to the fovea, and soft confluent drusen. Mild nuclear sclerosis does not explain the loss. Optical coherence tomography is unavailable here.
The left eye sees 6/9, with soft drusen but no fluid or haemorrhage, unchanged since July 2025. She has been given an Amsler grid to monitor it daily and to report any change at once.

She has hypertension treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily and no known allergies. She lives alone and does not drive, but her daughter can bring her at short notice. Colour photographs of both eyes are enclosed.

letters.re: Re: Master Liam Foster, aged 4 years 3 months, left convergent squint and amblyopia
body: I am writing to refer Liam for orthoptic and paediatric ophthalmology assessment and management of a left convergent squint with left amblyopia. Nursery staff raised a concern about his vision in July.

His mother has noticed the left eye turning inward for about a year. Uncrowded vision is right 6/6 and left 6/24 with matching pictures at three metres, unimproved by pinhole. Prism cover test shows a left esotropia of approximately 25 dioptres at near and 12 at distance. Stereopsis was not demonstrated; please repeat crowded acuity and stereoacuity.

Cycloplegic refraction with cyclopentolate 1 per cent gave right plus 2.50 DS and left plus 5.00 DS. This hypermetropic anisometropia of 2.50 D is the likely cause of the amblyopia, with an accommodative element driving the squint. Media, red reflexes, discs and maculae are normal in both eyes.
His father wore glasses and had patching as a child. Liam has no known allergies and takes no regular medicines.

I am prescribing full hypermetropic correction for all-day wear. I would be grateful for your assessment and advice on occlusion of the right eye once the glasses are established. I will review him in six weeks unless you advise otherwise.

body: I am writing to request urgent assessment of Mr Sharma, a taxi driver, for right proliferative diabetic retinopathy likely to need pan-retinal photocoagulation, ideally within two weeks.

Vision is right 6/12 and left 6/9, unimproved by pinhole. The right eye shows new vessels at the disc of approximately one third of a disc area, venous beading in two quadrants and a small preretinal haemorrhage, without traction. The left eye has moderate non-proliferative changes. Macular oedema cannot be excluded without OCT, and there are no iris new vessels.

He has had type 2 diabetes for fourteen years, on twice-daily mixed insulin and metformin 1 g twice daily, with a last HbA1c of 84 mmol/mol. He takes ramipril 10 mg daily; blood pressure today was 156/94. Cholesterol is raised with no statin listed. He has no known allergies.

He should return immediately if vision drops suddenly. His best acuity is below the Group 2 standard for taxi licensing, so he has been told to stop taxi driving until reviewed and to contact the licensing authority and the DVLA. His GP will review his control, including lipids; please coordinate any rapid glucose tightening, which can transiently worsen the retinopathy. Photographs are enclosed.

body: I am writing to refer Mrs Pryce for same-day assessment of suspected giant cell arteritis, following my telephone call at 2.40 pm. I would be grateful if you would start high-dose corticosteroids immediately, considering intravenous methylprednisolone, without waiting for inflammatory markers or biopsy, and involve ophthalmology today.

Over three days she has had two episodes of transient curtain-like loss of vision in the right eye, the latest this morning, each lasting a few minutes. She also reports a new right temporal headache for about ten days, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, weight loss of about 4 kg over two months, night sweats, and morning shoulder and hip girdle stiffness.

Today, vision is right 6/9 and left 6/6, with full colour vision and fields. There is no relative afferent pupillary defect, disc swelling or pallor. The right temporal artery is tender and thickened, with reduced pulsation. No bloods have been taken. An embolic cause should also be considered.
She has osteoporosis, relevant to steroid treatment, and takes weekly alendronic acid with daily calcium and vitamin D. She has no known allergies and weighs 61 kg.
She has been advised not to delay or drive; a neighbour is accompanying her.

commentary.selection: The visual episodes, the classic cranial and systemic symptoms, the normal eye findings today, the temporal artery signs and the osteoporosis are kept. Her librarian work, allotment, previous abrasion, hip replacement, mammogram and car-park request are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request, then symptoms, then examination findings, then medical background relevant to treatment, then practical safety advice.
commentary.tone: Urgent and direct, as between clinicians in an emergency, without dramatic language.

letters.re: Re: Mr Thomas Reilly, aged 34, suspected acute anterior uveitis, right eye
body: I am writing to refer Mr Reilly for prompt assessment and treatment of suspected acute anterior uveitis in the right eye. Posterior synechiae are already forming, so I would be grateful if he could be seen today for topical corticosteroid and cycloplegic treatment.

He has a three-day history of a deep aching red right eye with marked photophobia and mild blurring, without trauma or contact lens wear. Vision is right 6/12 and left 6/6. The right eye shows circumcorneal ciliary flush, anterior chamber cells graded 2+ with flare, fine inferior keratic precipitates and early posterior synechiae at the four and eight o'clock positions. Pressures are right 14 and left 15 mmHg, and the fundi are healthy with no vitritis. The left eye is normal.

He had a similar right episode about two years ago, treated at eye casualty, but did not attend follow-up. He also reports inflammatory-type lower back stiffness most mornings for over a year. Investigation for an HLA-B27 association and a rheumatology opinion may therefore be warranted.
He takes no medication and has no known allergies. He has been advised to attend follow-up and not to drive. His GP will receive a copy.

commentary.organisation: Request, then present episode and findings, then history pointing to a systemic association, then medicines, allergies and practical points.
commentary.tone: Clinical and concise, using standard grading terms a hospital ophthalmologist expects.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Joan Whitfield, aged 72, right cataract
body: I am writing to refer Mrs Whitfield for consideration of right cataract surgery. She has a dense nuclear sclerotic cataract that now limits her daily activities, and she is keen to proceed.

Over about twelve months she has noticed gradual right blurring, with marked glare and haloes from headlights, so she has stopped driving after dark. She can no longer manage the close needlework she does daily. Right vision is 6/18, improving to 6/12 with pinhole, and falls to 6/24 on glare testing; left vision is 6/9. Near vision is N12 right and N6 left. There is a myopic shift of 1.25 D in the right eye since 2024.

The right lens shows grade 3 nuclear sclerosis with some posterior subcapsular change. Anterior chambers are deep, pressures are right 15 and left 16 mmHg, and there is no pseudoexfoliation. The maculae appear healthy, although the right view is hazy.

She has well-controlled hypertension treated with bendroflumethiazide 2.5 mg daily, takes no alpha-blocker, and has no known allergies. She wears a hearing aid in the left ear, which is relevant to consent and communication in theatre. She can lie flat, and her daughter can help with drops.

commentary.opening: The request and the eye are named in the first sentence, followed by the functional impact and her wish for surgery, which are what a cataract service needs to accept a referral.
commentary.selection: Functional loss, acuity including glare, refraction change, lens grading, surgical risk factors (pseudoexfoliation, alpha-blocker, ability to lie flat) and the hearing aid are kept. The choir, cat, bunion surgery, bowel screening and her son in Canada are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request, then symptoms and measurements, then examination findings, then medical and practical points relevant to surgery.
commentary.tone: Routine and professional, with patient-centred detail about her needlework to justify the referral.

letters.re: Re: Mr Raymond Doyle, aged 64, suspected left central retinal vein occlusion
body: I am writing to refer Mr Doyle for same-day assessment of sudden painless visual loss in the left eye consistent with a central retinal vein occlusion, as agreed by telephone at 9.30 am.

He woke with blurred left vision, normal at about 11 pm, without pain, headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or neurological symptoms. Vision is right 6/6 and left 6/36, unimproved by pinhole, with a left relative afferent pupillary defect. The left fundus shows flame haemorrhages in all four quadrants, tortuous dilated veins, cotton wool spots and disc swelling, with probable macular oedema unconfirmed without OCT. No iris new vessels were seen; pressures are right 18 and left 19 mmHg.

He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and raised cholesterol, treated with metformin 1 g twice daily, ramipril 10 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg at night. He is allergic to penicillin. Blood pressure today was 168/98, and 165/96 on repeat.

Please also arrange, with his GP, a full systemic work-up including ESR and CRP to exclude an inflammatory cause of the disc swelling, and close follow-up for iris and angle new vessels, as the occlusion appears ischaemic. He has been advised not to drive; fundus photographs are enclosed.

commentary.selection: Onset, relevant negatives (including giant cell arteritis symptoms), acuity, RAPD, fundus signs, pressures, vascular risk factors, medicines, the penicillin allergy and today's blood pressure are kept. His fishing, family wedding, lid cyst, hernia repair, tinnitus and parking question are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request, then history and examination, then medical background and allergy, then the specific requests and practical points.
commentary.tone: Urgent, precise and professional, as appropriate to an on-call ophthalmologist.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Eileen Doherty, aged 64, suspected acute angle-closure, right eye
body: I am writing to request same-day assessment of Mrs Doherty for suspected acute angle-closure in the right eye. Following my telephone call at 9.05 pm, she is expected within the hour.

She has a three-hour history of severe right eye pain radiating to the forehead, with blurred vision, coloured haloes, nausea and one episode of vomiting. The onset was in a dimly lit cinema. Right vision is 6/36, reduced from 6/9, and left is 6/9. The right cornea is oedematous, with marked injection and a fixed, mid-dilated oval pupil. Intraocular pressure is 48 mmHg right and 17 mmHg left. Van Herick grading is 1 right and 2 left, so the left eye is also at risk and should be assessed for prophylactic peripheral iridotomy.

She is hypermetropic, and her mother had closed-angle glaucoma. The likely precipitant is an over-the-counter cold remedy containing an antihistamine and a decongestant, started two days ago; she has stopped it and is bringing the packet.

She has hypertension treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes. She is allergic to penicillin, which causes a rash. She has been advised not to drive, and her son is bringing her.

commentary.selection: Symptoms, acuity, pressures, angle grading, the fellow-eye risk, the precipitating medicine, the family history, current medicines and the penicillin allergy are kept. Her carpal tunnel release, knee pain, grandchildren, cinema habits and parking question are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request, then presentation and examination, then risk factors and precipitant, then medicines, allergy and transport.
commentary.tone: Urgent and factual, addressed by name to a consultant colleague.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Hyacinth Obiageli-Farnsworth, aged 57, recall for breast assessment
body: I am writing to let you know that Mrs Obiageli-Farnsworth has been recalled for further assessment after routine screening, and to ask whether you could see her before her assessment on 2 October at 09:40, as she is very distressed and not sleeping.

Her mammograms of 11 September showed architectural distortion of approximately 12 mm in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast, not present in 2022. There is no microcalcification, the right breast is normal and she has no symptoms. Assessment may include biopsy, and she has been advised not to drive if one is taken.

She has been told that most women recalled do not have cancer, that about one in four is found to have it, that we cannot say more before assessment, and that biopsy results take up to a week. A breast care nurse will telephone her on 27 September.

Her sister died of breast cancer at 46. She lives alone and has told nobody, including her son and employer, so please do not assume she has support at home. Please also assess her family history against the NICE familial criteria, referring her if they are met.

commentary.opening: The letter opens with the recall and the specific request, an appointment before 2 October, because the reason for writing now is her distress, not the result.
commentary.selection: The finding, what she has been told and her lack of support are kept, because the GP needs them to counsel her. Technical screening details (double reading, image quality), obstetric history, BMI and routine medication are left out as they do not affect what the GP must do now.
commentary.organisation: Request first, then the finding and the assessment plan, then exactly what she has been told, and finally the social picture and the family history request worded to the NICE criteria.
commentary.tone: Professional and compassionate, colleague to colleague, avoiding speculation about the outcome just as she has been told.

letters.re: Re: Master Aurelio Fitzgibbon-Nnamdi, aged 6 years and 2 months, cumulative imaging
body: I am writing about Aurelio to ask for a coordinated diagnostic plan and a single named clinician to oversee his imaging. Today's request for CT of the abdomen with contrast, for query intussusception, has been held rather than cancelled.

In fourteen months he has had three contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans, eleven abdominal and four chest radiographs, and two normal ultrasound scans. The requests came from different teams unaware of one another, and no unifying diagnosis has emerged. His estimated cumulative effective dose is approximately 15.5 millisieverts, and today's CT would add 4 to 5 more. This matters because a child's tissues are more radiosensitive than an adult's.

The paediatric registrar has agreed to ultrasound first, which answers the intussusception question well at his age, and this is booked for 15:30 today. I have placed a dose summary in his record, requested a medical physics dose assessment, and asked our paediatric radiologist to review the three CT scans together.

I would suggest radiation-free MRI enterography if inflammatory bowel disease is suspected, and joint protocol planning if further CT is needed. Finally, have his parents, who asked in January whether the scans were safe, been given an explanation?

commentary.opening: The request, a coordinated plan with one named clinician, comes first, with the reassurance that today's CT is held rather than refused, so the consultant does not read the letter as a refusal.
commentary.selection: The imaging count, the cumulative dose and the lack of coordination are the core facts. Exact dates of each scan, dose methodology, the background radiation comparison and social details are left out as they do not change the request.
commentary.organisation: Request, then the imaging history and dose, then what has been done today, then further suggestions and a final question about the parents.
commentary.tone: Respectful and collaborative: it makes no criticism of any single referrer and frames the problem as the total, not any one request.

letters.re: Re: Mr Ambrose Chukwuma-Delacroix, aged 24, missed scaphoid fracture
body: I am writing to inform you of a reporting discrepancy concerning Mr Chukwuma-Delacroix and to request that he be recalled urgently to the emergency department or fracture clinic, without waiting for a routine appointment.

He attended on 30 January after falling onto his outstretched right hand. His radiographs were recorded as normal, and he was discharged in a support without follow-up, despite documented snuffbox tenderness, pain on telescoping the thumb and reduced grip. On formal reporting today, I identified an undisplaced fracture of the waist of the right scaphoid, which a consultant musculoskeletal radiologist has confirmed.

He has been mobilising the wrist for three days. Delayed immobilisation increases the risk of non-union and avascular necrosis, which would be serious for a right-handed plasterer aged 24. On attendance, please immobilise him appropriately and consider MRI or CT rather than repeat radiographs.

We have not yet reached him directly, as his number is unobtainable. His mother and general practitioner have been asked to contact him, further calls are planned at 14:00 and 17:00, and a recorded delivery letter will follow. Please tell him openly what happened, and I am willing to speak to him myself.

commentary.selection: The missed fracture, the suggestive clinical findings, the three days of mobilisation and the failed contact attempts are kept. Projection details, analgesia, the address and the learning-system entry are left out as they do not change the action needed.
commentary.organisation: Request, then what happened and what the report shows, then why it matters and what to do on attendance, then contact attempts and the duty of candour.
commentary.tone: Factual and non-blaming between professionals, with clear urgency and a plain request for openness with the patient.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Georgiana Nwafor-Sutherland, aged 67, insulin plan for PET-CT
body: I am writing to request a written insulin plan for Mrs Nwafor-Sutherland for her urgent PET-CT on 20 February 2025 at 11:00, which will stage her newly diagnosed lymphoma before chemotherapy. The plan needs to reach her, and this department, by 17 February.

The tracer behaves like glucose, so our protocol requires a capillary glucose below 11 mmol/L at injection, a fast of at least six hours from 05:00, and no short-acting insulin within four hours of injection. Otherwise the scan may be uninterpretable, and the tracer cannot be reused.

She has type 1 diabetes and takes glargine 34 units at 22:00, with mealtime aspart and correction doses. Her readings range between 4 and 16 mmol/L, with two early-morning hypoglycaemic episodes in the past fortnight.

Please advise on the glargine dose on 19 February, which must not be omitted, whether any aspart should be taken that morning, and what she should do if her glucose falls below 4 or is above 11 on arrival. Please also confirm whether she takes metformin and, if so, whether to hold it. As she is anxious about hypoglycaemia during the fast and uptake period, please address this directly.
signoff: Nuclear Medicine and PET-CT Department, Wexbridge Hospital

commentary.opening: The request, the scan date and the deadline of 17 February are all in the first paragraph, because a late plan wastes the tracer and delays chemotherapy.
commentary.selection: The preparation rules, her insulin regimen, her hypoglycaemia and the four questions the plan must answer are kept. The detailed mechanism, other preparation instructions, retinopathy and transport details are left out as the GP does not need them to write the plan.
commentary.organisation: Request and deadline, then why the rules matter, then her current regimen and control, then the specific questions and her anxiety.
commentary.tone: Clear and courteous; it explains the radiographer's limit (she cannot write the plan herself) without over-explaining physics.

letters.re: Re: Miss Wilhelmina Okpara-Ravensworth, aged 29, CT pulmonary angiogram in early pregnancy
body: I am writing to inform you that Miss Okpara-Ravensworth underwent a CT pulmonary angiogram on 4 April 2025 while 9 weeks and 4 days pregnant, and to ask that the enclosed physics report be filed in her hand-held notes.
The scan confirmed a segmental pulmonary embolism in the right lower lobe, and she is on low molecular weight heparin. She had genuinely not known she was pregnant when asked.

Our medical physics expert estimated the fetal dose at 0.09 mGy, far below the 100 mGy threshold for deterministic effects. The additional childhood cancer risk is well under one in ten thousand, so there is no basis for considering termination, which she asked about directly. The maternal breast dose was approximately 20 mGy, so a perfusion scan should be considered first for any further imaging.

She has taken no folic acid and her BMI is 31, so please start folic acid 5 mg daily until 12 weeks. Please also confirm her anticoagulation plan for the rest of the pregnancy, at least six weeks after delivery, and the delivery itself. As she was frightened, please offer her the chance to ask questions again later in pregnancy.

letters.re: Re: Mr Ptolemy Uchendu-Blackwood, aged 71, repeated non-attendance for radiotherapy planning
body: I am writing about Mr Uchendu-Blackwood, who has missed three planning CT appointments for radical radiotherapy, to ask that your team contact him, by home visit if possible, before his referral is closed.

He has an inoperable squamous cell carcinoma of the right upper lobe, and 55 Gy in 20 fractions was agreed. He has not been planned, and six weeks have passed since consent. Further delay risks progression and loss of local control.

He answered one of six calls, saying he had got mixed up and was unsure about treatment. His brother, who has not seen him for three weeks, reports that he lives alone, was widowed in June and has been drinking heavily. He has no car, lives eleven miles away and would need to attend on twenty consecutive working days.

Please establish what is preventing him from attending. If he has declined treatment, please document this as a decision rather than non-attendance, and if transport is the obstacle, book it for the whole course. If he cannot be reached within days, please arrange a welfare check through his general practitioner, or the police if needed. Please also inform his general practitioner about his bereavement and drinking.

commentary.opening: The request, contact before the referral is closed, is made at once, because the default pathway would otherwise discharge him.
commentary.selection: The missed appointments, the clinical consequence of delay and the possible barriers (bereavement, alcohol, isolation, transport) are kept. Staging details, comorbidities and the cancelled mould room appointment are left out as they do not change what the nurse must do.
commentary.organisation: Request, then the treatment and why delay matters, then what is known of his circumstances, then the specific actions and what the department will do.
commentary.tone: Concerned and non-judgemental, making clear that non-attendance may hide a decision or a barrier rather than disengagement.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Cordelia Nwachukwu-Fairbairn, aged 46, MRI head and cervical spine not completed
body: I am writing to explain that Mrs Nwachukwu-Fairbairn's urgent MRI of the head and cervical spine could not be completed today because of severe claustrophobia, and to request your decision on an alternative.

Her safety screening was clear. She made three attempts, including feet-first positioning, but each time became distressed and breathless, with a pulse of 122. No diagnostic images were obtained and no contrast was given. A CT head would not answer the demyelination question.

The options are anxiolysis with an escort and no driving afterwards, which she is willing to try; general anaesthesia, with our next list on 9 July; or the wide-bore scanner at Ashcombe Park Hospital on 26 June, although this may fail for the same reason. A desensitisation pre-visit is arranged for 24 June.

Please send a new request card specifying your chosen route, and consider adding the thoracic spine, as both legs are affected. If sedation is chosen, please arrange the prescription in advance; she takes sertraline 50 mg and no sedative. Please also review the urgency, given a likely delay of two to four weeks. She knows to attend the emergency department for new leg weakness or bladder or bowel change.
signoff: Magnetic Resonance Imaging Department, Wexbridge Hospital

commentary.organisation: Purpose, then what happened, then the options, then the specific actions requested of the consultant.
commentary.tone: Factual and supportive of the patient, avoiding any suggestion of blame for the failed attendance.

letters.re: Re: Mr Ignatius Balogun-Ravenscroft, aged 79, renal function before contrast CT
body: I am writing to request an urgent serum creatinine, eGFR and urea and electrolytes for Mr Balogun-Ravenscroft, with a medication review, before his staging CT for sigmoid adenocarcinoma can proceed. Please arrange the bloods this week, within seven days of his rebooked appointment on 12 November at 09:30.

I did not give contrast today because his latest result, from 3 April 2025, showed an eGFR of 47 and is seven months old. He also reports an admission to Ashcombe Park Hospital in August with a urinary infection and dehydration. If you hold those results, please send them.

He takes undeclared metformin 1 g twice daily and has taken over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for five weeks. With ramipril and indapamide this raises the risk of acute kidney injury, and with apixaban the risk of bleeding, so I have advised him to stop it; please consider alternative analgesia, whether to hold indapamide, and his apixaban dose once the result is back. His fluid intake is poor. We withhold metformin for 48 hours after contrast if the eGFR is below 30 or there is acute kidney injury.

commentary.selection: The out-of-date result, the August admission, the undeclared drugs and their risks, the apixaban review and the metformin rule are kept. Contrast history, cardiac history, the slot release date and what he was told about the cancer are left out as they do not change the GP's tasks.
commentary.organisation: Request and deadline, then why the scan was postponed, then the medication findings and the specific decisions needed.

letters.re: Re: Mr Aurelian Kyriakou-Bramwell, aged 68, MRI lumbar spine postponed for implant safety
body: I am writing to explain why Mr Kyriakou-Bramwell's urgent MRI lumbar spine could not safely proceed today, and to ask you to confirm how urgent the imaging is clinically, so that the appropriate option can be chosen.

On screening, he disclosed a cardiac device implanted in March 2024 at Ashcombe Park Hospital. His identification card is illegible, and he is unsure whether it is a pacemaker or a defibrillator, or whether he is pacing-dependent. Today's chest radiograph suggests a dual-chamber pacemaker, but this is only an inference. Without the generator and lead models and confirmation that the whole system is MR-conditional, I cannot scan him. Their device clinic is closed until Tuesday.

If so, he could be scanned on our cardiac-supported list on 5 September with a cardiac physiologist and monitoring, which I recommend and have provisionally booked. Alternatively, CT myelography is available within four days, although it is invasive. Plain CT would not answer your question. If his foot drop needs imaging sooner, transfer to a centre linked with his implanting trust could be considered.
Please re-examine him now for cauda equina signs, which would make imaging an emergency, and send a revised card if you choose myelography.

commentary.opening: The first paragraph says at once that the scan did not happen and what the surgeon must do: judge the clinical urgency, because that decides the imaging route.
commentary.selection: The device history, the uncertainty about its type, the closed device clinic and the four options are kept, because the surgeon needs them to decide. Scar size, lead positions in detail, the negative screening answers and eGFR are left out as they do not change his decision.
commentary.organisation: Request, then the safety problem and why it blocks the scan, then the options with a recommendation, then the cauda equina check and the revised card.
commentary.tone: Professional and firm on safety, while showing the surgeon that the time-sensitivity of a progressive foot drop has been recognised.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Perpetua Onyekwere-Middlemiss, aged 63, radiotherapy skin reaction
body: I am writing to transfer the skin care of Mrs Onyekwere-Middlemiss, who completed breast and axillary radiotherapy today, and to request daily nursing visits for the first week, as she cannot see or reach her inframammary fold herself.

She has a grade 3 reaction, with moist desquamation of the inframammary fold and axilla, and erythema of the whole breast. There is no infection. Reactions peak seven to ten days after the final fraction, so worsening is expected and does not indicate infection. Healing may be slower because of her diabetes.

Please wash gently with water and a pH-neutral, unperfumed wash, and apply non-adherent silicone dressings held with a tubular garment. Avoid adhesive, talc, perfumed or metallic-based products, and apply emollient to intact skin only.

For dressing changes, she has oral morphine solution 2.5 mg as required, besides paracetamol and ibuprofen. Please contact the acute oncology 24-hour number for a temperature above 37.5 or below 36, spreading redness, purulent discharge, odour or uncontrolled pain.

Because of her lymphoedema risk, please avoid venepuncture, injections and blood pressure measurement on her left arm. Her radiotherapy review is on 28 October; please copy any skin plan changes to our department.

commentary.selection: The current reaction, its expected worsening, the dressing rules, analgesia for dressing changes, escalation criteria and the left-arm precaution are kept because the nurses act on them. Dose and fractionation, tumour details, full medication and late effects are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request, then the wound and what to expect, then care instructions, then pain and escalation, then lymphoedema precautions and follow-up.
commentary.tone: Clear and practical for nursing colleagues, with instructions written as polite requests.

letters.re: Re: Mr Emmanuel Trevalyan-Adeoye, aged 58, urgent review during chemoradiotherapy
body: I am writing to request your urgent review of Mr Trevalyan-Adeoye today, before fraction 22 of his chemoradiotherapy for left tonsil carcinoma, as several problems have developed, one affecting treatment accuracy.

Cone-beam imaging shows that his neck contour has changed, with shifts exceeding our 3 mm tolerance three times, reaching 6 mm. His shell no longer fits, so the plan is not being delivered as intended. I have provisionally booked a re-planning CT for 5 May. Today's fraction was delivered after online correction, agreed with the duty oncologist and physics.

He has lost 9.6 kg, 11.4 per cent of his planning weight. He is taking almost nothing solid and drank about 700 mL yesterday, and his sodium is 131, so his hydration needs assessing today. The dietitian recommends enteral feeding by gastrostomy or nasogastric tube. His grade 3 mucositis causes pain of 8 out of 10 on swallowing, so his analgesia and mouth care need review.

His eGFR is 58, below the usual threshold of 60 for full-dose cisplatin, and his magnesium is 0.61 mmol/L, needing replacement, before his third cycle next week. Two missed fractions need compensating. He has been tearful and has mentioned stopping treatment.

commentary.opening: The request and its deadline, review before fraction 22, come first, with the reason that one problem affects treatment accuracy, which is the radiographer's particular concern.
commentary.selection: The geometric problem, weight loss and dehydration, mucositis, eGFR against the cisplatin threshold, low magnesium, missed fractions and his thoughts of stopping are kept because each needs a decision. Full blood count, skin reaction, swab and referral details are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request, then the technical problem and actions taken, then nutrition and pain, then bloods, gaps and mood, each linked to the decision needed.
commentary.tone: Concise and technical, colleague to consultant, urgent but measured.

letters.re: Re: Mr Lysander Chukwuemeka-Bostock, aged 61, urgent dental assessment before radiotherapy
body: I am writing to request urgent dental assessment and treatment for Mr Chukwuemeka-Bostock within the next five working days, as head and neck radiotherapy begins on 3 February 2025 and any extractions must be completed by Friday 17 January at the latest.

His right mandible will receive a high dose for floor of mouth carcinoma, leaving it at lifelong risk of osteoradionecrosis, with permanently reduced saliva. Extraction after radiotherapy carries a substantial risk; beforehand the risk is much lower, provided at least fourteen days, preferably twenty-one, are allowed for healing.

He has not seen a dentist for seven years. The lower right first and second molars are grossly carious, and the lower left third molar has caused pericoronitis twice. Other teeth appear carious. He has type 2 diabetes and smokes, but takes no bisphosphonate or denosumab.

I would be grateful for a full assessment with radiographs, extraction of unrestorable or doubtful teeth, scaling, and high-concentration fluoride with trays if possible. The 26 January appointment offered is too late. He has also been referred to hospital restorative dentistry. Please tell us by return whether you can see him; if not, the start date must be reconsidered.

commentary.selection: The osteoradionecrosis risk, the healing interval, the problem teeth, diabetes, smoking and the absence of antiresorptive drugs are kept because they shape the dental plan. Doses to each structure, alcohol history, transport and the planning dates are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request and deadline, then the reason for the interval, then the dental findings and relevant history, then the specific treatment wanted and the reply needed.
commentary.tone: Courteous and professional to a dental colleague, firm about timing without criticising the practice.

letters.re: Re: Miss Anastasia Oyelowo-Kingsmill, aged 34, anaphylaxis to iodinated contrast
body: I am writing to hand over Miss Oyelowo-Kingsmill, who had anaphylaxis to iodinated contrast during her CT pulmonary angiogram today, and to request close monitoring overnight, together with two further tryptase samples.

At 15:27, shortly after the iohexol injection, she developed urticaria, facial swelling, stridor and hypotension. She received two doses of intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms, oxygen, intravenous fluid, chlorphenamine and hydrocortisone. She is now alert, although periorbital swelling remains.
Please take the second tryptase sample at 17:15 and arrange the third at least 24 hours after full recovery, as these are easily missed.

Continuous oximetry and cardiac monitoring are required for at least six hours, with observations every fifteen minutes for two hours, then half-hourly, then hourly. Because of the risk of a biphasic reaction, she needs at least twelve hours of observation from full resolution of symptoms, so she must stay overnight and have medical review before discharge. Report immediately any stridor, wheeze, urticaria, swelling or hypotension; sit her up for breathing difficulty, or lay her flat if hypotensive.
The CT excluded pulmonary embolism but showed a small right basal consolidation, which needs medical review. A contrast allergy alert and allergy clinic referral have been made.

commentary.selection: The reaction, treatment, current state, sample times, monitoring schedule, the observation period timed from resolution, positioning and warning signs are kept. Exact observations, injection rate, contraception and social details are left out as the ward will make its own observations.
commentary.organisation: Request, then what happened and treatment, then the samples most likely to be missed, then monitoring and escalation, then the scan result and record actions.
commentary.tone: Direct and clear for a nursing colleague, giving instructions politely but without ambiguity.

letters.re: Re: Mr Fitzwilliam Adekunle-Sharrocks, aged 76, completed palliative radiotherapy
body: I am writing to inform you that Mr Adekunle-Sharrocks completed palliative radiotherapy today for painful spinal and right femoral bone metastases, and to request your support at home, including reinforcing red flag warnings at every visit.

Benefit is expected two to six weeks after treatment. For a pain flare in the first week he has dexamethasone 8 mg daily for three days; if he takes it, his capillary glucose should be checked at least twice daily, as he is insulin-treated. His analgesia should not be reduced before three weeks.

He takes three to four breakthrough doses daily, so please review his background morphine and, given his chronic kidney disease, consider an alternative opioid. Please also add a stimulant laxative to his macrogol and check his calcium, as he takes denosumab.

New back pain, leg weakness, saddle numbness or bladder or bowel changes may indicate cord compression and require the same-day acute oncology number. New thigh or groin pain, or inability to bear weight, could indicate a fracture.
He wishes to remain at home, supported by his wife; this is not yet formalised, and I would be grateful if your team could revisit it. A DNACPR form is in the house.

commentary.selection: Timing of benefit, the flare plan with glucose monitoring, the opioid, laxative and calcium reviews, red flags and his preferred place of care are kept. Doses and fields, previous cancer treatments, imaging and response statistics are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request, then what to expect, then the medication reviews, then red flags, then advance care planning.
commentary.tone: Supportive and practical for a palliative nursing colleague, sensitive to his wishes.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Ottilie Nkemdirim-Ashworth, aged 91, CT head not performed
body: Further to our telephone conversation today, I am writing to confirm my advice that Mrs Nkemdirim-Ashworth be sent to the emergency department today for urgent CT head and clinical review, as she takes apixaban and has new decline since her fall. I would also ask for a coordinated plan.

Your requested CT head could not be performed. She arrived distressed, with an escort who did not know her. Despite repeated simple explanations, she could not retain information or give a consistent decision, and in my judgement she lacked capacity to consent. She became agitated and tried to leave. No restraint was used.

No information about a lasting power of attorney or next of kin was available, so no best-interests decision was made here. The emergency team may make an urgent best-interests decision if she still lacks capacity.

Only if they judge that imaging can safely wait, please start a full best-interests process with the home and her family. I have cancelled automatic rebooking, so please send us the outcome, a named contact and attorney details first. Please also review her apixaban dose, as only one dose-reduction criterion is confirmed.

commentary.opening: The letter opens by confirming the urgent telephone advice, because sending an anticoagulated patient with decline after a head injury to the emergency department today is the most important action.
commentary.selection: The reason the scan failed, the capacity assessment, the missing attorney information, the conditional plan and the apixaban dose review are kept. Journey times, the deceased husband, the trusted care assistant's name, the tailored appointment and premedication detail are left out.
commentary.organisation: Urgent confirmation and request, then what happened and capacity, then the legal position, then the conditional plan and what the department needs back.
commentary.tone: Professional and careful about the Mental Capacity Act, clear that urgency comes before the full process.

letters.re: Re: Mr Raymond Cole, aged 65, abdominal aortic aneurysm found on screening
body: I am writing to inform you that Mr Cole, who attended aneurysm screening today, has been referred urgently to vascular surgery. Please review his blood pressure and support him in stopping smoking.

Ultrasound showed an infrarenal aortic aneurysm of 5.7 cm, confirmed by a second screener, with no leak. As this exceeds the 5.5 cm intervention threshold, he will be seen by vascular surgery within two weeks; the screening office will confirm the date.

His father died of a ruptured aneurysm. Mr Cole and his wife know to call 999 immediately for sudden severe abdominal or back pain or collapse, and he carries a card. He should not drive himself to appointments; his wife will take him.

His blood pressure was 158/92, repeated at 154/90, but he had just smoked, so please confirm it with repeat or home readings before changing treatment. He takes amlodipine 10 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg and aspirin 75 mg daily.

He still smokes ten a day, and I explained that smoking speeds aneurysm growth. The local stop smoking service will contact him by telephone. He previously stopped nicotine patches because of vivid dreams, so an alternative may suit him.

letters.re: Re: Miss Hannah Okeke, aged 22, acute appendicitis on ultrasound
body: I am writing to refer Miss Okeke, a university student, for urgent surgical review, as ultrasound this afternoon has confirmed acute appendicitis.

She has had eighteen hours of pain, beginning around the umbilicus and localising to the right iliac fossa, with low-grade fever, anorexia and one episode of vomiting. At scanning, her temperature was 37.8 degrees Celsius and pulse 98. White cell count was 13.6 and C-reactive protein 42. Her pregnancy test was negative.

Graded compression ultrasound showed a blind-ending, non-compressible appendix of 9 mm outer diameter, with wall thickening, hyperaemia, fat stranding and a small volume of simple pelvic free fluid. There was no appendicolith or abscess, and both ovaries were normal.

She has been kept nil by mouth, having last eaten at about 17.00 the previous day, and has received analgesia. She has no known allergies, takes no regular medication and has never had a general anaesthetic.

CT is not indicated, as the ultrasound is diagnostic and further imaging would add radiation without benefit. She returned to the emergency department at 14.30 to await your team. Images and the report are on the hospital imaging system. She is anxious but agrees to surgical assessment.

letters.re: Re: Mr Frederick Naylor, aged 74, staging bone scan for prostate cancer
body: I am writing to report Mr Naylor's whole-body bone scan of 27 August 2026, which shows probable widespread skeletal metastases, and to advise prompt assessment of a right femoral lesion for fracture risk.

Mr Naylor has Gleason 9 prostate adenocarcinoma, diagnosed on 11 August 2026, with a PSA of 186 micrograms/L. He has had three months of thoracolumbar back pain, worse at night, but no neurological symptoms.

The scan showed multiple areas of increased uptake at T8, T11, L2 and L4, both iliac bones, the sacrum and the right proximal femur. The pattern is multifocal, asymmetric and predominantly axial, typical of metastatic disease.

The femoral lesion is intense and involves the intertrochanteric region. I recommend plain radiography or CT to assess fracture risk, as prophylactic fixation may be needed before a pathological fracture occurs. Correlation with his PSA, multidisciplinary team discussion and consideration of bone-targeted therapy are also advised.

He has been given written spinal cord compression advice and told to present immediately with leg weakness, numbness, urinary difficulty, bowel change or new band-like or radicular spinal pain. Until fracture risk is assessed, he should avoid heavy lifting and showing cattle. A copy is requested for his GP.

commentary.opening: The opening states the result and the most time-sensitive advice, the femoral fracture risk, so the urologist knows what to act on first.
commentary.selection: The diagnosis, PSA, symptoms, neurological status, distribution of uptake, the femoral lesion and the cord compression advice are kept. Farm life, hobbies, past operations, the injection technique and the radiation advice about his grandson are left out as they do not affect management.
commentary.organisation: Purpose, then clinical background, then scan findings, then recommendations, then safety-netting and the GP copy.
commentary.tone: Formal and precise for a consultant, using hedged wording ('probable') because the scan alone cannot confirm metastases.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Carol Mensah, aged 52, unruptured intracranial aneurysm
body: I am writing to refer Mrs Mensah for neurosurgical assessment of an unruptured intracranial aneurysm found on MR angiography on 26 August 2026, to consider treatment versus surveillance.

The scan, requested for recurrent migraine with a family history of subarachnoid haemorrhage, showed a 6 mm saccular aneurysm at the left middle cerebral artery bifurcation, with a neck of approximately 3 mm and the dome pointing superolaterally. There was no daughter sac, haemorrhage or further aneurysm.

Her sister had a ruptured aneurysm at 49, and a maternal aunt died of a brain haemorrhage. Mrs Mensah takes losartan 50 mg daily for hypertension; home readings of around 140/90 are above target and need prompt review. She smokes twenty a day but wishes to stop now. She takes sumatriptan 50 mg for migraine with aura; as triptans are cautioned in poorly controlled hypertension, please advise whether it should continue.

She has written advice to call emergency services for thunderclap headache. She knows that a small swelling which has not bled was found; discussion was deferred to your team. She was tearful, fears her sister's outcome and asked about gym activity.
Images and the report are available through the regional image-sharing system.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Geraldine Apt, aged 63, incidental left adrenal nodule on CT urogram
body: I am writing to advise you of an incidental left adrenal nodule on Mrs Apt's CT urogram of 25 August 2026, and to recommend biochemical screening rather than further imaging.

The scan was performed for one episode of painless visible haematuria. No upper tract tumour, calculus or hydronephrosis was found, but CT does not exclude a bladder tumour, so flexible cystoscopy is still required.

The nodule measures 2.8 cm, is round and smooth, without necrosis or calcification, and has an unenhanced attenuation of 4 Hounsfield units. This is below the 10 HU threshold and consistent with a lipid-rich benign adenoma, so further imaging is not required.

To exclude a functioning tumour, I recommend a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, with an aldosterone to renin ratio if hypertension develops. Plasma metanephrines are not routinely needed at this attenuation unless symptoms develop. She has no symptoms of hormone excess, her blood pressure was 124/76 and potassium 4.3 mmol/L. If biochemistry is normal, routine imaging follow-up is not mandated.
She tolerated contrast without reaction and has no known allergies. Metformin 1 g twice daily was withheld on the scan day, though not required at an eGFR of 84; she may restart it.

commentary.selection: The haematuria result, the CT limitation, the adenoma features, the suggested tests and the metformin advice are kept. Her teaching career, grandchildren, fractures, cholecystectomy, volunteering and the parking charge are left out as irrelevant to the urologist's decisions.

commentary.tone: Clear and formal for a consultant, reassuring about the benign features without dismissing the need for tests.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Patricia Holloway, aged 67, indeterminate liver lesions on staging CT
body: I am writing to advise you that Mrs Holloway's staging CT on 28 August 2026 showed two indeterminate liver lesions, and to recommend liver MRI with a hepatocyte-specific agent before the multidisciplinary team meeting.

Mrs Holloway has sigmoid adenocarcinoma, diagnosed at colonoscopy on 14 August 2026, and is awaiting surgery. CT showed circumferential sigmoid wall thickening over 5 cm, with no perforation or definite pericolic nodes above 8 mm, and no lymphadenopathy, lung nodule or peritoneal disease. Her CEA is 6.2 micrograms/L.

The liver lesions measure 12 mm in segment 7 and 8 mm in segment 4a. Both are too small to characterise reliably on CT, and although neither shows convincing features of metastasis, this cannot be excluded. No previous imaging is available. As a metastatic diagnosis would change the operative approach, characterisation is needed now.

No metastatic disease is confirmed, and she should not be told she has liver metastases on the basis of this scan. A former nurse, she asked detailed questions, and her daughter wishes to be present when results are given.
Her left knee replacement is recorded on the MRI safety questionnaire for confirmation at booking, and her previous contrast nausea is not a true allergy.

letters.re: Re: Mr Daniel Okoye, aged 58, incidental right lower lobe nodule
body: I am writing to inform you of an incidental lung nodule on Mr Okoye's abdominal CT of 27 August 2026, and to ask you to arrange a low-dose CT of the whole chest in three months and to counsel him promptly.
The CT, requested for right upper quadrant pain, showed no abdominal cause.

The included lung bases show a 9 mm solid nodule in the right lower lobe. It is smooth and homogeneous, without cavitation, calcification, pleural contact or lymphadenopathy. Its Brock risk is below 10%, so CT surveillance rather than PET-CT is appropriate. The upper lungs were not imaged, so further nodules cannot be excluded, and no previous imaging is available.

Mr Okoye is an ex-smoker of twenty-five pack-years who stopped four years ago, and has no haemoptysis, weight loss or cough. Referral to respiratory services is recommended if the nodule grows, if further nodules are found or symptoms develop.

He has not yet been told about the nodule and believes the scan was normal, so this conversation should happen promptly rather than at a routine appointment, as the main risk is that follow-up is never booked. The reporting radiologist is happy to discuss the images by telephone.

body: I am writing to advise you of an incidental thyroid nodule on Mr Bridges's CT after a road traffic collision, and to recommend a non-urgent thyroid ultrasound with thyroid function tests.
He was scanned on 30 August 2026. There was no cervical spine fracture, and he was discharged on 31 August 2026 with neck sprain advice.

The CT showed a well-defined 1.6 cm nodule in the right thyroid lobe, without calcification. The left lobe was normal, there were no enlarged cervical lymph nodes and the trachea was central. As CT cannot characterise thyroid nodules, ultrasound is needed to assign a U score.

He has no symptoms of thyroid dysfunction, no previous neck irradiation and no family history of thyroid cancer, although his mother has an underactive thyroid. Please note that he received intravenous iodinated contrast, which may affect thyroid function tests and any isotope thyroid study for several weeks, so results should be interpreted accordingly.

He has been told about the finding and understands that it is probably harmless but needs a scan. He should be reassured that most such nodules are benign, while still being followed up. He has asked for a copy of this letter.

body: I am writing to request urgent specialist assessment of Mr Ashford, whose left knee radiographs of 31 August 2026 show an aggressive lytic lesion of the distal femur, suspicious for a primary bone malignancy, most likely osteosarcoma.

He has had six weeks of left knee pain at rest and at night, with swelling for two weeks. There was no trauma. His parents report unintentional weight loss of approximately 4 kg over two months. He takes no medication and has no known allergies.

There is an ill-defined lesion approximately 6 cm long in the distal femoral metaphysis, with a poorly defined zone of transition, lamellated periosteal reaction, early Codman triangle and medial cortical breach with a soft tissue component. There is no pathological fracture, and the growth plate is not clearly crossed.

Please arrange whole-femur MRI and staging, including chest CT. No biopsy has been performed locally, to avoid compromising limb-sparing surgery. He has been advised to avoid contact sport and heavy loading, given the fracture risk.
He and his parents know that the bone is abnormal, but no diagnosis has been given. His mother's mobile telephone is the preferred contact. Images are on the regional image-sharing network.

commentary.opening: The first paragraph states the request (urgent specialist assessment) and the suspected diagnosis at once, because a possible sarcoma in a teenager is time-critical for the reader.
commentary.selection: The red-flag history (night pain, swelling, weight loss), the aggressive radiological features and the biopsy warning are kept. School, rugby position, family members, parking, the driving test and old minor injuries are left out because they do not affect the specialist assessment.
commentary.organisation: Request and suspected diagnosis, then the clinical history, then the imaging findings, then the specific actions and precautions, and finally what the family has been told and the practical contact details.
commentary.tone: Formal and precise between professionals, using correct radiological terms and conveying urgency without speculating beyond the report.

letters.re: Re: Lucas Brennan, aged 2 years 4 months, undisplaced spiral fracture of the left tibia
body: I am writing to report Lucas's left tibia and fibula radiographs of 29 August 2026 and to advise on interpretation and follow-up. They show a subtle undisplaced spiral fracture of the distal tibial shaft, typical of a toddler's fracture.
Lucas has refused to weight-bear on the left leg since a low fall while running in the garden the previous evening, which his mother witnessed. Her account has been consistent throughout.

The fracture is visible on the lateral view but only faintly on the anteroposterior view, so both views should be reviewed carefully. The fibula is intact, and there is no periosteal reaction to suggest an older or healing injury. There is no metaphyseal corner or bucket-handle lesion, and bone density is normal.

The reporting radiologist agreed with these appearances. There are no imaging features suggestive of non-accidental injury, and the mechanism fits the fracture pattern. However, imaging alone cannot exclude a safeguarding concern, so clinical correlation is still advised.

A below-knee walking cast or removable boot is recommended for comfort, with paediatric orthopaedic follow-up in one week to confirm the type. His mother has care advice and expects three to four weeks of immobilisation. Lucas has no known allergies.

commentary.opening: The purpose (reporting and advising) and the key finding are given together, so the emergency consultant knows immediately what was found and why the letter matters.
commentary.selection: The mechanism, the subtle appearance, the negative findings relevant to non-accidental injury, the safeguarding caveat and the plan are kept. Birth history, eczema, croup, nursery, parking, his sister's dental appointment and the distraction techniques are left out as irrelevant to interpretation or follow-up.
commentary.organisation: Purpose and finding, then the history and consistency of the account, then interpretation advice, then the safeguarding position, and finally the management plan.
commentary.tone: Collegial and measured; it reassures where the imaging allows but does not overstate what imaging can exclude.

letters.re: Re: Mr Stephen Vasquez, aged 38, obstructing right ureteric calculus
body: I am writing to inform you that Mr Vasquez was discharged from the emergency department on 1 September 2026 after CT showed an obstructing right ureteric stone. Please consider metabolic review, as this is his second episode.

He presented with sudden colicky right loin-to-groin pain and microscopic haematuria. Low-dose non-contrast CT KUB showed a 5 mm calculus at the right vesicoureteric junction, with mild proximal ureteric dilatation and minimal perinephric stranding, consistent with acute obstruction. No other calculus was seen, and appendicitis, diverticulitis and aortic aneurysm were excluded.
He had no fever, his creatinine was 92 with an eGFR above 90, and urine nitrites were negative. Diclofenac 75 mg was effective. He has no known drug allergies.

The stone is likely to pass spontaneously. He was discharged with oral analgesia, a urine strainer, tamsulosin 400 micrograms daily for up to four weeks, and advice to increase his fluid intake substantially, given his hot working conditions. No hospital follow-up has been booked, so please arrange imaging or urology review if the stone has not passed within four weeks.
He knows to return immediately if fever, rigors or uncontrolled pain develop, as infection behind an obstructing stone is a urological emergency.

commentary.opening: The letter opens with the discharge and the main finding, then states what the GP is asked to do, so the reader sees both the situation and her role at once.
commentary.selection: The stone size and position, the obstruction, normal renal function, the absence of infection, the discharge plan and the safety-net advice are kept. Times of arrival and scanning, his job details, football, family history, the Wi-Fi request and the holiday are left out as irrelevant to follow-up.
commentary.organisation: Purpose and request, then the presentation and CT findings, then the reassuring results and treatment given, then the discharge plan with the GP actions, and finally the red flags.
commentary.tone: Concise and professional for a GP colleague, with clear, polite requests.

letters.re: Re: Miss Amelia Dawson, aged 19, undisplaced right scaphoid waist fracture
body: I am writing to recommend orthopaedic fracture clinic review for Miss Dawson, as repeat radiographs today, 31 August 2026, confirmed an undisplaced fracture of the right scaphoid waist that was not visible on her first attendance.

She fell onto her outstretched right hand twelve days ago and has persistent snuffbox tenderness and pain on axial loading of the thumb. Her initial radiographs on 19 August 2026 did not include dedicated scaphoid views, and no fracture is visible on them even in retrospect. No splint was recorded after that visit, which has been referred for departmental review.

Today's dedicated scaphoid series shows the fracture on the ulnar deviation and oblique views, with no displacement, angulation or carpal instability. It is too early to assess for avascular necrosis.

A below-elbow cast including the thumb was applied today, analgesia was given, and circulation was satisfactory. A fracture clinic booking request has been sent electronically. She has been counselled on the risk of non-union and avascular necrosis if immobilisation is inadequate, and on likely six to twelve weeks out of netball. She must not remove the cast.
She is right-hand dominant, takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and has no known drug allergies.

commentary.opening: The recommendation and the reason for it come first, together with the key point that the fracture was not visible at the first attendance, which the GP needs to understand at once.
commentary.selection: The mechanism, signs, both sets of imaging, the absence of early immobilisation, the cast, the referral and the counselling on complications are kept. Her course, café job, examinations, netball fees, hay fever, old ankle sprain and transport are left out as irrelevant to orthopaedic management.
commentary.organisation: Recommendation, then history and explanation of the earlier normal films, then today's findings, then the treatment and referral already made, and finally relevant background.
commentary.tone: Professional and factual; it states plainly that scaphoid views were not taken and no splint was recorded, without blame and without over-reassurance.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Priya Sharma, aged 52, suspicious left breast mass on screening with an incomplete left study
body: I am writing to refer Mrs Sharma for urgent triple assessment following her screening mammogram on 28 August 2026, which showed a highly suspicious left breast mass, and to highlight that the left study is incomplete. She has accepted an appointment on 4 September 2026.

The left mediolateral oblique view was suspended because she could not tolerate compression, owing to severe pain and a recent left shoulder injury. Only the cranio-caudal view is therefore available on the left.

This shows a 14 mm spiculated mass in the outer left breast, with fine pleomorphic microcalcification extending approximately 8 mm beyond it. Its upper or lower position cannot be determined without the missing view. No skin thickening or nipple retraction is seen, and the right breast is normal. The left axilla was not examined.
Please consider a repeat left mediolateral oblique view or MRI at the visit, so that the left breast is fully assessed. Your clinic knows about her shoulder injury, so extra time can be allowed.
She is allergic to penicillin (rash) and takes levothyroxine 75 micrograms daily. Her mother had breast cancer at 61. She is anxious and would like to bring her daughter.

commentary.opening: The opening gives the request (urgent triple assessment), the reason, and the warning that the study is incomplete, so the limitation cannot be overlooked.
commentary.selection: The suspended view and its cause, the mass and calcification, the missing positional information, the allergy, medication, family history and anxiety are kept. Her job, the screening site, obstetric history, bunion surgery, the wedding and parking are left out as not relevant to assessment.
commentary.organisation: Request and limitation, then the technical problem, then the findings, then the specific suggestion for the visit, and finally safety and personal points.
commentary.tone: Formal and precise for a consultant radiologist, with appropriate mammographic terminology and a brief, sensitive note on the patient's anxiety.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Joan Pemberton, aged 58, suspicious right breast mass and axillary node
body: I am writing to summarise the assessment findings and biopsies for Mrs Pemberton, seen on 27 August 2026, ahead of the multidisciplinary team meeting on 3 September.

She was recalled from screening for a right breast asymmetry on her mammogram of 6 August 2026, and spot compression and magnification views confirmed it persists. Ultrasound showed a 14 mm irregular hypoechoic mass at the 10 o'clock position, 4 cm from the nipple, with spiculated margins, taller-than-wide orientation, posterior acoustic shadowing and internal vascularity, graded U4 to U5.
One indeterminate right axillary node measured 11 mm, with cortical thickening of 4 mm and partial loss of the fatty hilum. The left axilla was normal.

Under local anaesthetic, four ultrasound-guided cores were taken from the breast lesion and a marker clip placed, its satisfactory position confirmed on mammogram. Three cores were taken from the axillary node, as nodal status changes the treatment pathway. The node was not clipped, so please consider marking it before any neoadjuvant treatment.

She is allergic to penicillin (rash) and takes bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily, with no anticoagulant or antiplatelet medicines. Her mother had breast cancer at 70. A results appointment is booked the following week.

commentary.opening: The opening states the purpose and links it to the MDT date given in the task, so the surgeon knows the letter is preparation for that meeting.
commentary.selection: The lesion features and grade, the node findings, the biopsies and clip, the allergy, medication and family history are kept. Her volunteering, bowls, cataract and gallbladder surgery, the café question and wound-care advice are left out because they do not affect MDT discussion.
commentary.organisation: Purpose, then the breast findings, then the axilla, then the procedures performed, and finally safety background and the next step.
commentary.tone: Formal and concise for a consultant surgeon, using standard breast-imaging terms.
