letters.re: Re: Mrs Edith Lawson, aged 78, osteoporotic compression fracture of L1
body: I am writing to report an osteoporotic compression fracture of L1 in Mrs Lawson, imaged on 30 August 2026, recommending prompt bone-protective treatment, a DEXA scan and fracture risk assessment.
Sudden back pain began two days ago lifting a heavy bag, without a fall. She has no neurological symptoms, fever, weight loss or night pain.

Radiographs show a wedge fracture of L1 with approximately 30 per cent loss of anterior height. The posterior wall is intact without retropulsion. Bone density is generally reduced, with nothing to suggest malignancy or infection.

This is at least her second fragility fracture, after an uninvestigated wrist fracture in 2022, and the T12 wedging, of uncertain age, may be a third. She has taken prednisolone 5 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica for five years, with calcium and vitamin D but no bisphosphonate. Her mother fractured a hip. As she is at very high risk, treatment should not wait for DEXA. Prednisolone must not be stopped abruptly.

Early mobilisation with conservative pain relief is advised, as bed rest worsens bone loss. MRI is indicated only if neurological signs develop or malignancy is suspected. She has no known allergies, and her daughter will book a GP review.

commentary.opening: The first paragraph gives the finding and all three recommendations, so the GP knows immediately what action is expected.
commentary.selection: The mechanism, the red-flag negatives, the fracture features, the risk factors (steroids, previous fracture, family history), the very high risk and the gap in bone protection are kept. Her hearing aids, cataract surgery, sewing, lunch club, the café question and the knee query are left out as irrelevant to bone health.
commentary.organisation: Finding and recommendations, then the history, then the imaging, then the risk factors that justify treatment, and finally the management advice and follow-up.
commentary.tone: Clear and professional for a GP; the point about missing bone protection is made firmly but without criticism.

letters.re: Re: Miss Anneliese Okoro-Vandergraaf, aged 5 years 8 months, sensory and developmental concerns
body: I am writing to refer Anneliese, a Year 1 pupil, for a developmental assessment, including consideration of a neurodevelopmental referral. She was referred for difficulty with dressing and cutlery, but needs more than occupational therapy alone.

Her motor assessment was within normal limits on every item; her difficulties are sensory and behavioural. Dressing takes 45 minutes and ends in distress, as she tolerates only two garments. She eats six foods, covers her ears in noisy places, seeks movement constantly and takes two hours to settle.

At school on 26 January, she sat apart, left the classroom twice when noisy and spoke to no other child in two hours. Her teacher reports parallel play, no pretend play and distress at unexpected changes.

Her speech is advanced, vision normal, and she has no significant medical history or allergies. A maternal cousin has autism. As her sensitivity to sound is marked and her last hearing test was in 2023, please include a repeat hearing test. Sensory profiles are enclosed.
I will continue to support her and the school alongside your assessment. Her parents agree with this letter and ask whether assessment would label her; please address this at the first appointment.

commentary.opening: The request, a developmental assessment with consideration of a neurodevelopmental referral, comes first, followed at once by why the original motor referral understates the problem.
commentary.selection: The normal motor findings, the sensory and social pattern, the school observation, family history and the request for a repeat hearing test are kept because they justify and shape the work-up. Detailed strategies, birth and milestone dates are reduced or left out because the paediatrician can read the enclosed profiles.
commentary.organisation: Request, then why it is not a motor problem, then what was observed at school, then history and enclosures, then ongoing support and the parents' question.
commentary.tone: Professional and collegial, with a respectful note on the parents' worry about labelling.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Perpetua Delacroix-Nwosu, aged 84, seating and posture plan
body: I am writing to set out Mrs Delacroix-Nwosu's seating plan; please display these instructions where all staff can see them.

Her old chair was 100 mm too high and 120 mm too deep, so she slid onto her sacrum, causing Category 1 pressure damage with skin intact. A correctly sized chair with a right lateral support and a pressure-relieving cushion was delivered on 20 February and must not be adjusted without contacting me. I have referred her to district nursing for tissue viability review.

Her feet must be flat on the floor or a footstool, and her hips right back, with the lateral support firm at her lower ribs. Keep her upright for meals and one hour afterwards. Do not tilt the chair back. Reposition her every two hours, and return her to bed by hoist after two hours' sitting.
Please record the SSKIN care bundle and sitting time before any sliding, complete a MUST screen this week and weigh her monthly. Calling out may indicate discomfort.
Contact me if her skin has not improved within two weeks, or if she slides, the support marks her or her posture changes. I will review her seated on 21 March.

commentary.opening: The letter states its purpose and its main request, that every member of staff follows and can see the positioning instructions, in the first sentence.
commentary.selection: The cause of the sliding, the pressure damage and its referral, the new chair, the positioning and sitting-time rules, SSKIN and MUST monitoring and reasons to call are kept because staff must act on them. Individual body measurements and the account of past recording are left out as detail the manager does not need to act.
commentary.organisation: Purpose, then the cause and the new chair, then daily positioning, then monitoring, then when to contact and the review date.
commentary.tone: Clear and directive for a care home manager, explaining the reason behind each instruction without blaming staff.

letters.re: Re: Ms Bronwen Achterberg-Ilechukwu, aged 38, discharge from fatigue management
body: Ms Achterberg-Ilechukwu has been discharged from occupational therapy after 8 sessions; I am writing to ask you to support a phased return to work and review her mood.

On 6 September 2024 she was housebound and tolerated about 20 minutes of activity. With symptom-led pacing and a sleep routine, she now goes out five days a week, walks 25 minutes daily and manages about 90 minutes of activity. Her fatigue impact score fell from 68 to 41 out of 80.
She still cannot sustain a full day. Cognitive symptoms, worse with noise and time pressure, remain most limiting, and symptoms still worsen 12 to 24 hours after exertion.

A return to full duties in April, as her employer wants, would very likely cause a relapse. If medical evidence is requested, please support a phased return of no more than two half days weekly initially, non-teaching duties first, no cover or break duty and a quiet room, reviewed every four weeks and increased only if stable. My occupational health report is enclosed.
Her mood has been low this month about work; please include a self-harm risk screen. She declined referral in February but may accept one now. She may self-refer back.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Millicent Oyelowo-Trevithick, aged 83, discharge after right hip hemiarthroplasty
body: I am writing to refer Mrs Oyelowo-Trevithick, discharged home on 26 April 2025 after a right hemiarthroplasty, for continued rehabilitation and a home falls assessment.

Before admission she lived alone, walking with a stick, but had three unreported falls that year. She now walks 40 metres with a frame, transfers independently from a 46 cm chair and manages 13 stairs with a rail and supervision.

Her falls risk is high. She fears falling and froze at the top of her stairs at home. Her lying and standing blood pressure was 148/78 and 118/62, with dizziness; her GP has been informed and a medication review requested. She has been referred to fracture liaison and needs an eye test, last done in 2020.
Rails and two commodes are in place, and carers visit twice daily for four weeks. Until safe alone, she should use the stairs only when a carer is present.

Please continue progression to a stick, the six kitchen steps, which are her priority, and stair confidence. Please check hip precautions before reassessing the bath board. She weighs 51 kg on supplements. She has capacity and wants to stay home; discuss her son's care-home concern with her.

Itemised equipment, washing and dressing detail and the house layout are summarised or left out because the team will see them on the first visit.

letters.re: Re: Ms Rosalind Fennimore-Achebe, aged 44, return-to-work assessment
body: Thank you for referring Ms Fennimore-Achebe, seen for 9 sessions. With her written consent, I set out my assessment and recommend a twelve-week graded return from 1 July, with permanent adjustments.

She sustains 40 minutes of desk work before accuracy declines, manages one complex task at a time, and is slowed by interruption and noise. She is overwhelmed in groups of more than four. Written casework, colleague calls and planned deadlines do not trouble her. Her triggers are hostile members of the public, lone home visits and being named officer on imminent evictions.

I recommend two four-hour days of back-office work in weeks 1 to 3; three five-hour days adding client calls in weeks 4 to 6; four six-hour days adding accompanied face-to-face contact in weeks 7 to 9; and five days towards full hours in weeks 10 to 12, with home visits only in pairs. Build in a short break after each 40 minutes of desk work. Review at weeks 3, 6 and 12.
Permanent adjustments: no lone home visits, a quiet space, protected morning time, a named contact and routine debriefing after hostile incidents.
She fears a third absence, and asks whether colleagues would see her adjustments.

Clinical treatment is left out at her request, and session content is left out as not needed for the employer's decision.

commentary.tone: Formal and precise between professionals, discreet about her health and respectful of her wishes.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Cordelia Nwokolo-Bassingthwaighte, aged 57, protecting your joints and your equipment
body: This letter explains how to protect your joints and use your equipment and splints.

To protect your swollen knuckles and wrists, use the largest joint that can do the job, such as carrying a bag over your forearm, use both hands to share the load, and avoid gripping tightly for long. If pain lasts over two hours after an activity, change how you do it.
Your jar opener, tap turners, kettle tipper and key turner reduce the grip needed. Ask your pharmacist for easy-open medication packaging.
Wear your resting splints on both hands at night only. If redness lasts over 20 minutes after removal, stop and contact me. Wash them in cool water; keep them from heat.

Contact the rheumatology advice line the same day if one joint becomes hot, red and very painful, especially with fever, or with any sign of infection; if you cannot reach them, see your GP urgently or go to A&E. Call them urgently if a finger suddenly will not bend or straighten, and report night numbness or a flare lasting over a week.
With thicker needles and long-handled tools, you can keep knitting and gardening. I will see you on 24 September 2025.
signoff: Bassingthwaighte Community Occupational Therapy, Hand Clinic

commentary.selection: The joint protection principles, what the equipment does, easy-open medication packaging, the splint rules and all the warning signs are kept because she must act on them. Measurements such as grip strength are left out because they mean little to a patient and will be repeated at review.
commentary.organisation: Purpose, then joint protection, then equipment, then splints, then warning signs, then her hobbies and the review date.
commentary.tone: Warm, plain English addressed directly to the patient, with no jargon and clear instructions.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Winifred Ashgrove-Nkemdi, aged 86, package of care for discharge home
body: I am writing to request an urgent assessment for a package of care for Mrs Ashgrove-Nkemdi, so that her discharge home is not delayed further. She has been medically fit since 15 January.
Admitted on 3 January 2025 with a fractured left wrist and a chest infection, she was previously fully independent. She is left-handed, and her wrist is in a cast until 14 February.

She can wash her face and upper body seated, but not her back, left arm or hair, and cannot fasten buttons, a bra or shoes. She walks 40 metres with a gutter frame, approved by orthopaedics, and transfers from a 46 cm chair with arms. She cannot carry a full kettle, open packets or cut food, and slightly burned her right hand during assessment; this was treated and incident-reported.

She needs one carer three times daily: approximately 45 minutes each morning for personal care and breakfast, and 30 minutes at lunchtime and evening for meals and bedtime, until at least 14 February, then reassessment.
She has been referred to the fracture liaison service. She has capacity, wants to go home and accepts short-term help. Her daughter would like a call about the start date.

The equipment list and home layout are left out, since the assessor needs the care need rather than the inventory.

letters.re: Re: Mr Ignatius Farrell-Oduya, aged 62, level access shower recommendation
body: I am writing to request approval and a survey for a level access shower for Mr Farrell-Oduya, who has secondary progressive multiple sclerosis. I wish to attend, as seat and rail positions depend on his transfers.

Neurology confirms progression (letter enclosed). He walks about 4 metres indoors with a frame on good days and otherwise uses a wheelchair. He cannot lift his legs over the bath and has not bathed since December, and his wife, with a shoulder problem, can no longer help.

I recommend removing the bath, a level access shower with a linear drain, a drop-down seat with arms at 480 mm, grab rails, a thermostatic lever mixer at 1000 mm, a slip-resistant floor, and widening the door to 800 mm. Please also reinforce the wall for a hoist, allow space for a shower-commode chair, relocate the radiator, remove the threshold and raise the toilet.
A bath lift or cloakroom conversion would fail, and rehousing costs more. He will probably need assisted transfers within two to three years, so this layout avoids a second scheme.
He has agreed to the works. I have requested a carer's assessment for his exhausted wife, and would appreciate prompt approval.

commentary.selection: Progression, the failed bathing arrangement, the carer's strain, the specification including space for a shower-commode chair, and why alternatives fail are kept because they justify the adaptation. Most room measurements are left out because the surveyor will measure on site.
commentary.organisation: Request, then need, then specification, then alternatives and future-proofing, then consent and urgency.
commentary.tone: Formal and well-reasoned, written to support a funding decision.

letters.re: Re: Master Barnaby Okoye-Whitfield, aged 9 years 3 months, Year 4, motor coordination difficulties
body: I am writing to share my assessment of Barnaby, seen on 5 and 19 May 2025, and to ask the school to adopt these recommendations now.

Barnaby has motor coordination difficulty affecting handwriting, self-care and play, although his reading is above average. He writes 8 words per minute, against an expected 14 to 16, and his hand tires within four minutes. This is not laziness or a behaviour problem.

Please provide printed sheets instead of board copying, allow verbal answers, a scribe or a laptop, give extra time, and mark content rather than presentation. He should use the enclosed sloped surface and pencil grip, take movement breaks every twenty minutes, and have a lower chair. In PE, use a larger, softer ball and avoid public team picking.
I have shown his teacher a daily ten-minute fine motor programme. Please stop keeping him in at break, as he needs that activity and social time.

He has called himself "the stupid one", so pastoral support would help. I have suggested his GP refers him to community paediatrics, and his parents will book an eye test. I will review him on 22 September. His parents consented to sharing this letter.

commentary.opening: The SENCO needs to know at once what is being asked: that the school acts on the recommendations now, not after the summer.
commentary.selection: The key measurements, the reframing as a motor difficulty rather than reluctance, the classroom changes, the instruction to stop break-time detention, pastoral support and the onward paediatric and eye referrals are kept. Detailed scores for each motor test and the home dressing routine are left out because the school does not need them to act.
commentary.organisation: Purpose, then findings and what they mean, then classroom adjustments, then the programme and what to stop, then his wellbeing, review and consent.
commentary.tone: Professional and firm, especially in correcting the 'reluctant' label, while staying collaborative with the school.

letters.re: Re: Mr Rafael Ndukwe-Sandringham, aged 34, urgent wheelchair reassessment
body: I am writing to request an urgent assessment and reprovision of Mr Ndukwe-Sandringham's wheelchair. He has a complete T6 spinal cord injury, and his chair no longer fits, causing pressure damage and worsening posture.

He has gained 9 kg since 2020. His seated hip width is 470 mm against a 430 mm seat, and the original cushion has bottomed out. He has category 1 pressure damage over the right ischial tuberosity, unbroken but non-blanching, despite consistent pressure relief; this has been incident-reported.
The backrest hammocks by 60 mm, leaving him in a posterior pelvic tilt with a thoracic kyphosis. Both are still correctable, hence the urgency.

Please consider a chair matched to his measurements, a high-risk cushion with pressure mapping if available, and a tension-adjustable or solid back. It must be no heavier than now, so he can still load it into his car, and fit under a 720 mm desk.

I issued a temporary cushion on 6 June and advised off-loading and pressure relief every 15 minutes. Tissue viability review is on 4 July, sooner if no better. He knows the signs of autonomic dysreflexia and carries an emergency card. He can attend any weekday after two o'clock.

commentary.opening: The request and its urgency come first, with a one-line reason, so the clinical lead can prioritise the referral immediately.
commentary.selection: The mismatch in measurements, the failed cushion, the skin damage and its reporting, the correctable posture, autonomic dysreflexia awareness and the weight limit for car loading are kept because they shape the prescription and his safety. His full job details, home doorways and his emotional question are left out as less relevant to the seating assessment.
commentary.organisation: Request, then fit and skin, then posture and why it is urgent, then what the new chair must achieve, then interim measures and appointment availability.
commentary.tone: Clinical and precise between colleagues, using correct seating terminology.

letters.re: Re: Mr Ambrose Lindqvist-Nwokolo, aged 77, self-neglect and safeguarding concern
body: I am writing to request a safeguarding enquiry under the self-neglect pathway, with a multi-agency approach, for Mr Lindqvist-Nwokolo, who lives alone. I visited him on 14 and 28 August 2025 for a bathing assessment after his knee replacement.

Two heaters, one with a damaged cable, stood against stacked paper, and there were no working smoke alarms. Walking routes were about 400 mm wide, and he sleeps in an armchair. His knee wound dressing, due on 8 August, was soiled. There was evidence of incontinence, weight loss and no food preparation. He has missed two post-operative appointments, and some medication was out of date. I informed his GP about these.

He declined a care package, district nursing, cleaning and a fire service visit, but later accepted the fire service referral, which I have made. With his agreement, I took the damaged heater out of use. He appears to have capacity, as he repeats back the risks, but he did not move the heaters as he said he would, so a formal, decision-specific capacity assessment is needed.
He has no family contact. He accepts my visits, and I will continue them and attend any meeting.

commentary.selection: Observed risks are grouped (fire, falls, wound, nutrition, medication), the GP notification and the heater made safe are stated, and the capacity view is kept with the reason a formal assessment is needed. His quotations and the medication names are left out as the team can obtain them.

commentary.tone: Objective and factual, reporting observations rather than judgements, and respectful of his right to decide.

letters.re: Re: Mr Casimir Oyelaran-Braithwaite, aged 41, phased return to work after a right hand injury
body: With Mr Oyelaran-Braithwaite's written consent, I recommend a phased return to work from 4 September, with the adjustments below.

He sustained a crush injury to his dominant right hand at work on 4 March 2025, with metacarpal fractures and index tendon and nerve injuries. His grip is 50% of the left, and his index finger has reduced flexion and sensation, with marked cold intolerance. He cannot yet handle parts under 10 mm or sustain grip beyond about fifteen minutes.

I recommend 4 hours a day, 4 days a week in weeks 1 and 2, limited to inspection, documentation and quality checks, with no fine assembly, vibrating tools or cold store. Weeks 3 and 4: 6 hours daily, assembling larger components one hour at a time. Full hours follow in weeks 5 to 8, vibrating tools last, after review.

Please provide a supported forearm bench, warmth or gloves, and an unrecorded five-minute break hourly. As he may not feel burns or cuts, he needs gloves for hot or sharp parts. Reviews are booked for 2 and 30 October.
His fine assembly role may need permanent change, best discussed early. Please confirm the injury was reported under RIDDOR.

commentary.opening: Consent and the purpose — a phased return from a specific date — are stated first, because the adviser can share only what he has agreed to.
commentary.selection: Function is translated into what matters at work: grip, small parts, sustained grip, cold and protective sensation. Raw measurements such as pinch strengths, peg test times and two-point discrimination are left out because the adviser needs work implications, not test scores. The RIDDOR point is kept as the employer's duty.
commentary.organisation: Purpose, injury and current function, the week-by-week plan, adjustments and reviews, then prognosis.
commentary.tone: Clear and practical for a non-specialist health colleague, honest about prognosis without speculating on his employment.

header: Wife and main carer of Mr Reginald Pemberton
letters.re: Re: Mr Reginald Pemberton, aged 79, the morning routine we agreed
body: Thank you for welcoming me. I am writing to ask you to keep using the morning routine we tried together on 26 September, as it made mornings much calmer for you both.

Please wake Reginald later, around eight, and give him a cup of tea before the bathroom. Make sure the bathroom is warm and lit. Give one instruction at a time, then wait, counting to ten, before repeating it. Always tell him what you are about to do before touching him, and let him do what he still can, such as washing his face and arms. Lay his clothes out in order. If he resists, stop and try again ten minutes later.
Please remove the dark mat at the bathroom door, and keep the furniture where it is. He should use the bath board only with you supervising. The community alarm pendant is for you to wear.

Please also look after yourself. Your carer's assessment should include your own lifting and falls risk. The support group meets on the first Tuesday at the library, and day care is offered weekly from October. I would like you to have time out alone. I will visit again on 24 October.

commentary.opening: The letter opens warmly and states its purpose: to record the agreed routine and ask her to keep using it.
commentary.selection: The practical steps that worked on 26 September, the key home safety points, the alarm pendant and support for her, including her own lifting and falls risk, are kept. header: Team Manager, Community Mental Health Team
letters.re: Re: Ms Rosanna Ibeh-Winterbourne, aged 29, low mood and functional decline
body: I am writing to request an assessment by your team for Ms Ibeh-Winterbourne, who has had a marked functional decline over four months which appears to have a mental health rather than physical cause. She has agreed to this referral.

Her GP referred her for fatigue after normal investigations. She resigned in May, has not left her flat since 14 August, sleeps until the afternoon, rarely showers and eats one meal a day. She has no interest or enjoyment in anything and feels worse in the mornings.

On 22 September and 6 October, she described thoughts that she "would not mind not waking up", with no plan or self-harm. She named her mother as protective, but has not answered her calls for three weeks. She lives alone and has no stockpiled medication. Her GP started an antidepressant on 29 September and reviews her on 6 October, within one week. Her written crisis plan covers her GP and me in hours, the crisis line out of hours, and 999 or A&E.
I will continue weekly visits and help her claim benefits, as savings are running out. She does not answer the telephone, so please write or visit any afternoon.

commentary.selection: Functional decline, depressive symptoms, a full risk summary including the doubtful protective factor, the one-week GP review and the crisis plan are kept, as the team needs them to triage. Her blood results, the relationship ending and the university episode are left out or summarised as the team can explore them at assessment.
commentary.organisation: Request, then function and symptoms, then risk and current management, then relevant background, then ongoing support and how to contact her.
commentary.tone: Professional and measured, giving risk information clearly and quoting her words where they matter.

letters.re: Re: Mr Osgood Fairweather-Nkemdi, aged 72, discharge home after a stroke
body: I am writing to request early community rehabilitation for Mr Fairweather-Nkemdi, who will be discharged on 8 November 2025 after a left middle cerebral artery infarct, with right hemiparesis, expressive dysphasia and right visual field loss.

Please visit early because of his right homonymous field loss: he does not scan into it, walked into a door frame twice and leaves food on the right of his plate. He must not drive and has informed the licensing authority.

He walks 25 metres with a stick and supervision only, needs supervision for toilet transfers, and needs help with washing, socks and shoes. A downstairs bed, a 46 cm commode with arms and a call bell for his wife at night are in place. Carers visit twice daily from 9 November. He has a normal diet and fluids.

Please continue right upper limb work, visual scanning, simple meal preparation, stair practice and fatigue management. His goals are to reach his own bed, make his wife tea and walk to the postbox. Allow him time to speak. His low mood needs formal screening for post-stroke depression. His wife, who has arthritis, is awaiting a carer's assessment.

header: Daughter and main carer of Mr Walter Holloway
letters.re: Re: Mr Walter Holloway, aged 79, home safety and daily routine
body: Thank you for meeting me on 27 August 2026. As you asked, here is practical advice on your father's safety, routine and equipment.

The kitchen is the most urgent concern, as the gas ring has been left lit three times in a month. I have referred him today for a cooker isolation device or monitored cooker. Please also keep worktops clear, and remove clutter from the hallway and landing.

At night, a door sensor linked to your bedroom, rather than a call centre, will alert you if he goes to the front door. Night lights to the toilet, contrasting signs and a coloured toilet seat will help him find it. His GP will review his frequent night-time urination, which adds to his wandering.

A routine with activities in the same order each day helps most. Keep laying out his clothes in order, and give one calm, simple instruction at a time without rushing him. Music and gardening, which he still enjoys, are worth including daily.
Please look after yourself too. You are entitled to a carer's assessment in your own right, and I encourage you to request one. I will review your father in eight weeks.

commentary.opening: The letter thanks Mrs Holloway for the visit and states at once what she asked for and will receive: practical advice on safety, routine and equipment.
commentary.selection: Only what she must act on or understand is kept: the cooker risk and referral, night wandering and the door sensor, toilet aids, the nocturia review, routine and communication tips, meaningful activity and her own carer's assessment. History, medication, mobility and the blue badge and remote control queries are left out because they need no action from her or were already dealt with.
commentary.organisation: Purpose, then the most urgent risk (the cooker), then night safety, then daily routine and activity, and finally support for the carer and the review date.
commentary.tone: Warm, plain English for a family carer, with no jargon; practical rather than sympathetic, as she asked.

letters.re: Re: Mr Reginald Oduya, aged 70, discharge from occupational therapy after stroke
body: I am writing to inform you that Mr Oduya's occupational therapy ended on 31 August 2026, his goals having been met, and to ask you to monitor his mood and support his home programme.

Following his right middle cerebral artery ischaemic stroke on 27 June 2026, which weakened his non-dominant left side, he is now independent in washing, dressing, toileting and simple meals using one-handed techniques and aids.

His left arm is improving, with shoulder flexion to 90 degrees, but grip is 6 kg compared with 32 kg on the right, and release is slow. He has no shoulder pain or subluxation; the arm should stay supported when seated. He continues four armchair exercises and task-specific practice for twenty minutes twice daily, plus mirror therapy.
His perching stool, grab rail, bath board and kitchen aids are secure, and he knows how to arrange repairs. No further equipment is needed.

His mild low mood relates to losing his driving licence and allotment. As this is common after stroke and treatable, please monitor it. Please refer him back if function plateaus or declines, or if his hand improves enough for task retraining, as gains are possible for up to a year.

commentary.selection: The stroke, current independence, the left arm findings, the exercise programme, the equipment and the mood concern are kept, with the re-referral triggers. His medication, comorbidities, physiotherapy, hobbies and family details are left out, as the GP already holds them or they need no action.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Margaret Lindqvist, aged 71, discharge home after stroke
body: I am writing to hand over Mrs Lindqvist, discharged home today, 26 June 2026, for continued home-based rehabilitation, equipment follow-up and review once her ordered adaptations are installed.

Her left middle cerebral artery ischaemic stroke on 2 June 2026 caused weakness of her dominant right side and mild expressive dysphasia, which is improving. She has some difficulty sequencing multi-step tasks, but no neglect.

She feeds herself with built-up cutlery, dresses her upper body and transfers independently. She needs supervision for lower-body dressing and bathing, and walks indoors with a four-wheeled walker. She lives alone and cannot manage the stairs to the only bathroom, so a temporary bed and commode are downstairs. A twice-daily care package started this morning, with a key safe.
A perching stool, long-handled sponge, raised toilet seat, bed lever and raisers are in place. A stairlift and grab rails are expected within four weeks.

Please continue daily living and upper-limb retraining and carer education with her daughter, and review her after installation with a view to reducing care. Please act sooner if she falls, if installation is delayed beyond four weeks, or if her function declines. She must not drive for at least one month.

letters.re: Re: Mr Hassan Qureshi, aged 29, discharge after first episode of psychosis
body: I am writing to hand over Mr Qureshi, whose discharge from Willow Ward is planned for 2 September 2026, and to ask you to support his daily routine, graded return to study and social confidence.

Admitted informally on 12 July 2026 with a first episode of psychosis, he has settled on olanzapine 10 mg at night, though he has gained 4 kg; the physical health clinic will continue his monitoring. His insight is improving, and he can name early warning signs, including poor sleep and staying in his room. His relapse plan is shared with his family, and there is no current risk.

He is independent in self-care and laundry, cooks four simple meals, shops and travels into town alone. He budgets with prompts but needs support with longer-term planning. He sleeps seven hours, and has stopped cannabis, though two friendships make abstinence harder.

His agreed timetable for the first month includes the walking group and cooking two meals weekly. He hopes to resume his IT course in January, but has not told the university and is anxious about seminars. He would like you to accompany him to a support-services meeting before term. His care coordinator is Mr David Osei.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Eileen Forsythe, aged 68, discharge from occupational therapy after right total hip replacement
body: I am writing to inform you that Mrs Forsythe was discharged from occupational therapy on 28 August 2026 following her right total hip replacement, and to ask you to monitor her analgesia and wound.

Her elective posterior-approach replacement on 16 August 2026 was uncomplicated. She must maintain hip precautions until 27 September 2026: no bending past 90 degrees, no crossing her legs, no twisting on the operated leg and no lying on the operated side. She and her husband understand these, and she transfers correctly.

She washes and dresses independently with long-handled aids, walks with one crutch indoors and two outdoors, and manages the stairs with the second rail. Her raised toilet seat, perching stool, and chair and bed raisers should remain until the precautions lift.

She takes apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, due to stop on 20 September, paracetamol 1 g four times daily, and codeine 30 mg at night only, which she is keen to stop. Please note that she is allergic to aspirin, which causes wheeze. Her wound was clean and dry today.
Her orthopaedic review is at six weeks. Please refer her back if she has difficulty resuming any activity after the precautions lift.

letters.re: Re: Mr Stanley Pickering, aged 81, recurrent falls at home
body: I am writing to refer Mr Pickering, whom I assessed at home on 29 August 2026, for a falls-prevention assessment, a strength-and-balance programme and a home hazard review.

He has fallen four times indoors in three months: twice rising from his armchair and twice at night going to the toilet. The latest fall, on 21 August, caused a forehead laceration needing three sutures, and a neighbour had to help him up. He lives alone without a personal alarm, so I have referred him for one.

He walks with a stick and is unsteady on standing. Contributing factors include nocturia three times nightly, cataracts awaiting surgery, worn backless slippers, loose rugs, a trailing lead, a dim hallway and a low sofa. As he takes amlodipine, ramipril and tamsulosin, a medication review, lying and standing blood pressure, and expedited cataract surgery have been requested.
I have started removing the rugs and lead, and requested chair raisers, back-step grab rails, a toilet frame and a bedside lamp.
His cognition is intact, and he is motivated to regain his confidence and return to his club. He is happy for you to contact him directly, and his daughter would like to be kept informed.

body: I am writing to refer Mr Okafor, a right-hand-dominant carpenter, for specialist orthosis adjustment and graded active mobilisation after flexor tendon repair.

On 18 June 2026 he cut the volar aspect of his right index finger on a circular saw. Flexor digitorum profundus was repaired in Zone 2 on 19 June 2026 with a four-strand core and epitendinous suture; the digital nerve was intact. He is allergic to penicillin.

His dorsal blocking orthosis holds the wrist in neutral and the metacarpophalangeal joints at 60 degrees of flexion, with the interphalangeal joints extended. The wound is clean, the finger well perfused, with mild oedema. He understands the precautions: no active resisted flexion, no gripping and no orthosis removal. He performs passive flexion exercises but, fearing re-rupture, does fewer than prescribed, risking adhesion.

Please adjust the orthosis as oedema settles, progress mobilisation to a recognised protocol, and begin scar management after suture removal, expected around 2 July 2026. Please see him urgently if he suddenly loses active flexion, which may indicate rupture.
He is self-employed without sick pay, so needs telling clearly and early that full carpentry duties are unlikely before around twelve weeks. He prefers appointments after 10 am.

letters.re: Re: Mr Trevor Aldington, aged 63, right Dupuytren's fasciectomy
body: I am writing to ask you to remove Mr Aldington's sutures on 2 September 2026, monitor his wound and reinforce his night splint and exercises, as compliance in the first eight weeks determines the result.

His limited fasciectomy of the right ring and little fingers on 19 August 2026 achieved full passive extension. The wound is healing well, with mild swelling and no infection; a light non-adherent dressing was applied today. His type 2 diabetes, HbA1c 58 mmol/mol, may slow healing, so please watch for erythema, discharge or increasing pain.

His thermoplastic splint, holding the fingers in full extension, should be worn nightly for eight weeks, by day only if an extension lag develops. It fits well, and he can check for pressure marks. He does active flexion, extension and tendon-gliding exercises, ten repetitions hourly when awake, with elevation.
Once the wound has healed, please begin scar massage and silicone, as in the written instructions.

Please refer him back if extension worsens, a contracture recurs, or he develops disproportionate pain, swelling and skin change, which may indicate complex regional pain syndrome. His hand therapy review is in two weeks, and he prefers a morning appointment for suture removal.

commentary.opening: The opening gives the nurse her three tasks, with the suture removal date, and explains why her reinforcement matters.
commentary.selection: The operation, the wound state, diabetes as a healing risk, the splint regimen, the exercises, scar care and the referral triggers including CRPS are kept. His career, hobbies, family, parking and pre-operative history are left out as not needed for wound and splint care.
commentary.organisation: Request, then surgery and wound care, then splint and exercises, then scar management, and finally red flags and appointments.
commentary.tone: Practical and collegial for a practice nurse, with clear instructions she can follow at the appointment.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Rosa Calderon, aged 52, home adaptations for progressive multiple sclerosis
body: I am requesting a priority major home-adaptations assessment for Mrs Calderon, whom I assessed at home on 30 August 2026. She has secondary progressive multiple sclerosis and has fallen twice on the stairs in six weeks; the next fall is likely to cause injury.

She walks approximately 8 metres indoors with two sticks and uses a wheelchair outdoors. Lower-limb strength is 3+ out of 5 bilaterally, with right-leg spasticity, reduced sensation in both feet and fair standing balance. Fatigue worsens in the afternoons. She goes upstairs on her bottom and has strip-washed for four months because she cannot step into the bath.

Her bedroom and only bathroom are upstairs in an owner-occupied terraced house with a narrow staircase. The rear dining room could take a single bed. Her husband works full time and is out from 7 am to 6 pm.

Please assess her for a stairlift or, if the staircase is unsuitable, for downstairs living with a through-floor lift or a downstairs bedroom and wet room, plus a level-access shower and grab rails. Meanwhile, I have offered a temporary downstairs bed, a commode and a falls pendant. She prefers telephone contact in the mornings.

commentary.opening: The request and its urgency come first: two stair falls in six weeks justify asking for priority, so the reader learns at once why this case should move up the list.
commentary.selection: Mobility, strength, balance, fatigue, the falls, bathing and the layout of the house are kept because they decide which adaptation is possible. Hobbies, children, past ankle sprain, screening, the cat and the blue badge question are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request and risk, then function, then the house and who is at home, then the specific options to assess with interim measures.
commentary.tone: Professional and direct between occupational therapists, firm about priority without exaggeration.

letters.re: Re: Mason Albright, 7 years 5 months, query developmental coordination disorder
body: I am referring Mason, seen with his parents on 26 August 2026, for an occupational therapy assessment of fine and gross motor coordination using a standardised measure, as developmental coordination disorder is suspected.

His handwriting is slow and illegible, with an immature four-finger grasp and inconsistent letter formation with reversals. Hand pain develops after five minutes and settles on stopping. He cannot copy a diamond, cannot use a knife and fork together, and needs help with buttons and laces.
He bumps into furniture, takes stairs one at a time, catches and throws poorly and falls more often than peers. Hearing and vision were normal in March 2026, with no regression of any skill.

He is verbally bright and reads at the expected level or above, but written work is far behind. Extra time and a pencil grip have had limited effect; school would trial a laptop if recommended. Nightly practice at home is causing tension, and he now says he is bad at writing.

I would be grateful for advice for school and home and a handwriting and dressing programme that reduces pressure at home. His parents consent to information-sharing with school and prefer after-school appointments.

commentary.organisation: Request, fine motor and self-care, gross motor and screening, school and emotional impact, then the specific help wanted and consent.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Yolanda Estrada, aged 55, hand flare of rheumatoid arthritis
body: I am writing to refer Mrs Estrada, a right-handed school administrator with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, for hand and upper-limb assessment, joint-protection education and splinting after a six-week hand flare.

She has bilateral wrist and metacarpophalangeal swelling and tenderness, with early ulnar drift that is passively correctable; her thumbs are stable. Morning stiffness lasts approximately 90 minutes, and grip strength has fallen to 8 kg right and 7 kg left, from 14 kg in January. Fatigue is her most limiting symptom. She drops objects and struggles with buttons, jars, kettles, writing and keys.
She types for four hours a day and is worried about keeping her job, with a sickness meeting pending and no occupational health involvement.

She takes methotrexate 20 mg weekly, hydroxychloroquine, and prednisolone 7.5 mg daily, recently increased. She is allergic to sulfasalazine, which caused a rash. Rheumatology has been copied in to review the flare.

I would be grateful if you could provide joint-protection education, resting splints for night and working splints for typing, adaptive equipment, a hand exercise programme within the limits of the flare and fatigue management. With her consent, workplace advice and employer liaison would also help. She would prefer Friday appointments.

commentary.opening: The opening states the three things wanted — assessment, joint protection and splinting — and the trigger, a six-week flare.
commentary.selection: Joint findings, grip loss, fatigue, work demands and the relevant medicines and allergy are kept. Thyroid history, appendicectomy, screening, family events, hobbies and the car park question are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request, clinical findings and function, work concerns, medication and allergy, then the detailed plan.
commentary.tone: Precise and collegial for a specialist hand therapist, using correct anatomical terms.

letters.re: Re: Mr Callum Whitfield, aged 34, traumatic brain injury
body: I am writing to hand over Mr Whitfield, who transfers from inpatient neuro-rehabilitation today, so your team can continue his cognitive and functional rehabilitation at home. He sustained frontal and right temporal contusions in a cycling collision on 22 June 2026.

He is independent in self-care and mobility. However, attention and working memory are impaired, insight is reduced, and he is impulsive, having twice left the ward unannounced. He left the hob on twice during kitchen assessment, so it should stay isolated at home until supervised retraining shows it is safe. He cannot yet be left alone for extended periods.
He is frustrated, with brief evening verbal outbursts towards his partner but no physical aggression. He is not driving; the licensing authority has been notified.
He takes levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily, which needs medical review as it may contribute to irritability, and sertraline 50 mg daily. He is allergic to latex.

Please continue his phone reminders and structured routine, fatigue management with an afternoon rest, and education for his partner, particularly about reduced insight; she needs support herself. Vocational referral should wait until he is ready. His partner asks for visits on her days at home.

commentary.organisation: Purpose and injury, cognition and safety, mood and driving, medication and allergy, then what the team should continue.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Constance Mbeki, aged 64, metastatic ovarian cancer
body: I am writing to hand over Mrs Mbeki, who has metastatic ovarian cancer with spinal, pelvic and lung metastases, so you can support her comfort, fatigue management and meaningful activity at the day hospice. Treatment is now for symptom control.

She has severe fatigue, is best between 10 am and midday, and rests most afternoons. She is breathless on exertion and manages stairs slowly with one rest. Neuropathy has reduced her grip, so she drops things and struggles with a fine brush. She has a shower chair, perching stool, raised toilet seat and bed lever.
Her goals are to stay at home, to attend her granddaughter's wedding on 10 October and stand for the photographs, and to keep painting. She values doing things herself.

She and her husband know to contact acute oncology immediately if new back pain, leg weakness or numbness, or bladder or bowel change develops, as these may indicate spinal cord compression. She is intolerant of metoclopramide, which caused a dystonic reaction.

Please continue pacing built around these priorities, breathlessness strategies, adapted painting grips, equipment review, and planning for the wedding, including a wheelchair and a rest space. Her daughter may attend sessions.

commentary.opening: The first paragraph gives the diagnosis, the palliative intent and what the hospice OT is asked to do, so the reader can plan the first session.
commentary.selection: Fatigue pattern, breathlessness, grip, equipment, her goals, the spinal cord compression red flags and the metoclopramide intolerance are kept. Career history, exhibitions, the dog, the son in Canada and the garden question are left out.
commentary.organisation: Purpose, current function, the patient's goals, safety information, then the specific plan.
commentary.tone: Warm but professional, keeping the patient's own priorities and dignity at the centre.

letters.re: Re: Mr Liam Donoghue, aged 41, return to work after lumbar disc prolapse
body: I am writing to refer Mr Donoghue, a scaffolder, for a work-capacity assessment against his actual job demands and a phased graded return-to-work plan. He has been off work for four months after an L5/S1 disc prolapse, sustained lifting at work on 24 April 2026. His statutory sick pay ends in early November, so this is time-sensitive.

His sciatic symptoms resolved in July, and he has no red-flag symptoms. He completed a twelve-session graded-activity programme and now walks for 30 minutes. However, standing beyond about twenty minutes, bending and lifting over approximately 5 kg remain limited by pain.

His job involves climbing, working at height and routinely carrying loads of up to 25 kg on ten-hour shifts, well beyond his current capacity. He has no other trade but holds a scaffolding supervisor card.
He has low mood related to inactivity, without suicidal ideation, and his fear-avoidance beliefs are reducing. He takes naproxen and paracetamol as required and is intolerant of codeine.

I would be grateful for ergonomic and manual-handling advice and liaison with his supportive employer about modified duties; a supervisory or yard role may be a realistic bridge. He consents to employer contact and would prefer early shifts.

commentary.opening: The opening states the assessment wanted, the injury and why it is time-sensitive, so the reader understands both the task and the deadline.
commentary.selection: Current tolerances, absence of red flags, job demands, mood, medicines and the codeine intolerance are kept, because the gap between capacity and demands is the crux. Old injuries, hobbies, darts, fishing and the evening appointment question are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request and urgency, clinical progress and capacity, job demands, mood and medication, then the specific plan.
commentary.tone: Professional and practical for a vocational colleague, balanced between his limits and his motivation.

letters.re: Re: Ms Dawn Eccleston, aged 47, urgent seating and cushion reassessment
body: I am writing to request an urgent reassessment of Ms Eccleston's wheelchair and pressure-relieving cushion, as she has a Category 2 pressure ulcer and a deteriorating sitting posture. She has an incomplete C6 spinal cord injury, ASIA scale C, and is a full-time manual wheelchair user.

The ulcer, over the left ischial tuberosity, has been present for three weeks and measures 2 cm by 1.5 cm, with no infection. Sensation there is markedly reduced, so she cannot reliably feel deterioration; until it heals, she should minimise sitting on it. She has a history of autonomic dysreflexia, which the ulcer could trigger, and carries an emergency card.

She has a new, partly correctable pelvic obliquity, left side lower, and a developing left-leaning trunk. Her four-year-old cushion is visibly compressed, and the chair lacks lateral supports; these almost certainly caused the ulcer.
Right shoulder pain for six months is limiting propulsion and needs review. She is allergic to adhesive dressings such as Elastoplast; please use silicone-based products.

I would be grateful for postural support before the trunk lean becomes fixed, and a repositioning review with tissue viability. Any new chair should fit under her desk. She prefers morning appointments.

commentary.selection: The injury level, ulcer details, sensation, the advice to minimise sitting on the ulcer, the autonomic dysreflexia history with her emergency card, posture, the old cushion, shoulder pain and the adhesive allergy are kept. Continence routines, hobbies, pets, visitors, screening and the chair colour request are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request and diagnosis, the ulcer, the posture and its cause, shoulder and allergy, then the specific requests and practical details.
commentary.tone: Professional and urgent for a seating specialist, with clear causal reasoning.

letters.re: Re: Mr Casimir Odugbemi-Fairweather, aged 45, persistent left plantar heel pain
body: I am writing to refer Mr Odugbemi-Fairweather for a progressive, supervised plantar fascia and calf loading programme. His left plantar heel pain has improved only partially with podiatric treatment and has plateaued.

His pain began eleven months ago, when he changed to a warehouse job standing for eight to nine hours on concrete. It is sharpest on his first steps in the morning and returns as an ache by mid-afternoon. He is tender at the medial calcaneal tubercle, with a positive windlass test and tight gastrocnemius. Ultrasound on 3 February 2025 showed fascial thickening of 6.8 mm with no tear. Squeeze and Tinel's tests were negative.

Over seven months he has had custom orthoses, footwear advice, taping, stretching and an anti-fatigue mat at work. His first-step pain has fallen from 8 to 5 out of 10, but the afternoon ache is unchanged since January.

Importantly, he manages only 8 single-leg heel raises on the left, compared with 21 on the right; this strength deficit now limits his recovery. Please also assess his proximal strength and single-leg control, and advise on managing load in a job he cannot change. He hopes to run again.

commentary.opening: The request comes first and is named precisely (a supervised plantar fascia and calf loading programme), with the reason in the same paragraph: podiatric treatment has plateaued.
commentary.selection: The physiotherapist needs the diagnosis, what has already been tried, the outcome scores and above all the heel raise asymmetry, which is the reason for referral. Negative tests that exclude a stress fracture or nerve entrapment are summarised in one sentence; detailed angles, girth and navicular drop are left for the physiotherapist's own assessment.
commentary.organisation: Request, then history and findings, then treatment and outcome, then the key finding with the specific requests, ending with the patient's goal of running.
commentary.tone: Collegial and concise between allied health professionals, using clinical terms the physiotherapist shares.

letters.re: Re: Mr Anselm Kirkbride-Achebe, aged 63, peripheral neuropathy of unknown cause
body: I am writing to ask you to investigate a significant symmetrical peripheral neuropathy which I found in Mr Kirkbride-Achebe at a private callus appointment today. He is not known to be diabetic and has never been investigated.

Over three years, numbness has spread from his toes to his ankles, with night burning for eighteen months. He cannot feel bath water temperature and has twice walked on objects unnoticed. The monofilament was not felt at 7 of 10 sites on the right and 6 of 10 on the left. Vibration sense and ankle reflexes were absent, with impaired proprioception, a positive Romberg's test and mild toe extension weakness. Circulation is normal.

Relevant factors include a partial gastrectomy in 1999, omeprazole for fifteen years, a restricted diet, approximately 25 alcohol units weekly and past solvent exposure. As subacute combined degeneration is possible, please check vitamin B12 promptly and, if it is low, treat urgently before any folate. Please also consider folate, HbA1c, thyroid, renal and liver function, full blood count, protein electrophoresis and copper, neurological referral if no cause is found, and alcohol review.
I have debrided a pre-ulcerative callus and placed him on our high-risk pathway with eight-weekly review.

commentary.opening: The GP is told at once what is wanted (investigation of the cause) and why it matters: a significant neuropathy in a man who is not known to be diabetic and has never been investigated.
commentary.selection: The progression, the safety events and the key objective findings show severity, including the signs of large-fibre and possible dorsal column involvement. Because a positive Romberg's test after gastric surgery and long-term omeprazole may mean B12-related subacute combined degeneration, the request for a prompt B12 check, and urgent treatment before any folate, is given its own sentence. The other tests are grouped; vascular figures are reduced to one sentence saying the circulation is normal.
commentary.organisation: Request, then history and findings, then risk factors with the suggested investigations, then what the podiatrist has already done.
commentary.tone: Professional and respectful of the GP's role: tests are offered for consideration rather than instructed.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Philomena Achterberg-Dunwoody, aged 89, foot care plan
body: This foot care plan for Mrs Achterberg-Dunwoody is for all staff and replaces any previous instructions. She is at high risk of foot ulceration because of nerve damage and poor circulation, and her dementia means she cannot reliably report pain.
Her skin is intact today. I have asked her doctor to consider assessing her circulation, respecting her wishes and best interests.

Staff should inspect and record both feet, including heels and between the toes, morning and evening. Wash them daily in water tested with a thermometer or the carer's forearm, and dry thoroughly. Apply emollient once daily, never between the toes. Keep the right fourth toe space dry, using the gauze separator supplied, changed twice daily. She must wear the supplied socks and slippers out of bed, and heel devices in bed or reclining.
Staff must not cut her nails, use corn plasters or foot products, place any heat source near her feet, or let her transfer barefoot.

Telephone the podiatry line the same day for any skin break, blister, persistent redness, swelling, discharge or colour change, or out-of-hours services. Also report non-fading heel redness under your pressure ulcer policy. My next visit is on 3 January 2025.

commentary.opening: The purpose is stated in the first sentence, together with the fact that this plan replaces earlier instructions, so the manager knows it overrides anything already in the file. The reason for high risk follows at once, in plain words.
commentary.selection: Care staff need actions, not measurements, so the monofilament, Doppler and toe pressure figures are left out and summarised as nerve damage and poor circulation. Every 'do' and 'do not' instruction and every escalation trigger is kept, including keeping the macerated toe space dry rather than applying cream, and reporting non-blanching heel redness under the home's pressure ulcer policy. The request to her GP about vascular assessment is mentioned so the home knows it has been made.
commentary.organisation: Purpose and risk, today's condition, what staff should do, what staff must not do, then escalation and the review date.
commentary.tone: Clear, direct and non-technical, suitable for a care home manager who will brief staff of varying clinical background.

letters.re: Re: Mr Barnabas Ngozi-Cholmondeley, aged 84, unstageable left heel pressure ulcer
body: I am writing to request a joint review within one week of Mr Ngozi-Cholmondeley, who has an unstageable pressure ulcer of the left heel, and agreement on whether to debride it, given his poor circulation.

He was discharged four days ago after hip hemiarthroplasty; the ulcer was not in his discharge documentation, so I have reported it as an incident and to safeguarding. It measures 46 mm by 39 mm, with 70 per cent black eschar, moderate exudate, rolled edges and non-blanching erythema. As the eschar is unstable and infection cannot be excluded, I have also telephoned the diabetic foot service, who will see him within one working day. His right heel has category 1 damage.
He has type 2 diabetes, dense neuropathy and peripheral arterial disease, with a left toe pressure of 38 mmHg. He has lost 6 kg, his albumin is 28 g/L and he takes apixaban.

Today I applied an antimicrobial dressing without debridement, issued heel offloading boots and requested urgent mattress reassessment. I have referred him to the vascular service and requested dietetic input.
I would also welcome advice on dressings and maceration, and a full pressure risk assessment, as I have not examined his sacrum.

commentary.opening: The reader learns immediately what is asked (a joint review within one week) and the key clinical question (whether to debride an ischaemic heel).
commentary.selection: Wound measurements and characteristics, the at-risk right heel, the vascular and nutritional factors and the actions already taken are kept because they shape joint management. Because the eschar is not stable and infection or osteomyelitis cannot be excluded, the same-day telephone referral to the diabetic foot service is stated, and the incident and safeguarding report is mentioned because the ulcer was missing from the discharge documents. The admission history is reduced to one sentence.
commentary.organisation: Request, then background and wound description, then healing risk factors, then actions taken, closing with the further requests.
commentary.tone: Collaborative and precise between specialists, using wound-care terminology the tissue viability nurse expects.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Henrietta Balogun-Winterbourne, aged 71, warfarin and planned nail surgery
body: I am writing to request your written advice on Mrs Balogun-Winterbourne's warfarin before a planned bilateral partial nail avulsion with phenolisation of both hallux nails. I will not proceed without it.
She has recurrent ingrowing toenails, with six infections in fourteen months despite full conservative care. The right toe is currently inflamed, and she has worn sandals since November, a fall risk.

She takes warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve and has permanent atrial fibrillation. Her yellow book records a target range of 2.5 to 3.5, lower than usual for this valve, so please confirm her target. Recent results range from 2.4 to 4.2, with two of the last five above range. She reports no bleeding and takes no antiplatelet drug.
The procedure uses a ring block with plain lidocaine and phenol, normally with a digital tourniquet, and the nail beds then weep for two to four weeks.

Please advise whether I may proceed on her usual dose with an INR check within twenty-four hours beforehand and, if so, at what maximum INR; whether a tourniquet is acceptable; and whether hospital is preferable. I have told her not to stop warfarin unless your service advises it.

commentary.opening: The letter opens with the request for written advice and the planned procedure, and makes clear that surgery will not go ahead without it.
commentary.selection: The pharmacist needs the indication, target range, recent INR variability, bleeding history and the bleeding profile of the procedure. Because the recorded range looks low for a mechanical mitral valve with atrial fibrillation, the letter quotes it as written and asks the service to confirm the correct target. Podiatric detail such as nail curvature and vascular findings is left out because it does not affect anticoagulation advice.
commentary.organisation: Request, then why surgery is needed, then anticoagulation details, then procedure details, ending with the three specific questions.
commentary.tone: Courteous and precise, deferring to the specialist service on anticoagulation decisions.

letters.re: Re: Mr Radovan Ajayi-Postlethwaite, aged 58, footwear after left partial first ray amputation
body: I am writing to request urgent bespoke footwear and offloading for Mr Ajayi-Postlethwaite, who has a pre-ulcerative lesion beneath his left second metatarsal head fourteen weeks after a partial first ray amputation.

The amputation, on 2 June 2025 for osteomyelitis, healed on 19 August 2025. Since then, new callus has formed beneath the second and third metatarsal heads, with a haemorrhagic focus under the second, and his second toe has clawed and drifts medially. In-shoe peak pressure at that site is 412 kPa, against 198 kPa on the right.
He has diabetes, dense bilateral neuropathy and arterial disease, placing him at high risk; if the lesion breaks down, I will refer him to the foot service within one working day.

He needs a rigid rocker sole, a total contact insole offloading the second and third metatarsal heads with a medial column filler, and adequate depth for the clawed toe. His right foot, also neuropathic and now carrying more load, should be included, and two pairs are needed because he perspires heavily.
He refuses shoes that look like hospital footwear, so please discuss appearance openly at fitting. He remains on two-weekly podiatry review until the footwear is supplied.

commentary.opening: The request and its urgency are stated together, with the reason for urgency (a pre-ulcerative lesion) in the first sentence.
commentary.selection: The orthotist needs the surgical change, the new pressure areas, the pressure measurements, the risk category and the writer's footwear specification. Medication, retinopathy and kidney disease are left out as they do not alter the prescription; the patient's view on appearance is kept because it decides whether the footwear will be worn.
commentary.organisation: Request, then surgical history and current findings, then risk, then the footwear specification, ending with concordance and follow-up.
commentary.tone: Professional and specific, offering a clinical view while leaving the final design to the orthotist.

letters.re: Re: Mr Desmond Achterberg-Quaye, aged 61, infected right plantar ulcer, probe to bone
body: Further to my telephone discussion with your team at 09:55, I am sending Mr Achterberg-Quaye for same-day admission with an infected diabetic foot ulcer and suspected osteomyelitis, for bloods, blood cultures, imaging and intravenous antibiotics.

The ulcer, beneath his right first metatarsal head, measures 32 mm by 24 mm and 9 mm deep, and a probe reaches bone. There is heavy purulent exudate, forefoot swelling and erythema extending 6 cm, which I have marked. His temperature is 37.9 degrees, pulse 104 and capillary glucose 19.4 mmol/L. He has no protective sensation, hence no pain.
Circulation is also poor, with absent dorsalis pedis on Doppler and a toe pressure of 42 mmHg, needing vascular assessment.
He reports a childhood rash with penicillin, without swelling or breathing difficulty, which should be verified before antibiotics are given. He takes metformin, gliclazide and aspirin, and smokes.

I debrided the wound, sent a deep tissue sample for urgent culture and applied a non-adherent dressing. I deliberately did not apply a total contact cast. He has crutches, and was told not to weight-bear or drive, and to attend the emergency department if unwell. He asked about Saturday's holiday; I said this must await your assessment.

commentary.opening: Because the patient carries the letter today, the opening confirms the telephone agreement and the purpose (same-day admission) and names the expected management, so the receiving team can act without reading further.
commentary.selection: The probe-to-bone finding, signs of spreading infection, systemic observations, ischaemia and the penicillin allergy are all safety-critical and kept. Detailed neurological measurements and social history are reduced or left out, as the team will reassess.
commentary.organisation: Purpose, then the wound and systemic findings, then circulation, then allergy and medication, then treatment given and advice, ending with the patient's question about his holiday.
commentary.tone: Urgent, factual and economical, as expected in an emergency referral between clinicians.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Rosalind Mbeki-Trelawny, aged 74, right leg rest pain
body: Further to my telephone call today with your on-call registrar, who accepted her urgently, I am writing to confirm the referral of Mrs Mbeki-Trelawny for urgent assessment. She has developed rest pain in her right foot, suggesting critical ischaemia which I believe is unrecognised.

She has had right calf claudication for fourteen months, her walking distance falling from about 400 to 60 metres. For five weeks she has had burning forefoot pain at night, relieved by hanging the leg down, and she has slept in an armchair for nine nights.

Right foot pulses are absent apart from a faint monophasic posterior tibial signal. Her ankle brachial pressure index is 0.38 on the right and 0.71 on the left, and the right toe pressure is 26 mmHg. Buerger's test is positive. A new 4 mm dusky area has appeared on her right fourth toe within three weeks. Sensation is intact.
She has diabetes, hypertension and a previous myocardial infarction, and takes clopidogrel.

I have advised her not to elevate the leg, and to attend the emergency department the same day if the toe breaks down or the pain becomes constant. Her GP will review analgesia, as paracetamol has not helped.

commentary.opening: The letter opens by confirming the same-day telephone referral to the on-call vascular team, so the surgeon knows the case has already been accepted, then gives the new feature that makes it urgent (rest pain) and the concern that the disease has not been recognised.
commentary.selection: The vascular surgeon needs the progression of symptoms, the objective arterial measurements, the new toe discolouration, cardiovascular risk factors and antiplatelet therapy. Neurological figures are reduced to 'sensation is intact', which is enough to show the pain is ischaemic, and social detail is left out.
commentary.organisation: Request, then symptom history, then examination and measurements, then relevant history, ending with the safety-net advice given.
commentary.tone: Concise and clinical, conveying urgency through the findings rather than through emotional language.

letters.re: Re: Mr Kwabena Lindqvist-Osei, aged 49, suspected active Charcot neuroarthropathy
body: I am writing to request urgent assessment of Mr Lindqvist-Osei, a plasterer with type 1 diabetes, for suspected active Charcot neuroarthropathy of the right foot. Your specialist podiatrist accepted the referral by telephone today, with triage by the next working day.

At routine screening, his right foot was swollen, red and hot, measuring 34.8 degrees at the mid-foot against 30.1 degrees on the left. The medial arch has dropped, with a new plantar prominence. He denies pain, but twisted the foot approximately seven weeks ago. There is no wound or fever, and the erythema reduces on elevation.
He has dense bilateral neuropathy. Pulses are bounding and toe pressure is 96 mmHg. He has no known allergies.

Today I fitted a removable knee-high walker, issued crutches, advised non-weight-bearing and recorded baseline temperatures. I advised him not to drive while wearing the walker, and to contact us the same day if any skin break appears.

My main concern is concordance: he has two jobs booked and asked to wear the boot only in the evenings. I would be grateful if you could address this directly and consider a non-removable total contact cast, alongside urgent X-ray and further imaging.

commentary.opening: The letter names the suspected diagnosis and the urgency at once, and confirms the telephone acceptance, so the reader knows the triage clock is already running.
commentary.selection: The temperature difference, the change in foot shape, the absent pain, the neuropathy and the vascular status are kept because they make the diagnosis and rule out ischaemia. Because he wants to wear the removable walker only in the evenings, the request to consider a non-removable cast is stated, and the advice not to drive in the walker is included. Monofilament counts, ABPI, HbA1c, retinopathy and family detail are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request, then the key findings, then neurovascular status and background, then what was done today, and finally the concordance problem as the specific thing the clinic must address.
commentary.tone: Professional and direct between foot-care colleagues; urgency is shown through facts rather than emphatic language.

letters.re: Re: Miss Oluwaseun Hardcastle-Adeyemi, aged 38, changing pigmented band, right hallux nail
body: I am writing to request urgent assessment of Miss Hardcastle-Adeyemi, aged 38, for a changing pigmented band in the right hallux nail. She has an appointment within two weeks under the urgent pathway.

During routine nail care today I found a longitudinal brown-black band from the proximal nail fold to the free edge. It measures 7 mm proximally and 4 mm distally, compared with 3 mm proximally in a photograph from 21 August 2024. The colour is not uniform, the border is irregular, and brown pigment now extends approximately 3 mm onto the nail fold skin, which was absent in August. The nail plate is intact and painless.

She reports no injury and no other pigmented lesion on her feet, but I have not examined the rest of her skin and would ask that this be done. Her mother was treated for melanoma. She takes levothyroxine and a combined oral contraceptive, and has no known allergies.

I deliberately did not debride, file or sample the nail, and advised her not to varnish, cut or file it before she is seen. Both photographs are attached. She is anxious and asks that her appointment avoid a school inset day.

commentary.selection: The measured widening, the irregular colour and border, and the pigment on the nail fold are kept because these are the worrying features. Normal neurovascular findings, footwear and the varnish timeline are left out as they do not change the dermatological decision.
commentary.organisation: Request, then the lesion and its change over time, then relevant history and the request for a full skin check, and finally what was deliberately not done and the patient's concerns.
commentary.tone: Precise and objective for a specialist reader, with a brief, respectful note of the patient's anxiety.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Bettina Oyelaran-Whitcombe, aged 56, painful left hallux valgus
body: I am writing to request a surgical opinion for Mrs Oyelaran-Whitcombe, aged 56, a theatre nurse with painful left hallux valgus that has not responded to eighteen months of conservative management.

Her medial eminence pain scores 7 out of 10 by the end of a working day. Since September 2024 she has had more disabling pain beneath the second and third metatarsal heads, and since January, second interspace numbness with a positive Mulder's click, suggesting a neuroma.

The hallux valgus angle has increased from 34 to 41 degrees. The radiograph of 8 April 2025 shows an intermetatarsal angle of 17 degrees and first metatarsophalangeal joint degeneration, with dorsiflexion limited to 22 degrees. The second toe has a fixed hammer toe, and plantar callus reforms within four weeks of debridement. Neurovascular status is normal.

Orthoses with a metatarsal dome, appropriate footwear, debridement, a toe prop, a night splint and analgesia have given limited benefit. She now works four shifts weekly and cannot walk from the car park without stopping.
Codeine causes nausea and vomiting, though this is not a true allergy. She understands that the decision about surgery is yours, and asks whether the second toe could be corrected simultaneously.

commentary.organisation: Request, then symptoms, then measured and radiographic findings, then treatment already tried and functional impact, and finally the codeine intolerance and the patient's question.
commentary.tone: Formal and concise, as appropriate for a consultant, and careful not to presume the surgical decision.

letters.re: Re: Mr Ferdinand Achampong-Blyth, aged 78, healed neuropathic ulcer, high-risk foot
body: I am transferring the foot surveillance of Mr Achampong-Blyth to your team. His right plantar neuropathic ulcer has been healed for eight weeks, but he remains at high risk of recurrence, so please inspect both feet weekly at an existing visit.

The ulcer, beneath the fifth metatarsal head, healed on 1 October 2024. He has dense neuropathy, deformity and type 2 diabetes. Neither he nor his wife can inspect his soles, so please check between the toes and both heels.

Please telephone our direct line, not a routine referral, if you find any skin break or blister, redness persisting twenty minutes after removing footwear, dark or marked callus, new swelling, or a warmth difference between the feet. A 9 mm callus over the site could ulcerate beneath itself.

Please confirm at each visit that he wears his prescribed shoes and insoles indoors, as he has previously reverted to a slipper. Do not debride callus, cut nails, use adhesive corn treatments or apply emollient between the toes.
We continue four-weekly reviews, next on 24 December 2024 with toe pressures, and will see him within one working day of any new problem, or the same day if infection is suspected.

commentary.organisation: Purpose and request, then the background that explains the risk, then the warning signs to report, then instructions and prohibitions, and finally the podiatry arrangements retained.
commentary.tone: Clear and practical for nursing colleagues, using polite requests ('please') for each instruction so the actions are easy to follow.

letters.re: Re: Ms Marguerite Ilesanmi-Corrigan, aged 34, suspected inflammatory arthritis
body: I am writing to request early assessment of Ms Ilesanmi-Corrigan, whose bilateral forefoot pain appears inflammatory rather than mechanical, without waiting for the routine GP pathway.

Her pain has lasted eleven weeks, with forty to sixty minutes of morning stiffness, improvement with activity, and swelling for six weeks. She also reports four weeks of a swollen left second toe and six weeks of right Achilles insertion pain, and unusual tiredness for three months, without fever or weight loss.

The metatarsal squeeze test is positive bilaterally, with tenderness at the second to fourth metatarsophalangeal joints and swelling at the second and third. The left second toe shows dactylitis, and the right Achilles and plantar fascia insertions are tender. There is no callus at the painful sites.
She has nail pitting on three nails, right hallux onycholysis with mycology awaited, and a 3 cm scaly plaque at the natal cleft. Her father has psoriasis.

She takes ibuprofen 400 mg as required, with good relief, and has no known allergies. I have provided cushioned insoles for relief only. Her GP has been asked for inflammatory markers, full blood count, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP and uric acid; please do not wait for them.
