commentary.selection: The inflammatory pattern, dactylitis, enthesitis, nail and skin changes and the family history of psoriasis are kept because together they point to psoriatic arthritis. Occupation details, children and normal neurovascular findings are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request, then history, then joint examination, then skin, nail and family features, and finally medication, what has been done and the blood tests requested.
commentary.tone: Formal and well-reasoned for a consultant, presenting the pattern without stating a firm diagnosis.

letters.re: Re: Master Ptolemy Farquharson-Nkemelu, aged 12 years and 4 months, painful rigid right flat foot
body: I am writing to request imaging and an orthopaedic opinion for Ptolemy, aged 12, whose right flat foot is rigid and painful and has not responded to seven months of appropriate conservative management.

His pain began fourteen months ago without injury, at the sinus tarsi, lateral ankle and mid-foot, and is worse on uneven ground, scoring 6 out of 10 after games. He has stopped football, and the ankle gives way about once a fortnight, with two falls.

The central finding is rigidity. On the right, the arch does not reform on Jack's test or tiptoe, and the heel does not invert. Hindfoot valgus is 18 degrees, against 7 on the left. Subtalar movement is approximately 8 degrees and painful, against 30 degrees on the left, and the peroneals are tight and tender. Neurological examination is normal.

Despite orthoses, stretching, strengthening, footwear change and activity modification, his pain is unchanged, subtalar movement has decreased by approximately 6 degrees, and giving way is more frequent. I have mentioned a possible bony bar to the family.
He takes no medication and has no allergies. Meanwhile, I have advised avoiding uneven ground and contact sport, leaving school games to your clinic.

commentary.opening: The opening asks for imaging and an opinion and explains why at once: the foot is rigid, painful and has failed conservative care.
commentary.selection: The rigidity tests, the side-to-side comparisons and the worsening despite treatment are kept, as they are what distinguishes this from a simple flexible flat foot. Gait details, callus, centiles and Beighton score are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request, then the history, then the central examination finding, then treatment and its failure, and finally interim advice.
commentary.tone: Professional and measured, using comparison with the normal left foot to make the findings clear to a specialist.

letters.re: Re: Mr Aurelio Bankole-Hetherington, aged 67, acute cellulitis of the left leg
body: I am writing to request that Mr Bankole-Hetherington be seen this morning for antibiotic treatment of acute cellulitis of the left lower leg and foot. He has a 10:20 appointment with your duty doctor and is bringing this letter.
Please note that he has a verified penicillin allergy, with anaphylaxis requiring hospital admission in 1991.

Erythema extends from the malleoli to approximately 12 cm below the knee and onto the foot. I marked the border at 08:55. The left calf measures 41 cm, against 36 cm on the right, with two intact bullae and tender inguinal nodes. At 08:50 his temperature was 38.1 degrees and pulse 98.
The likely entry point is a fissure from long-standing tinea pedis between his left toes. This is his third episode in this leg. He has type 2 diabetes and lymphoedema; circulation is adequate.
I would be grateful if you would also consider a deep vein thrombosis, review his empagliflozin and metformin under sick-day guidance, and consider antibiotic prophylaxis once the tinea is treated.
I removed his compression hosiery, which should not be reapplied until you see him, and advised emergency attendance if he worsens or the redness passes the mark.

commentary.opening: The request, the timescale and the booked appointment come first, so the GP knows the patient is on the way and what is needed today.
commentary.selection: The penicillin anaphylaxis is given its own paragraph because it directly affects the antibiotic choice. The marked border, observations, portal of entry and recurrence are kept. A short paragraph adds what a febrile patient on empagliflozin and metformin, with a 5 cm calf difference and a third episode, also needs: DVT considered, sick-day review, and prophylaxis once the tinea is treated. Full doses, ABPI values and venous history are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request, then the allergy, then the findings and observations, then cause and background, then the further requests, and finally what was done and the safety-netting advice.
commentary.tone: Brisk and professional, suited to a same-day clinical handover between colleagues.

letters.re: Re: Mr Ian Forsyth, aged 52, right insertional Achilles tendinopathy with suspected partial tear
body: I am writing to refer Mr Forsyth, reviewed on 28 August 2026, for urgent ultrasound or MRI and a surgical opinion on his right insertional Achilles tendinopathy, as a partial tear is now suspected.
He has had posterior heel pain for nine months. On 14 August he stumbled off a kerb and felt a pull; since then he cannot walk beyond about ten minutes or manage stairs normally.

The tendon is thickened and tender at the insertion, extending 3 cm proximally, with a Haglund prominence. The Simmonds-Thompson test produces plantarflexion and there is no palpable gap, so complete rupture is unlikely, but a significant tear is not excluded. He managed only three painful right single heel raises, against twenty on the left.
Eccentric loading and heel-raise orthoses gave limited benefit, which the injury has since reversed.

Ciprofloxacin for prostatitis earlier this year may have contributed; he has been advised to avoid further fluoroquinolones unless unavoidable. He takes tamsulosin 400 micrograms daily and has no known allergies.
He is on relative rest with a bilateral heel raise and no eccentric loading until imaging. He hopes to avoid surgery but is open to advice. I will review him on 25 September 2026.

commentary.opening: The first paragraph states exactly what is wanted, urgent imaging and a surgical opinion, and why: a partial tear is now suspected on top of a chronic tendinopathy.
commentary.selection: The acute change, the key tests for and against rupture, the failed conservative care and the ciprofloxacin link are kept, because they shape the specialist's decision. His family, house, hay fever, knee arthroscopy, badminton and the parking question are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request, then the history of the change, then examination, then treatment so far, then the drug risk and medication, and finally the interim plan and review date.
commentary.tone: Concise and clinical between professionals, presenting the fluoroquinolone link as possible rather than proven.

letters.re: Re: Ms Rebecca Lyons, aged 34, bilateral arch ache and anterior knee pain
body: Thank you for referring Ms Lyons, whom I assessed on 26 August 2026. I am writing to advise you of my biomechanical findings and her custom orthotic plan; no orthopaedic referral is needed.
Her bilateral medial arch ache and anterior knee pain began about six weeks ago, after she increased her running from 10 to 30 kilometres weekly before a half marathon in late November 2026.

Examination showed bilateral excessive pronation, with a Foot Posture Index of plus 9 and a navicular drop of 12 mm. The flatfoot is flexible and the tibialis posterior tendon is intact. She also has gastrocnemius equinus, tight hamstrings and right hip abductor weakness. Her knee pain is patellofemoral, with stable ligaments.

I have prescribed bespoke functional orthoses, due for fitting on 16 September 2026, with a graded break-in schedule. She has stretching and hip strengthening exercises and needs new running shoes. Her running will be reduced by a third for four weeks, then increased by no more than ten per cent weekly, with knee pain recorded after each run.
I will review her eight weeks after fitting, on 11 November 2026, and discuss onward physiotherapy if her symptoms have not improved.

commentary.opening: As the GP referred her, the letter thanks the doctor, states its purpose (findings and plan) and answers the GP's likely question at once: no orthopaedic referral is needed.
commentary.selection: The training change that triggered the symptoms, the key foot, hip and knee findings and the full management plan are kept. Her job, partner, old ankle sprain, screening history, parking question and the many normal measurements are left out.
commentary.organisation: Purpose, then the cause of the problem, then examination findings, then the management plan, then follow-up and the next step if it fails.
commentary.tone: Informative and collegial; technical terms are used because the reader is a doctor, but the plan is explained clearly.

letters.re: Re: Mr Raymond Clarke, aged 58, suspected acute Charcot neuroarthropathy, right foot
body: I am writing to confirm my telephone referral today of Mr Clarke for urgent assessment of suspected acute Charcot neuroarthropathy of the right foot. He needs immobilisation in a total contact cast, which is not available here, and an MRI.
He has had type 2 diabetes for nineteen years, with an HbA1c of 74 mmol/mol, and confirmed peripheral neuropathy. He has no previous ulcer or Charcot.

For twelve days his right midfoot has been red, warm and swollen. The skin is intact and he is afebrile. The foot is 4.2 degrees Celsius warmer than the left, the erythema blanches on elevation, and there is early loss of the medial arch with a developing rocker-bottom deformity. Today's radiograph shows only soft tissue swelling, which does not exclude acute Charcot.
He takes metformin, empagliflozin, atorvastatin and ramipril, and is allergic to penicillin (rash). His diabetes team should review empagliflozin if ulceration or infection develops.

I have advised strict non-weight-bearing and issued crutches. Although reluctant, he understands the risk of midfoot collapse and amputation, and has agreed to stop driving and loading pending your review and not to drive in a cast. He can attend at short notice.

commentary.opening: The letter confirms the same-day telephone referral, as NICE expects suspected acute Charcot to reach the specialist service within one working day, and names the urgency, the diagnosis and the two things needed (a total contact cast and MRI).
commentary.selection: The neuropathy, the hot swollen foot with a 4.2-degree difference, the developing deformity and the limits of the normal radiograph are kept as they support the diagnosis. Family, the wedding, fishing, carpal tunnel surgery, eye screening and bowel screening are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request and telephone referral, then background risk, then the presenting signs and imaging, then medication, allergy and the SGLT2 inhibitor point, and finally the interim measures, driving advice and his availability.
commentary.tone: Urgent and precise, as between specialists, without overstating a diagnosis that is still to be confirmed.

letters.re: Re: Mr Trevor Okonkwo, aged 64, non-healing neuroischaemic ulcer, right foot
body: Following my telephone call today, I request urgent vascular assessment of Mr Okonkwo, with a view to revascularisation, as possible limb-threatening ischaemia is preventing his right plantar ulcer from healing.

He has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 79 mmol/mol) and peripheral neuropathy. His seven-week ulcer beneath the right first metatarsal head measures 2 cm by 1.5 cm, 4 mm deep. It has mild malodour but does not probe to bone, without cellulitis. Its area has not reduced over four weeks despite offloading, dressings and conservative debridement.

Right pedal pulses are absent, with monophasic Doppler signals and an ABPI of 0.6. The foot is cool and pale (capillary refill four seconds). He has right calf claudication at approximately 100 metres but denies rest pain, which neuropathy may mask. Toe pressures would help, as calcification can make the ABPI falsely reassuring.

He is an ex-smoker (thirty pack-years) taking atorvastatin 80 mg and ramipril 10 mg but no antiplatelet; please consider clopidogrel 75 mg daily unless contraindicated. He is allergic to penicillin (rash).
Weekly care continues here, next on 7 September 2026; he will report any signs of infection at once. He has mild hearing loss and prefers written information.

commentary.opening: The letter follows a same-day telephone call, as the ischaemia may be limb-threatening, and opens with the urgent request and its reason, so the vascular surgeon knows at once that ischaemia, not infection or offloading, is blocking healing.
commentary.selection: The wound findings, failure to heal despite good care, the vascular evidence (absent pulses, monophasic signals, ABPI 0.6, claudication), the request for toe pressures and the missing antiplatelet are central. His bus career, hernia repair, cataract surgery, allotment, family news and parking are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request and telephone call, then diabetes and the wound with treatment so far, then the vascular findings and toe pressures, then risk factors, medication with the antiplatelet request and allergy, then ongoing care, infection watch and communication needs.
commentary.tone: Urgent but measured, giving objective measurements so the specialist can triage.

letters.re: Re: Mr Abdul Karim, aged 67, neuropathic ulcer, right first metatarsal head
body: I am writing to transfer the care of Mr Karim, who moved to your area on 30 August 2026, and to ask you to continue weekly offloading, debridement and wound management of his neuropathic plantar ulcer.
He has type 2 diabetes with established peripheral neuropathy; his HbA1c was 69 mmol/mol in July 2026. His ABPI is 1.0 bilaterally.

The ulcer has been present for seven weeks. When last seen on 27 August 2026, it measured 12 mm by 10 mm, more than halved from 18 mm by 14 mm over four weeks, with a granulating base, no infection and no probing to bone. However, the callus rim reforms within a week.

The main obstacle to healing is poor adherence to his removable walker, which he takes off at home and at the mosque. I would recommend a total contact cast or a rendered-irremovable walker; he would consider a cast if it were explained to him.

He will need district nurse support for twice-weekly foam dressings and has only about one week of stock, so needs a new prescription promptly. He has no known allergies. Photographs are enclosed, and his vascular status should be rechecked in three months.

letters.re: Re: Miss Chloe Bennett, aged 22, partial nail avulsion, right hallux
body: I am writing to inform you that Miss Bennett, whom you referred on 10 July 2026, has been discharged from podiatry following a partial nail avulsion, and to outline her ongoing self-care. No routine follow-up is needed unless the problem recurs.

She had a recurrent ingrown toenail on the lateral border of the right hallux, despite two courses of antibiotics and conservative care. On 24 August 2026, a partial nail avulsion with phenolisation was performed under a digital block of plain lidocaine 2 per cent, without complications.
Today the area is healing well, with the expected serous discharge and no sign of infection. She is walking normally and is pain-free.

She is continuing salt-water soaks and daily dressing changes, and has enough dressings for two weeks. She understands that discharge may continue for four to six weeks and is expected, and that she may return to netball once the area is dry and comfortable. She now cuts her nails straight across.

She has been advised to contact the surgery if increasing redness, swelling, discharge or fever develops. The recurrence rate is under five per cent; please re-refer her if the treated border regrows. She has no known allergies.

letters.re: Re: Mr Gordon Mackenzie, aged 70, healed neuropathic ulcer, right second toe
body: Mr Mackenzie was discharged from active podiatry treatment on 28 August 2026 into our high-risk foot surveillance pathway. Please amend his allergy record and continue his glycaemic and vascular risk management.

His neuropathic ulcer, first seen on 8 April 2026, was complicated by cellulitis in May, which resolved fully after fourteen days of flucloxacillin. There was no bone involvement. The ulcer healed in mid-July and has remained closed for six weeks.

Your record lists a penicillin allergy, but his earlier reaction was confirmed as nausea only, and he then tolerated flucloxacillin. Please amend this to penicillin intolerance (nausea), as it affects future prescribing.

His neuropathy persists, with the monofilament absent at eight of ten sites, so he remains at high risk; pedal pulses are palpable (ABPI 1.0). His HbA1c has improved to 58 mmol/mol from 76 in March. He wears extra-depth shoes with insoles indoors and out. Please review his dapagliflozin if a new ulcer or infection develops.
He and his wife check his feet daily; he will report any skin break the same day. His next surveillance appointment is on 9 October 2026, with podiatry review every 1 to 2 months.

letters.re: Re: Mr Joshua Bennett, aged 23, recurrent ingrown toenail, right hallux
body: I am writing to refer Mr Bennett, an apprentice electrician whom I saw on 29 August 2026, for partial nail avulsion with phenolisation of the lateral border of his right hallux, as repeated conservative treatment has failed.

This is his third episode of onychocryptosis in twelve months, and the November 2025 episode required oral antibiotics. The current episode began about ten days ago. Today the lateral nail fold is swollen and inflamed, with serous exudate and approximately 4 mm of hypergranulation tissue that bleeds on contact. Erythema is confined to the nail fold, there is no spreading cellulitis and he is afebrile. His involuted nail and deep lateral sulcus explain the recurrences.
Packing, nail filing, cutting education and footwear advice have each given only temporary relief.
He is fit and well, with no diabetes, good perfusion and intact sensation. He takes no medication and has no known allergies.

He has been counselled about the procedure and is keen to proceed. He would prefer a date after 26 September, when his current site job finishes. Meanwhile, he will keep the toe dressed and elevated with daily salt-water soaks, and will return sooner if spreading redness, throbbing or fever develops.

letters.re: Re: Tom Whitfield, aged 11, Sever's disease (heel pain)
body: I am writing to ask for your help in supporting Tom, who joins your school in September, with his heel pain during physical education and sport. His mother has consented to this letter.

I saw Tom on 27 August 2026 with heel pain in both feet for about four months. He has Sever's disease, a growth plate traction injury common in active children during a growth spurt. It is self-limiting, causes no lasting damage and usually settles between thirteen and fifteen.

Heel raises have been fitted to his school shoes and football boots, and he does calf and hamstring stretches three times daily. Please allow him to wear supportive trainers rather than plimsolls indoors.

During a flare, which he recognises as heel pain that makes him limp, I suggest modified participation rather than exclusion, reducing running and jumping while keeping him active. Swimming, cycling and upper-body activities are good alternatives, and a cool pack he brings himself would help afterwards. Complete rest is neither necessary nor helpful.
Tom is self-conscious, so adjustments should be made discreetly. His mother can be contacted through the school office, and I will review him in eight weeks.

commentary.selection: The diagnosis, its benign course, the footwear and stretching plan and the specific school adjustments are kept, because they are what the nurse will act on. Examination measurements, growth figures, his old wrist sprain, grommets, his sister and the car park question are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request and consent, then the diagnosis in plain clinical terms, then current treatment and footwear, then how to manage a flare at school, then his feelings, contact and review.
commentary.tone: Warm and practical, written for a nursing colleague who is not a foot specialist, so the diagnosis is explained briefly without jargon.

letters.re: Re: Lucy Adeyemi, aged 4 years 2 months, in-toeing gait
body: Thank you for referring Lucy, whom I assessed on 26 August 2026 for in-toeing gait. She has a normal developmental variant, her parents have been reassured and I have discharged her from podiatry.

Examination confirmed a mild, symmetrical in-toeing gait due to bilateral internal tibial torsion, with a thigh-foot angle internally rotated 10 degrees on each side. Hip rotation was full and symmetrical, her feet were structurally normal and neurological examination was normal, with no leg-length discrepancy. She has no pain, her development is normal, and the tripping is already less frequent than a year ago. Her brother had similar in-toeing, which resolved untreated.

Internal tibial torsion unwinds spontaneously with growth, usually by around eight years of age. I explained that orthoses, splints, corrective footwear and exercises do not change its natural history, and her parents, who had considered corrective boots, accepted this with relief. Any comfortable, well-fitting shoe is suitable.

No treatment or further appointment has been arranged. Her parents know to return if she develops pain, if the in-toeing becomes asymmetrical, if any skill is lost, or if there is no improvement by around age eight. They will receive a copy of this letter.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Pauline Hardy, aged 71, suspected critical limb ischaemia, right leg
body: Following my call to the on-call vascular team today, I request urgent assessment of Mrs Hardy, as new right foot rest pain with an ABPI of 0.52 raises the question of critical limb ischaemia.

She has a six-month history of right calf claudication, now at about 100 metres, from around 400 metres in the spring. For three weeks, right forefoot pain has woken her most nights, eased by hanging the foot out of bed. There is no tissue loss.

The right foot was cool, with a positive Buerger test, absent pedal pulses and capillary refill of five seconds at the hallux. ABPI was 0.52 right and 0.78 left, with monophasic Doppler signals at the right ankle.

She smokes twenty cigarettes daily, has now accepted stop smoking referral, and has hypertension and hyperlipidaemia without diabetes. She takes amlodipine 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg at night and aspirin 75 mg daily; please review these, as NICE advises atorvastatin 80 mg and clopidogrel 75 mg. She has no known allergies.
Please arrange duplex imaging and revascularisation assessment. Her son can bring her at short notice. I will avoid sharp debridement until your review and see her in four weeks.

letters.re: Re: Mr Steven Walsh, aged 45, persistent right plantar heel pain
body: I am writing to refer Mr Walsh for a structured progressive loading programme for persistent right plantar heel pain, which has responded only partially to ten weeks of podiatry care.

He has a five-month history of pain at the medial calcaneal tubercle, worst on first steps and after sitting, and worse again late in the day. It began after he took up running in January, quickly reaching four sessions weekly; he also sits at a desk for around nine hours daily. The windlass test was positive, with no neural, radicular or inflammatory features.
He has marked gastrocnemius equinus, with ankle dorsiflexion of 3 degrees with the knee extended and 12 degrees flexed, and a weaker right calf raise. His body mass index is 31.

Heel cushioning, taping, off-the-shelf orthoses and load management have reduced first-step pain from 7 out of 10 to 5 out of 10, but late-day pain is unchanged and his stretching has been sporadic. He stopped running in July. He takes occasional ibuprofen and has no known allergies.
I would be grateful for supervised gastrocnemius stretching and a gait and running review before any return to running. Orthoses should continue. He prefers evening or Friday appointments.

body: I am writing to refer Miss Davenport for consideration of advanced verruca treatment, as her plantar verruca has failed to respond to conservative therapy and is limiting her activities.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Geraldine Foster, aged 64, progressive rheumatoid forefoot deformity
body: I am referring Mrs Foster to the multidisciplinary foot clinic for progressive rheumatoid forefoot deformity, as an early pre-ulcerative lesion beneath her right second metatarsal head means ulceration is likely within months without intervention.
Her seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, diagnosed in 2011, is well controlled (DAS28 2.4). Over a year, forefoot pain, worse on the right, has limited her to about ten minutes on her feet.

Examination showed marked bilateral hallux valgus, clawing of the lesser toes with dorsal subluxation at the metatarsophalangeal joints, and distal displacement of the plantar fat pad. The pre-ulcerative lesion is macerated callus with underlying haemorrhage, skin intact. Pulses and sensation were normal, with no infection. Her narrow, heeled shoes contribute significantly.

She takes methotrexate 20 mg weekly on Mondays, folic acid 5 mg weekly on Thursdays, adalimumab fortnightly and omeprazole 20 mg daily, and is allergic to sulfasalazine (rash). Her immunosuppression raises the stakes should an ulcer become infected.

I debrided the callus, offloaded the lesion with felt padding and will review her in two weeks. I would be grateful for bespoke orthoses, a footwear assessment and consideration of a surgical opinion, with perioperative methotrexate and adalimumab planned with rheumatology; she would prefer orthoses first.

letters.re: Re: Mr Terence Boyle, aged 62, infected right hallux ulcer, suspected osteomyelitis
body: I am referring Mr Boyle urgently for admission with a deep infected right hallux ulcer and suspected osteomyelitis. After my call to the diabetic foot service at 11.00 am, he is travelling by emergency ambulance.

He has type 2 diabetes, neuropathy, an HbA1c of 81 mmol/mol and a healed 2024 ulcer on the same toe. Over three weeks, a blister from new shoes has become a deep plantar ulcer, 15 mm in diameter, which probes to bone, with purulent, malodorous exudate, erythema extending 3 cm and dactylitis. The radiograph shows cortical erosion of the distal phalanx.

Unwell for four days, he was shivering last night. Temperature was 38.1 degrees, pulse 96 and blood pressure 132/78. CRP was 96 mg/L, white cell count 14.2 x 10^9/L and capillary glucose 16 mmol/L. His sepsis screen was positive.
Please take blood cultures and a deep tissue sample on arrival and start intravenous antibiotics without delay, not withholding them to protect cultures. MRI and debridement are probably needed.

He takes metformin 1 g twice daily, insulin and atorvastatin 40 mg at night, and has no known allergies. Please withhold metformin and manage glucose with insulin. He is non-weight-bearing; his wife is with him.

commentary.opening: An urgent admission letter states the diagnosis and the action already taken in the first lines, so the registrar knows the patient is on his way and why.
commentary.selection: Diabetes control, the ulcer and probe-to-bone result, the radiograph, signs of systemic infection, blood results, the sepsis screen, medication and allergies are kept. His job, flat, car, keys, employer and the ward television are left out as irrelevant to his acute care.
commentary.organisation: Urgent request and transfer by ambulance, then the history and local findings, then systemic findings and results, then the immediate actions requested, then medication with the metformin advice and transfer details.
commentary.tone: Direct and urgent, using precise figures and clear instructions for a hospital doctor.

letters.re: Re: Miss Seraphina Okorie-Dunmore, aged 6 years and 3 months, absence of speech at school
body: I am writing to request joint management of Seraphina, whom I assessed on 21 January and 4 February 2025, with your service leading on her anxiety and mine on a graded speaking programme.

At home she talks freely in English and Igbo, yet she has not spoken to any adult at school since starting Reception in September 2023. She speaks only to one classmate when no adult is near, and freezes when addressed.

Her receptive and expressive language standard scores are 108 and 104, her speech sounds are age-appropriate and her hearing was normal in November 2024, so a language disorder can be regarded as excluded.

In my view, anxiety is the primary problem and extends beyond speaking: she does not eat, drink or use the toilet at school, separation is worsening, and she worries constantly about tomorrow. I have asked her GP to check her hydration, bowels and urinary symptoms, and the school to stop recording her accidents as behavioural. Rewards and direct questioning increased her distress; removing pressure has helped.
Please assess her, plan graded exposure with me within a formulation, and support her parents, who have waited seventeen months. There are no safeguarding concerns.
signoff: Wexbridge Community Speech and Language Therapy Service

commentary.opening: The first paragraph names the request and the division of roles at once: psychology to lead on the anxiety, speech and language therapy on the speaking programme, so the reader knows this is joint working rather than a hand-over.
commentary.selection: The situational pattern, the normal language scores and the features beyond speaking are kept because together they make the case that anxiety is the primary problem. Birth history, milestones and the detail of the forty-minute observation are left out as they do not change what psychology must do.
commentary.organisation: Request, then the pattern that defines the difficulty, then the evidence that language is normal, then the wider anxiety and what has made it worse, then the specific requests.
commentary.tone: Professional and confident between clinicians, firm about what is established while respectful of the psychologist's own assessment.

letters.re: Re: Mr Fitzgerald Adewale-Kinnersley, aged 66, communication needs and plan
body: I am writing to set out the communication plan for Mr Adewale-Kinnersley, now under your care, and to ask that every visitor first reads his communication passport.

He has no voice, and it will not return, but his cognition and hearing are intact. Please speak at normal volume and pace, let him write without finishing his sentences, and never direct questions to his wife in his presence.

Writing is his best method, although his hand tires. He also has an alphabet board, a night bell and a tablet with key phrases. Recordings of his own voice are stored there; please do not mention them in front of his wife.

As the tumour lies above his tracheostomy, he cannot be oxygenated via the mouth. A spare tube, suction and a bed-head sign are in the house, and the family will call 999 for a blocked or dislodged tube; please confirm this plan at your first visit.

He eats small amounts for pleasure, with feed and medication via gastrostomy, a decision made with capacity. A DNACPR is in place and he wishes to die at home. Please begin advance care planning while he can still write. I will review him fortnightly.

commentary.opening: The letter opens with its purpose and the single action every visitor must take, reading the communication passport before the first visit, because the team is taking over today.
commentary.selection: The guidance for visitors, the tools, the tracheostomy emergency plan, the swallowing decision and the end-of-life details are kept because they govern every visit. Tumour staging, treatment history and co-morbidities are left out as already known to the palliative team.
commentary.organisation: Purpose and passport, then how to communicate with him, then the tools he uses, then the tracheostomy emergency plan, then eating, advance decisions, advance care planning and review.
commentary.tone: Warm but precise between professionals, conveying his dignity and stated wishes without sentimentality.

letters.re: Re: Master Octavian Rutherford-Chinweze, aged 6 years and 8 months, hypernasality after adenoidectomy
body: I am writing to refer Octavian for instrumental assessment of velopharyngeal function, including nasendoscopy and, if available, videofluoroscopy, for persistent hypernasality that began after adenoidectomy and has not responded to therapy.

His speech was normal until his adenoidectomy and grommet insertion on 9 January 2025. Within a week, his mother noticed a nasal voice and nasal regurgitation of fluids, and neither has changed in nine months.

He has moderate, consistent hypernasality, rated 3 on a 5-point scale by two therapists independently, with audible nasal emission, nasal turbulence and a mild nasal grimace. Glottal stops have developed for /k/ and /g/, and intelligibility to an unfamiliar listener is 68 per cent. Although I found no bifid uvula, zona pellucida or palpable notch, I cannot exclude an occult submucous cleft unmasked by surgery, and a maternal cousin has a cleft palate.
After twelve sessions of articulation therapy, /k/ and /g/ are established in words, but resonance is unchanged. He now avoids speaking in class and has been teased.
I would be grateful for your view on surgery and on what therapy should address meanwhile. His hearing was normal on 22 August 2025, but should be re-checked if ear symptoms return.
signoff: Wexbridge Community Speech and Language Therapy Service

commentary.opening: The opening names the investigations requested and the reason in one sentence, so the surgeon can triage the referral immediately.
commentary.selection: The timeline after surgery, the resonance findings, the possible submucous cleft with the family history, and the failed therapy trial are kept because they justify instrumental assessment. Mirror-test detail, voice findings and social history are left out as they add nothing to the decision.
commentary.organisation: Request, then the timeline, then the findings and the suspected cause, then the therapy outcome and impact, then the remaining requests.
commentary.tone: Formal and specific, as suits a referral to a consultant surgeon, while making the child's distress clear.

letters.re: Re: Mr Percival Adeyemi-Hollingsworth, aged 43, eating and drinking with acknowledged risks
body: I am writing to set out the eating and drinking plan for Mr Adeyemi-Hollingsworth, agreed on 4 December, so that everyone supporting him works to one document.

He has progressive dysphagia, coughing on thin fluids and dry or mixed textures. On 27 November, he was found to have capacity for this decision. Understanding that aspiration could cause a fatal chest infection, he chose thin fluids and a normal diet. This is his decision, not a best interests one.

Staff should offer softer options and mildly thick fluids without pressing him, and avoid dry bread, biscuits and mixed consistencies; crisps are allowed if softened. He must be upright at the table and for 30 minutes afterwards, with his pace slowed. Mouth care twice daily and after meals is essential.
His drinks were thickened without his knowledge. Please consider whether this meets the safeguarding threshold under the Care Act 2014, and record the outcome.

Please weigh him monthly, reporting any loss over 2 kg. His general practitioner should be contacted the same day for fever, breathlessness or a productive cough, and has been asked to review his omeprazole. He may change his mind at any time. Review is six-monthly.
signoff: Wexbridge Community Speech and Language Therapy Service

commentary.opening: It opens by stating that the plan has been agreed and asking that everyone works to one document, which is exactly what a social work manager needs to coordinate the network.
commentary.selection: The capacity assessment and the fact that this is his decision are given prominence because they are the legal basis social care must understand. The covert thickening is raised as a possible safeguarding concern because social work must decide on it. The trial-by-trial swallow results are condensed, and the full history is left out as not needed by social work.
commentary.organisation: Purpose, then the risk and the capacity decision, then what staff must do, then the safeguarding question, then monitoring, escalation and review.
commentary.tone: Clear and respectful of the client's autonomy, firm on the protective measures and on the covert thickening that must not recur.

letters.re: Re: Master Aurelius Ogundipe-Thackeray, aged 13 years and 9 months, Year 9, stammering
body: I am writing, at Aurelius's request and with his written consent, to set out the adjustments he needs, and to ask that this letter is shared with all his teachers, including cover staff, but not read out to him in a meeting.

He has stammered since the age of 4. He substitutes words constantly, so his difficulty is easily underestimated. He has not volunteered an answer since Year 7, and told me he "would rather be thought stupid than be thought a stammerer".

He does not want to be excused from speaking, but to be given time. Please wait for blocks to end without finishing his words, keep natural eye contact, and never tell him to slow down, breathe, relax or think. Give notice of reading aloud, and let him answer the register in his own way, as his name is his hardest word.
He has taken four detentions rather than read aloud. This is a disability-related difficulty (Equality Act 2010), so please review those sanctions.
He wants to take the spoken language endorsement, with preparation, a smaller audience and extra time. He begins fluency group sessions on 14 April, and I will review him in July 2025.
signoff: Wexbridge Community Speech and Language Therapy Service

commentary.opening: The opening establishes his consent, the purpose and the most important request, sharing the letter with every teacher, because he said this matters more than any single adjustment.
commentary.selection: The hidden avoidance, his own words, his wishes, the practical adjustments and the detentions are kept because they change what teachers do. Stammering percentages, secondary behaviours, his option choices (not yet his to share) and family background are left out.
commentary.organisation: Purpose and sharing, then a short profile with his own words, then the adjustments in his own terms, then the detentions, then the examination arrangement, therapy and review.
commentary.tone: Plain and professional for teachers, respecting the young person's voice and avoiding clinical jargon.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Emmelina Bassey-Fotheringay, aged 71, progressive dysphagia
body: Having assessed Mrs Bassey-Fotheringay today, I believe her difficulty is oesophageal rather than oropharyngeal, and I would be grateful if you could refer her urgently for gastroscopy on the suspected upper gastrointestinal cancer pathway.

Over four months her dysphagia has progressed from solids to soft foods and, for ten days, to fluids. She localises the sticking to the lower sternum and regurgitates undigested food about three times a week, including twice at night. She has had retrosternal pain on swallowing for six weeks and has lost 11 kg unintentionally, from 65 kg to 54 kg.
Her cranial nerves, voice and oropharyngeal swallow were normal, so I have not started therapy, which would only delay investigation.
She has long-standing reflux on omeprazole 20 mg, never reviewed, and Barrett's oesophagus was noted in 2006, without surveillance since.

I spoke to your duty doctor at 13:40 today. She should attend the emergency department if she cannot swallow saliva, vomits blood or food sticks completely, and needs same-day medical assessment if she cannot keep up her fluid intake. She should raise the head of her bed. I would also suggest a full blood count, ferritin, and review of her omeprazole, codeine and lapsed surveillance.
signoff: Wexbridge Community Speech and Language Therapy Service

commentary.opening: The writer redirects the referral and states the urgent request in the first sentence, because the GP referred for therapy and must now act differently.
commentary.selection: The red-flag features, the normal oropharyngeal findings and the lapsed Barrett's surveillance are kept as they justify the urgent pathway, with the fluid and night-time safety-netting and the medication review. Trial-by-trial bedside results and other co-morbidities are left out as not affecting the referral.
commentary.organisation: Request, then the history and red flags, then the reason therapy is not appropriate, then relevant background, then actions taken and further requests.
commentary.tone: Direct and collegial, conveying urgency without alarm and without overstepping into diagnosis.

letters.re: Re: Mr Casimir Adebowale-Thorncroft, aged 64, urgent referral for progressive hoarseness
body: I am writing to request urgent laryngeal examination for Mr Adebowale-Thorncroft, whose progressive hoarseness has features of concern. Following my call to your coordinator today, he has an appointment on 22 April.

His hoarseness has progressed over five months without any period of normal voice. For nine weeks he has had constant left-sided throat discomfort, with referred left ear pain for six weeks and difficulty swallowing solids for seven weeks. He has lost 8 kg unintentionally, from 79 kg to 71 kg.

Today he had severe dysphonia, GRBAS grade 3, with diplophonia and a maximum phonation time of 4 seconds. I also found a firm, mobile left level II node of approximately 2 cm. He has no stridor, but will attend the emergency department immediately if noisy breathing or breathing difficulty develops.

He has smoked sixty-one pack-years and drinks at least 60 units a week, so he is at risk of alcohol withdrawal if admitted; please assess this and consider thiamine. He has type 2 diabetes, treated with metformin 1 g twice daily, and no known allergies.
I have not started voice therapy. He has been referred for smoking cessation and has asked that his partner is not telephoned.
signoff: Wexbridge Community Speech and Language Therapy Service

letters.re: Re: Mrs Theodosia Nwankwo-Ellersley, aged 87, eating and drinking plan
body: This plan for Mrs Nwankwo-Ellersley replaces the plan dated 4 March 2025, which should be removed from her file. She will not remember it, so it is entirely the staff's responsibility.

All drinks, including those with medication, must be mildly thick, IDDSI Level 2, and all food pureed, IDDSI Level 4, with no mixed consistencies. Do not use straws, spouted beakers or syringes. She must sit upright at 90 degrees, and remain so for 30 minutes after eating or drinking, under seated one-to-one supervision. Mouth care twice daily and after meals is equally important.

No tablet should be crushed into a drink before pharmacist review, and her anticoagulant must not be crushed or opened. Please keep a daily fluid chart. Her general practitioner will review her insulin, as her intake may fall.

Contact our service if coughing increases, her voice stays wet or her alertness changes, and her general practitioner the same day for a temperature above 37.5, breathlessness or a productive cough. Weigh her weekly, reporting any loss over 2 kg in a month.
Her son, who holds lasting power of attorney, agrees. She has been referred to a dietitian; I will review her on 6 September.

letters.re: Re: Miss Anouska Villanueva-Okereke, aged 2 years and 7 months, suspected hearing loss
body: I am writing to request a full hearing assessment for Anouska, seen twice for delayed speech. I strongly suspect an uninvestigated hearing loss; her passed newborn screen appears to have been taken as settling the question.

She uses approximately eighteen single words, without combinations, and is poorly understood by strangers. Significantly, quiet high-frequency sounds such as /s/, /f/ and /sh/ are absent, while louder low-frequency sounds are present. She follows instructions only when watching the speaker. Her receptive score was below the 2nd centile, but her social communication is good, with no features of autism.
Her family report that she turns the television up, ignores calls from another room and is startled by arrivals.
She has had six episodes of otitis media and two of ear discharge, latest June 2025, and a persistent blocked nose. Her grandmother has adult-onset hearing loss. She has no medication or allergies.

Although glue ear is likely, a sensorineural loss must also be excluded. Therapy continues meanwhile. Her general practitioner has been asked to refer her to ENT or paediatrics for suspected obstructive sleep apnoea, as she snores nightly with breathing pauses.
signoff: Wexbridge Community Speech and Language Therapy Service

commentary.organisation: Request and reason, then the language and speech evidence, then the family's observations, then the medical history, then the differential, the therapy running alongside and the sleep apnoea referral.
commentary.tone: Clear and professional between clinicians, giving evidence rather than a diagnosis and leaving the hearing assessment to the specialist.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Ottavia Blackwood-Nnaji, aged 59, progressive dysarthria and dysphagia
body: I am writing to request urgent neurological assessment of Mrs Blackwood-Nnaji, whose speech and swallowing are deteriorating over weeks. Following my call to your registrar at 15:10 today, an appointment has been offered on 19 June.

Speech change began around November 2024 and is now present from waking. Over seven weeks, her intelligibility has fallen from 88 per cent to 61 per cent. Most importantly, her tongue shows marked wasting with fasciculations at rest. She also has a brisk jaw jerk, hypernasality and a mixed spastic and flaccid dysarthria. Cognition and language are intact.

She has had left-hand weakness since May, twitching in both upper arms and two episodes of uncontrollable laughter. She reports no breathlessness, orthopnoea or disturbed sleep, and will seek same-day help if these develop.

She coughed on 3 of 5 thin fluid trials, and her weight has fallen from 66 kg to 58 kg. She has capacity and has declined modified textures; she has had swallow safety advice, and I have requested an instrumental swallow assessment and referred her to the dietitian.
She takes levothyroxine 50 micrograms and has no known allergies. No diagnosis has been named to her.
signoff: Wexbridge Community Speech and Language Therapy Service

letters.re: Re: Barnaby Oyelaran-Whitlock, aged 7 years and 1 month, Year 2, developmental language disorder
body: Thank you for referring Barnaby. He has a significant developmental language disorder, and I ask that the classroom recommendations below be adopted. In my assessment, the behaviour you described results from this difficulty, not a separate problem.

His understanding is below the 3rd centile: he manages single instructions but not those with two or more parts or words such as "before" or "unless". His sentences are short and word finding is markedly difficult. Clear speech and average non-verbal reasoning explain why this was missed. In class he copied others and was reprimanded for not listening when he had not understood, yet followed single instructions at his desk immediately.

Please gain his attention by name, give one step at a time, allow ten seconds' processing time, and support speech with visuals. Check understanding by asking what he will do, as he will always say yes. Pre-teaching key topic words a week ahead would help most. Please treat non-compliance as non-comprehension before any sanction.

A therapy assistant will begin six weekly sessions on 8 January, staff training is offered for 15 January, and review is planned for July 2025. I support an education, health and care needs assessment application.
signoff: Wexbridge Community Speech and Language Therapy Service

letters.re: Re: Mr Ignatius Farrowdale-Achike, aged 68, aphasia after left middle cerebral artery infarct
body: I am writing to transfer Mr Farrowdale-Achike, discharged home today, to your service for continued community aphasia rehabilitation. He had a left middle cerebral artery infarct on 12 September 2025, causing moderate-severe non-fluent aphasia, mild apraxia of speech and mild right hemiparesis.

He understands everyday one-to-one conversation in quiet surroundings but struggles with noise, groups and rapid speech. He speaks in short phrases, averaging 2.4 words, and word finding remains severely impaired. Fluent automatic speech can overstate his ability. His insight is full; he is frustrated, not confused. Please give him time, use yes or no questions, write key words, and avoid speaking loudly or finishing his sentences. He uses gesture, drawing and his own communication book.
His swallow has recovered, but please reassess if he deteriorates neurologically.

His goals include using his communication book in shops, telephoning his daughter and returning to his allotment committee. His wife needs continued partner training. Please consider the local aphasia support group.
He has been tearful on eight occasions. Please screen his mood with an aphasia-friendly tool, such as the SADQ-H10, and refer him to stroke psychology if positive.

commentary.tone: Professional and collegial, with respect for the patient's dignity in how his frustration is described.

letters.re: Re: Master Rafferty Osei-Wainwright, aged 4 years and 9 months, feeding difficulty and weight loss
body: I am writing to request joint management of Rafferty's feeding. He has spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy, and over four months his mealtimes have become longer and less safe, while his weight has fallen.

He weighed 13.1 kg on 19 February, compared with 14.2 kg on 3 May 2024, and is well below the 2nd centile. He has had three chest infections since October, one requiring admission. Meals took up to 58 minutes, yet his fluids totalled only about 400 mL in a day. As he is newly drowsy, I have asked his paediatrician for a medical review this week.

He coughs on thin fluids and mixed consistencies, so I have changed his diet to IDDSI Level 4 pureed with Level 2 mildly thick fluids, and limited mealtimes to 30 minutes. At home he is fed semi-reclined because his chair is too small, and an urgent seating review has been requested.

Please provide a nutritional assessment, advice on fortification and your view on supplementary feeding, not yet raised by the family, and attend his videofluoroscopy on 11 March if possible. His constipation is poorly controlled. He takes sodium valproate, macrogol and a vitamin supplement, and has no known allergies.
signoff: Wexbridge Community Speech and Language Therapy Service

letters.re: Re: Miss Rosalind Nkemdirim-Pargeter, aged 34, muscle tension dysphonia
body: I am writing to update you on Miss Nkemdirim-Pargeter, whom I assessed today, and to ask the practice to review her omeprazole and her mood.

Nasendoscopy on 18 December 2024 showed healthy, mobile vocal folds with no lesion, but marked supraglottic constriction, consistent with muscle tension dysphonia. She has understood the normal findings to mean her problem is imaginary, so please reinforce that this is a real, treatable condition.

Her voice has worsened over fourteen months, and she has lost it completely on eleven days this academic year. I found moderate strained dysphonia; her voice improves within seconds on humming, a favourable sign.
She began eight fortnightly therapy sessions today, and I have written to her school recommending an amplifier and timetable changes.

She has taken omeprazole 20 mg since March 2024 without benefit or confirmed reflux; should it continue? She became tearful twice today about a workplace capability process and lives alone, so please screen her mood, ask about risk and consider psychological support, as she asked. Please also support any occupational health referral, and re-refer to ENT if red flags such as dysphagia or haemoptysis appear.
signoff: Wexbridge Community Speech and Language Therapy Service

letters.re: Re: Mr Aurelio Chikwendu-Marchbanks, aged 52, speaking valve plan and swallow status
body: I am writing about Mr Chikwendu-Marchbanks, transferred today, to set out his speaking valve and swallow plans. He has a size 7 cuffed tracheostomy, cuff deflated at all times.

The cuff must be fully deflated before the valve is placed, as a valve on an inflated cuff obstructs expiration. If uncertain, do not place it. He may wear it for up to four hours each morning and afternoon, never at night. Remove it if he becomes breathless, strained or asks, and record observations before, during and after each period. Never suction through a fenestrated inner cannula.

He should take a Level 5 minced and moist diet with Level 1 slightly thick fluids, only with the valve on, so he is nil by mouth whenever it is off. He must sit upright at 90 degrees; no thin fluids or straws. During overnight nasogastric feeds, keep the bed head raised to at least 30 degrees. Mouth care four times daily is essential.

His overnight CPAP plan will be set by the respiratory and tracheostomy teams before his first night. Please contact us for coughing at meals or falling valve tolerance, and the tracheostomy or outreach team urgently for breathing difficulty.

commentary.selection: The life-threatening cuff rule, the valve timings and stop signs, the diet and fluid levels, mouth care and escalation are kept. The ICU history, FEES details and valve progression figures are left out as background the nurses do not need to act on.
commentary.organisation: Purpose and tube, then the valve plan with its safety rules and the suction rule, then swallow, feeding position and mouth care, then the overnight plan and escalation.
commentary.tone: Direct and instructional for nursing colleagues, with firm wording where a mistake could be fatal.

letters.re: Re: Master Daniel Petrov, aged 8 years 4 months, high-tech AAC assessment, trial and funding
body: I am referring Daniel for a formal augmentative and alternative communication assessment, an extended trial of an eye-gaze speech-generating device and a funding application. He has spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy (GMFCS level V) with severe dysarthria, and his speech is under 10 per cent intelligible to unfamiliar listeners.

Formal testing is not possible, but his receptive language is functional on eye-gaze arrays, his yes and no responses are reliable, and his cognition is not considered as impaired as his speech suggests. His 24-symbol picture board is outgrown, and he is so often misunderstood outside the family that he has begun to stop trying.

In a four-session trial in July and August 2026, he calibrated reliably, navigated pages and generated three- and four-word messages, including a spontaneous request. Selection slowed after about thirty minutes because of fatigue. Upper limb access is not viable because of dystonia; his wheelchair already has a mounting point.

His epilepsy is well controlled, with no seizures during eye-gaze use. School and family are committed to daily use, supported by our implementation training. Delay matters, as communication failure at his age begins to shape behaviour and self-image. Trial data and video are available with parental consent.

Swimming, parking, the sister's age, reflux, grommets and hip X-rays are left out as irrelevant to device funding.

commentary.tone: Formal and persuasive but factual, as befits a funding referral to a specialist service.

letters.re: Re: Mr Trevor Aldous, aged 68, community aphasia rehabilitation after left MCA stroke
body: I am writing to refer Mr Aldous for community aphasia rehabilitation following a left middle cerebral artery ischaemic stroke. He was admitted on 18 August 2026 and discharged home on 30 August 2026, and I would be grateful for twice-weekly outpatient therapy.

He has Broca-type expressive aphasia, with slow, effortful speech of one to three words and mild verbal apraxia. Naming is markedly impaired (Boston Naming Test 12 of 60), with phonemic cues helping about half. Comprehension holds for single-stage commands but not for longer instructions or complex grammar. Fatigue prevented a fuller battery.

He communicates with single words, gesture, drawing and an alphabet board; yes and no responses are reliable. He is motivated but visibly frustrated. No mood screen was done before discharge; please complete an aphasia-friendly screen early, such as the SADQ-H10 with his wife. Swallowing is normal.

His goals are to talk with his grandchildren, use the telephone and order in a café. His wife, who answers for him, is keen for supported conversation training. He takes apixaban, is allergic to penicillin and has been advised not to drive for at least one month. He prefers mornings; a six-week review with repeat naming measures is planned.

commentary.selection: The aphasia profile, communication strategies, the outstanding mood screen, goals, the wife's role and the driving advice are kept because they shape therapy and safety. His postal career, allotment, hernia, cataract, flu vaccine, parking and stroke club are left out as not needed for planning aphasia therapy.
commentary.organisation: Request, then language profile, then communication and the mood screen request, then goals, partner training, safety facts and practical arrangements.
commentary.tone: Collegial and concise between therapists, using shared clinical terms without over-explaining.

letters.re: Re: Master Liam Okoro, aged 4 years 6 months, developmental stuttering
body: I am writing to refer Liam for specialist assessment and management of developmental stuttering, including consideration of the Lidcombe Program or a comparable early-intervention approach. In my view he needs timely treatment rather than watchful waiting.

His stammer began at around three years of age, approximately eighteen months ago, and has increased in frequency and effort over the past six months without remission. In a ten-minute play sample, he stammered on 9 per cent of syllables, with part-word repetitions, prolongations and silent blocks accompanied by facial tension, eye closure and jaw tremor. He sometimes taps or stamps to force words out.

He is now aware of the problem, telling his mother that his words get stuck, and has begun to avoid speaking and swap words. His kindergarten teacher reports reluctance in group time. A paternal uncle stammers into adulthood. His language, speech sounds and hearing are age-appropriate.

His parents are anxious but understand they have not caused it, and their advice to slow down was addressed today. His father can attend weekly sessions, both parents will practise daily, and kindergarten staff will follow advice. Together, the duration, tension, avoidance and awareness make natural recovery less likely.

commentary.opening: The request and the recommended approach come first, together with the clinical judgement that he needs timely treatment, so the team can prioritise him appropriately.

His interests, friends, chickenpox, the fluency app and the waiting-area question are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request, then history and severity, then impact and risk factors, then family readiness and the reason for urgency.
commentary.tone: Professional and evidence-based, firm about priority without overstating it.

letters.re: Re: Mr Jaymon Reeves, aged 24, cognitive-communication difficulties after severe traumatic brain injury
body: I am writing to refer Mr Reeves for ongoing management of cognitive-communication difficulties following a severe traumatic brain injury. He leaves inpatient rehabilitation on 3 September 2026, and I would be grateful if you could continue his outpatient therapy.

He sustained frontal and temporal contusions in a motorcycle accident on 21 July 2026. His language is structurally intact, but he loses the thread of conversation after about three minutes and has impaired verbal memory. His conversation is tangential and disinhibited, with poor topic maintenance and turn-taking, and impulsive responses.

Importantly, his insight is reduced and he reports no communication problems, which limits progress in all disciplines. Direct correction makes him irritable, but he accepts video feedback and an agreed discreet signal. He fatigues after 30 minutes, so morning sessions with a break are advised.

Therapy should target attention in conversation, pragmatics and compensatory memory strategies using his diary and phone. Partner education for his family and, with consent, employer is recommended. He hopes to return to his apprenticeship, but not before a formal work assessment. He has been advised not to drive and to notify the DVLA. Neuropsychology is booked for later in September; please coordinate with occupational therapy.

commentary.selection: The cognitive-communication profile, the insight problem, fatigue, what helps, the therapy goals and the driving advice are kept. The clavicle fracture, childhood asthma, football, his brother, the motorcycle being written off and parking are left out as irrelevant to communication therapy.
commentary.organisation: Request, then injury and communication profile, then insight and fatigue as the factors that shape therapy, then goals, partners and coordination.
commentary.tone: Clear and collegial; the insight problem is highlighted with 'importantly' so it is not missed.

letters.re: Re: Mr Stanley Ovenden, aged 79, communication and mealtime strategies
body: Thank you for asking me to review Mr Ovenden, who has advanced Alzheimer's dementia. I would be grateful if staff could follow the communication and mealtime strategies below.

He understands only short, familiar phrases and communicates with single words, expression and pointing. His hearing aid battery was flat, so please check it daily. Staff should use his preferred name, Stan, introduce themselves, approach from the front at eye level and give one instruction at a time. Please allow at least ten seconds, then repeat the same words.

He holds food in his mouth for up to thirty seconds, occasionally clears his throat on thin fluids and is at risk of aspiration if rushed or distracted. Please seat him upright at 90 degrees away from the kitchen door, with the television off and dentures in. Feed unhurriedly, one mouthful at a time, prompting him to swallow. I recommend a trial of IDDSI Level 6 soft and bite-sized food, avoiding dry, crumbly and mixed-consistency foods; thin fluids continue.
Every meal should be supervised, followed by oral care. Please contact me before the six-week review if you notice coughing, a wet voice, breathing changes, a chest infection or weight loss.

commentary.opening: The letter opens by acknowledging the request and immediately asks staff to follow the strategies, explaining briefly that he is at risk at meals so the purpose is clear.
commentary.selection: Only practical, actionable advice is kept: how he communicates, the hearing aid, specific communication techniques, the swallowing risk, positioning, texture and warning signs. His career, family visits, past surgery, podiatry, flu vaccine and food preferences are left out as they do not change what staff must do.
commentary.organisation: Request, then communication strategies, then mealtime findings and strategies, then supervision and when to call back.
commentary.tone: Clear, practical and instructional, written for nursing staff to act on, with polite imperatives ('please check').

letters.re: Re: Mrs Doris Pemberton, aged 77, unintentional weight loss on a texture-modified diet
body: I am referring Mrs Pemberton for nutritional assessment, as she has lost 4 kg unintentionally over eight weeks on a texture-modified diet. I would be grateful for advice on high-energy, high-protein modified-texture options, fortification and small frequent meals. She would prefer a home visit, as travelling tires her.

She has bulbar-onset motor neurone disease. Since videofluoroscopy in June 2026, she has been safest on IDDSI Level 6 soft and bite-sized food with Level 2 mildly thick fluids. Her cough is weak, so aspiration may be silent, and risk is highest in the last third of each meal.

Meals now take up to 45 minutes, she eats about half, and her weight is 54 kg, down from 58 kg. She finds the textures and thickened drinks unappealing and restricts fluids, so hydration is borderline. She prefers sweet flavours and cold puddings. Nobody is present for her evening meal.

She is anxious about a feeding tube and does not want to be fed by a machine, but has no advance decision. A joint discussion of nutrition goals, gastrostomy and advance care planning, with her niece present, is needed within weeks, after respiratory assessment and while she can fully take part.

commentary.opening: The weight loss and the precise dietetic request are in the first paragraph, together with her wish for a home visit, so the dietitian can triage and plan the visit at once.
commentary.selection: The letter keeps the textures she must stay on, the aspiration and fatigue risks, intake, weight, hydration, food preferences, the unsupervised evening meal and the urgent joint discussion, now including gastrostomy and a prior respiratory assessment. Her career, gallbladder, wrist fracture, cat, church group, breast screening and birthday tea are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request, then the swallowing restrictions, then the nutritional picture, then the feeding-tube concern and the time-sensitive joint discussion.
commentary.tone: Collegial and precise, sensitive in reporting her wishes about tube feeding while making the time pressure clear.

letters.re: Re: Miss Sofia Bianchi, aged 6 years 2 months, discharge after treatment for phonological disorder
body: I am writing to inform you that Sofia was discharged from speech pathology on 27 August 2026 following successful treatment of a phonological disorder. No further routine review is needed, but I would be grateful if you could re-refer her should either concern below arise.

She was referred on 20 October 2025 with unintelligible speech. Assessment showed a moderate to severe phonological disorder with fronting, stopping and final-consonant deletion, and intelligibility to unfamiliar listeners was approximately 40 per cent. Her hearing, oromotor structure and language were normal, with no signs of childhood apraxia of speech.

She attended eighteen sessions over ten months using minimal-pairs and cycles approaches, supported by a home programme. All target processes have resolved, intelligibility is now estimated at 90 per cent, and percentage of consonants correct has risen from 62 to 94 per cent. Her teacher reports improved confidence and participation.

Occasional distortion of /r/ and use of /f/ for th remain, both developmentally appropriate. Her parents have been advised to re-refer if /r/ is not acquired by age seven, or if literacy concerns emerge, because a history of phonological disorder increases the risk of later reading and spelling difficulty. The school is aware.

commentary.opening: A discharge letter states the outcome first; the request is then made explicit (no routine review, but re-refer if specific concerns arise) so the GP knows what action, if any, is expected.
commentary.selection: Key measures before and after therapy, the treatment approach and the two re-referral triggers are kept. Ear infections in infancy, thumb-sucking, chickenpox, gymnastics, the grandmother in Italy and the younger brother are left out as they do not affect the GP's role.
commentary.organisation: Outcome and request, then original findings, then treatment and progress, then residual features and safety-netting advice.
commentary.tone: Formal and concise, appropriately positive, with clinical terms a GP will understand.

letters.re: Re: Baby Amara Nguyen, aged 4 months, feeding and communication advice, cleft lip and palate
body: I am writing with feeding and communication advice for Amara, whom I reviewed at the regional cleft centre on 25 August 2026. I would be grateful if you could monitor her weight, hydration and hearing at routine checks, and encourage her parents to continue their current feeding technique.

She has a complete left unilateral cleft lip and palate. Her lip was repaired on 24 July 2026 and healed well; palate repair is planned at ten to twelve months. She feeds with a specialised cleft teat and squeezable bottle, held upright at approximately 60 degrees, with paced feeding, rhythmic squeezing and frequent burping. Feeds of 150 mL now finish within 30 minutes, without coughing, colour change or distress.
She weighs 6.0 kg, tracking along the 25th centile, with six wet nappies a day. Mild nasal air escape during vocalisation is expected before palate repair.

Because she is at risk of middle-ear effusion, please watch for ear infection or reduced response to sound, as hearing loss could affect later speech. Audiology review is due in October 2026. Babbling and turn-taking are developing well. She will be reviewed at the multidisciplinary cleft clinic in six weeks, with speech assessment after palate repair.

commentary.selection: The cleft repair timeline, the exact feeding technique, intake, growth, hydration and the hearing risk are kept. Antenatal detail, breastfeeding history, scar massage, the brother's singing, car seats, parking and school-run timing are left out as they do not change community care.

commentary.tone: Supportive and practical between professionals, reassuring that the current approach works while making the hearing watch clear.

letters.re: Re: Mrs Eileen Forsythe, aged 84, dysphagia management on transfer
body: I am writing to hand over the swallowing management of Mrs Forsythe, who transfers to your care on 2 September 2026 after recurrent aspiration pneumonia, so that her dysphagia precautions continue unchanged.
She has advanced Parkinson's disease. Videofluoroscopy showed silent aspiration on thin fluids. She does not cough when aspirating, so absence of coughing never indicates safety.

Please provide IDDSI Level 5 minced and moist food with IDDSI Level 2 mildly thick fluids. She must sit upright at 90 degrees for all intake and 30 minutes afterwards, with one-to-one supervision at every meal. Prompt her to alternate solids and fluids and take a second dry swallow. Time meals approximately 45 minutes after a levodopa dose, offering smaller, more frequent portions. Crush medications in puree only if the pharmacist permits. Provide oral care after meals and at bedtime.
Her GP, Parkinson's nurse and pharmacist should review her long-term domperidone, with an ECG; do not stop it abruptly.

Arrange prompt medical review for a wet voice, coughing with meals, prolonged meals, raised temperature, breathlessness or refusal to eat. Weigh her weekly; she weighed 51 kg on 1 September 2026. We will review her in four weeks, sooner if chest symptoms develop.

commentary.opening: The first paragraph names the transfer date and the request at once: the nursing team must keep every precaution in place from the day she arrives.
commentary.selection: Only what the nurses need to care for her safely is kept: the silent aspiration, the textures, seating, supervision, prompts, timing with levodopa, crushing, oral care, the domperidone review, warning signs, weight and review. Her hobbies, past surgery, family visiting questions and the television request are left out.
commentary.organisation: Purpose, then the key risk (silent aspiration), then the daily instructions in one practical paragraph, then the medication review, then warning signs and monitoring, then follow-up.
commentary.tone: Clear and directive but courteous between professionals; instructions are phrased as requests with reasons where safety depends on them.

letters.re: Re: Mr Bernard Castellano, aged 64, discharge after laryngectomy rehabilitation
body: I am writing to inform you that Mr Castellano was discharged from speech and language therapy on 28 August 2026 after completing rehabilitation following total laryngectomy, and to ask you to re-refer him if the concerns below arise.

His laryngectomy on 15 December 2025, for T3 laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma, was followed by radiotherapy, completed in March 2026. His ENT review on 5 August 2026 showed no recurrence, and surveillance continues under the head and neck team.

He now has fluent tracheo-oesophageal speech, intelligible in most settings including on the telephone. He eats a normal diet without aspiration or leakage through the prosthesis, and his weight is stable at 78 kg. He is independent with stoma care, heat-moisture exchanger use and prosthesis cleaning, as is his wife.

His prosthesis, fitted on 10 June 2026, is working well. Routine replacement remains with the ENT clinic, and his next review is booked for October 2026. He carries a spare plug for leakage and a neck-breather alert card, and his family have resuscitation information.
Please re-refer him if his voice deteriorates, leakage through or around the prosthesis develops, swallowing worsens, or new throat, neck or stoma symptoms arise.

Hobbies, holidays, grandchildren, old operations, the car park query and well-controlled diabetes details are left out, as the GP already holds or does not need them.

letters.re: Re: Leo Hartman, aged 5 years 2 months, discharge from speech and language therapy
body: I am writing to let you know that Leo Hartman, who joins your Year 1 class in September 2026, was discharged from our service on 28 August 2026, and to suggest classroom strategies to support his progress.

Leo was referred because of delayed expressive language and unclear speech. After therapy and a parental home programme, his understanding and use of language are now within normal limits for his age. He speaks in full sentences, tells a simple story in order, and is understood easily by unfamiliar listeners. He speaks English and Tamil, and continuing Tamil at home has supported both languages.

He may occasionally simplify consonant clusters in long words, for example saying "pider" for "spider" when excited. This is common at his age and is expected to fade. When it happens, please model the correct word naturally rather than asking him to repeat it, allow him time to process what he hears, and encourage clear speech without pressure. Please re-refer him if clusters are still reduced in everyday speech by around age 6.
Given his early language history, please also re-refer him if any literacy difficulties emerge during Year 1. His parents have our contact number.

letters.re: Re: Mr George Aldridge, aged 74, post-stroke dysphagia and weight loss
body: I am writing to refer Mr Aldridge for nutritional assessment and planning of his texture-modified diet, following his videofluoroscopy on 29 August 2026. He transfers to the community caseload today.

He had a left middle cerebral artery ischaemic stroke six weeks ago. The study showed trace silent aspiration on thin fluids only. He requires an IDDSI Level 4 pureed diet with IDDSI Level 2 mildly thick fluids, upright at 90 degrees for all intake and 30 minutes after, with supervised meals.

His weight has fallen from 74 kg to 70 kg since admission (height 183 cm, body mass index 21). He eats about half of each meal, finds modified food bland and would "rather not bother". Fluid intake is low, at about 1.2 litres a day, and no oral nutritional supplements have been started. He enjoyed well-spiced food, and his wife would welcome written recipe ideas.
He has right-hand weakness and feeds himself left-handed after set-up. He has type 2 diabetes on metformin; the pharmacist is reviewing his tablet format. He is allergic to penicillin.
Please advise on calorie and protein intake and monitoring of his weight and, particularly, hydration. Weekly swallow therapy continues, aiming to upgrade textures.

commentary.opening: The request for nutritional assessment is stated in the first sentence, linked to the swallow study that made it necessary.
commentary.selection: The dietitian needs the textures and precautions, the weight loss with height and BMI, intake, appetite, low fluids, supplements, food preferences, self-feeding, his diabetes (relevant to supplements) and the pending tablet review. Blood pressure, eye screening, hernia repair, the dog, the cricket and parking are left out as irrelevant.
commentary.organisation: Purpose, then diagnosis and swallow findings with the resulting textures, then the nutritional concern, then feeding ability and allergy, and finally the specific requests.
commentary.tone: Professional and collegial, with precise figures a dietitian will use for calculations.

header: The Head and Neck Speech Pathology Team
letters.re: Re: Mr Gordon Halliwell, aged 61, pre-laryngectomy counselling
body: I am writing to refer Mr Halliwell for pre-operative counselling and communication planning before his total laryngectomy on 21 September 2026. He should ideally be seen within a week, allowing time for a second appointment; mornings suit him.

He has T3 squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx, with neck dissection also planned. He has mild stridor on exertion, worsening over three weeks; this was reported to the surgical team today, and he has been told to call 999 for stridor at rest or breathing difficulty. He has moderate COPD and is allergic to sulfa drugs. His alcohol intake exceeds recommended limits; possible withdrawal has been flagged to the surgical and anaesthetic teams.

He is very anxious and believes he will be permanently mute; he had not heard of a voice prosthesis. Please explain the anatomical changes, including permanent breathing through a stoma and loss of smell, and introduce the alaryngeal communication options. A post-operative communication plan with a writing board, and baseline voice and swallow measures, are needed.
As a self-employed plumber taking all his business calls, he is keen to keep working, which should shape his goals. He would like to meet someone who has had a laryngectomy.

commentary.opening: The request, the operation date and the time frame are all in the first paragraph, because the counselling must happen before 21 September and ideally twice.
commentary.selection: The diagnosis, the worsening stridor with its emergency advice, COPD, the allergy, the alcohol risk already flagged for the peri-operative period, his misconception and anxiety, the content to cover and his work goals are kept. Old injuries, hobbies, the caravan, the football ticket and parking are left out.
commentary.organisation: Purpose and timing, then clinical background and airway risk, then his understanding and what the session should cover, then personal goals.
commentary.tone: Collegial and specific, conveying urgency about the airway and empathy about his fear without dramatising.
