letters.re: Re: Master Kwame Mensah, aged 5 years 4 months, developmental language disorder
body: I am writing to transfer the care of Kwame Mensah, who has developmental language disorder, to your service for classroom-embedded language support as he starts Year 1 in September 2026.

We have seen Kwame since June 2025. His hearing is normal and his speech sounds are age appropriate. On 14 August 2026, he followed one-step instructions reliably and two-step instructions with visual support, but struggled with complex grammar. He uses three-to-four-word sentences, with word-finding difficulties and errors in verb tense and plurals. His vocabulary standard score was 78. His scores have improved but remain below average.

He responds well to a visual timetable, picture cues, new words pre-taught with a picture, an action and repetition, and single-step instructions. A first-sound cue helps his word finding. He always answers yes to "do you understand?", so please check understanding by asking him to show or tell back what to do. He concentrates best near the front.

We recommend regular liaison with his class teacher and an annual review with his teacher and parents. We would be happy to attend a joint meeting in the first half-term, and previous reports are available, as consent has been obtained.
signoff: Community Speech and Language Therapy Service

commentary.opening: The transfer and its purpose, continuing language support as he starts Year 1, are stated in a single opening sentence.
commentary.selection: A receiving therapist needs his current profile, what has worked and how to check understanding. The Ghana trip, his brother's lisp, hobbies, uniform and lunch questions are left out as they do not affect therapy.
commentary.organisation: Purpose, then history and current assessment, then effective strategies, then the ongoing plan and offer of liaison.
commentary.tone: Collegial and specific, therapist to therapist, using appropriate terms such as standard score and word finding.

letters.re: Re: Ms Priya Sandhu, aged 34, progressive dysphonia
body: I am writing to request laryngoscopy and stroboscopy for Ms Priya Sandhu, a primary school teacher with five months of progressive hoarseness, to confirm the diagnosis and guide management before voice therapy begins.

Her hoarseness began in the spring term without a preceding infection. Her voice deteriorates through the school day, with vocal fatigue by midday, habitual throat clearing, a mild throat ache and occasional complete aphonia. She has no dysphagia, haemoptysis, weight loss, neck lump or otalgia, and has never smoked.

On assessment on 29 August 2026, her voice was rough and breathy, with reduced loudness and pitch range, hard glottal onsets, clavicular breathing and neck tension. Her maximum phonation time was 9 seconds and her Voice Handicap Index 42. I suspect bilateral vocal fold nodules, although polyps or cysts remain possible.

She teaches thirty children without amplification and also runs a choir. She has untreated mild reflux and allergic rhinitis with post-nasal drip, for which she takes loratadine 10 mg as required. She has no known allergies.
Vocal hygiene advice has been given; therapy will start after your examination. Her term begins on 3 September 2026, and she can attend at short notice during the autumn half-term.

commentary.opening: The specific investigations requested and the reason, confirming the diagnosis before therapy, are given in the first sentence.
commentary.selection: Duration, pattern, absence of red flags, smoking status, perceptual and objective findings, vocal load and contributing reflux and rhinitis are kept. Her husband, hometown, ankle fracture, exercise, the wedding and the café question are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request, then history and red-flag screen, then assessment findings and impression, then contributing factors, then current management and availability.
commentary.tone: Concise and clinical for a surgeon, using standard voice terminology.

letters.re: Re: Corinthian, Irish Sport Horse gelding, aged 11 years, chronic left forelimb lameness
body: I would be grateful if you would assess Corinthian for magnetic resonance imaging of the left fore foot, and advise on treatment and a realistic prognosis for return to work.

He has had a gradual-onset left forelimb lameness since November 2024, worse on hard ground and on the left rein. On 8 April he was grade 4 out of 10 on the left rein. A palmar digital nerve block on 24 March gave 70 per cent improvement, localising the pain to the palmar foot. I have left the distal interphalangeal joint and navicular bursa unblocked for you.

Radiographs show enlarged, irregular navicular synovial invaginations, flexor cortex irregularity and medullary sclerosis, which do not explain the lameness. Corrective farriery has improved balance but not the lameness. Phenylbutazone helped only while given and was stopped on 17 March. No bisphosphonate or intra-articular medication has been given, and an NSAID should not accompany one.

I would also value your view on the right fore, which is sound but shares the same imbalance. Mrs Adeyinka-Bramhall is insured to £5,000 per condition. She has asked whether he will compete again; I have deferred this until after imaging and would ask for the same care.

commentary.opening: The specialist needs to know at once what is being asked, so the first paragraph names MRI of the left fore foot as the main request, together with a treatment plan and a prognosis.
commentary.selection: The letter keeps the lameness pattern, the nerve block that localised the pain, the key radiographic findings, the response to treatment and the date phenylbutazone was stopped, which the hospital needs before repeat blocks or MRI. Detailed grading on each surface, palpation findings, the 2021 hind limb injury and the list of radiographic views are left out because the enclosed records cover them.
commentary.organisation: Request first, then history and localisation, then imaging and treatment response with the NSAID washout and the bisphosphonate warning, and finally the right fore and the owner's practical and emotional situation.
commentary.tone: Collegial and precise between vets, with a tactful but clear request about how the prognosis is discussed with the owner.

header: Specialist in Cattle Health and Production
letters.re: Re: Hollowfield Farm, 240 Holstein-Friesian dairy cows, transition cow disease
body: I am writing to request a full herd-level transition cow investigation for Mr Ogundipe-Threadgold's herd, having investigated it over three visits without resolution.

Since August 2025, disease within 21 days of calving has risen markedly: 14 left displaced abomasums against 3 last year, 22 cases of clinical ketosis against 7, retained membranes in 19 per cent of calvings and 11 cases of milk fever. Two cows died within 10 days of calving, neither examined post mortem.

Metabolic profiles on 26 October showed raised non-esterified fatty acids in 5 of 6 fresh cows and subclinical hypocalcaemia, consistent with negative energy balance. Mean body condition at drying off was 3.6, which I believe is central. The dry group is overstocked, with 58 cm of feed space per cow, shares one ration with far-off cows, and its DCAB and mineral specification are unknown.

I would be grateful for your assessment of the as-fed dry cow ration, the DCAB approach, stocking density, grouping and the timing of the move after calving, together with a monitoring protocol the farm can run. Please note that he will invest in feed but will not build. He has agreed to future post mortem examinations.

commentary.opening: The letter opens by asking for a herd-level investigation, not an opinion on individual cows, because that is the specific service the specialist is being asked to provide.
commentary.selection: Disease figures, the metabolic profile findings, body condition and housing problems are kept because they define the problem and point to its cause; the negative energy balance rests on the profiles, not the bulk-milk ratio, which is only marginally raised. Detailed forage analysis, trace elements, milk yield and cell count are left out as enclosed or not part of the problem.
commentary.organisation: Request, then the size of the problem, then the evidence for its cause, then the specific questions and the client's constraint.
commentary.tone: Professional and data-led between colleagues, with an honest admission of what is unresolved.

letters.re: Re: Ptolemy, German Shepherd Dog crossbreed, male entire, aged 3 years 2 months, escalating aggression
body: I would be grateful if you would assess Ptolemy for escalating aggression, with a diagnosis, a realistic management plan and an honest risk assessment.

Over fourteen months, barking at visitors has progressed to lunging and snapping. On 11 January 2025 he bit a family friend who reached for his collar under a table (Dunbar level 3); on 17 January he air-snapped at the owner's adult son, who tried to move him off a bed. All incidents occurred indoors, on approach while he was confined or on furniture, after missed avoidance signals.

Clinical and laboratory examinations were unremarkable, radiographs showed only mild hip remodelling, and a two-week NSAID trial, now stopped, made no difference. He needs a muzzle for examination. I have not started psychopharmacological treatment and would value your guidance.

The family, who have children aged 9 and 12, ask whether he is safe with them; please answer plainly. Meanwhile, I have advised in writing: move his bed off the through route, never approach or move him when confined or on furniture, and never leave the children with him unsupervised. Mrs Delacroix-Umeh is not insured but wishes to proceed, and asks that euthanasia be a conclusion, not a starting point.

commentary.opening: The opening states the three things the behaviourist is asked for, assessment, plan and risk assessment, so the purpose is clear before the history.
commentary.selection: The escalation, both incidents with their common pattern, the medical exclusions, the stopped NSAID, the interim safety advice and the unanswered safety question are kept. Detailed test results, early history, exercise routine and the failed trainer are left out as enclosed or for the family to describe.
commentary.organisation: Request, then the behaviour and its pattern, then medical work-up and medication, and finally the children's safety, the interim advice and the owner's position.
commentary.tone: Professional and careful, recording facts without judging the family, and firm about the need for a plain answer on risk.

letters.re: Re: Marigold, Netherland Dwarf rabbit, female neutered, aged 4 years 2 months, dental disease with mandibular lysis
body: I would be grateful if you would see Marigold for computed tomography of the skull, to define her apical dental disease and left mandibular lysis, and advise on possible abscessation and surgical management.

She has lost 240 grams, 18 per cent of body weight, over four months, and now takes only syringe-fed recovery formula, given competently by her owner. Her body condition score is 1.5 out of 5, and two episodes of absent faecal output resolved with treatment.

Under anaesthesia on 9 January, I reduced elongated cheek teeth with sharp spurs, one of which had penetrated the tongue. Radiographs showed apical elongation, with focal lysis at the left mandibular swelling. The left nasolacrimal duct is obstructed, with purulent material on flushing; please assess both incisor and cheek teeth apices as its cause. She continues on meloxicam 0.6 mg/kg once daily, with hydration monitored. I have deliberately withheld antibiotics so that samples are diagnostic.

I would also value a long-term plan and an honest prognosis. Miss Okonjo-Fairweather is not insured and would like a written estimate. She has been told that poor early dietary advice, not she, caused this, and asks to be told plainly if the outlook is poor.

commentary.opening: CT is the principal reason for referral, so it is named first, with the mandibular lysis as the finding that drives it.
commentary.selection: Weight loss, dependence on syringe feeding, gut stasis episodes, the key dental and radiographic findings, current medication and the withheld antibiotic are kept. The detailed dental chart, husbandry history and vaccination status are left out as enclosed or not needed for the specialist's decision.
commentary.organisation: Request, then her current condition, then findings and treatment, then the long-term questions and the owner's wishes.
commentary.tone: Collegial and clinical, with a respectful request that the owner's reassurance is not undone.

letters.re: Re: Three dogs kept by Mr Redvers Ashcombe-Onwuka (Ranger, Sable and Willow), clinical welfare concerns
body: I am writing to report clinical concerns about three dogs kept by Mr Ashcombe-Onwuka, examined on four occasions between 4 September and 27 November 2025. I report only what I examined and recorded.

Ranger, about 6 years old, had a body condition score of 1 out of 9, severe demodicosis with pyoderma, otitis and ingrown nails. Despite dispensed treatment and written feeding advice, his weight fell from 18.2 kg to 17.5 kg; the keeper stated that medication had not been given.

Willow, aged about 12 months, has entropion causing a right corneal ulcer. Surgery, recommended in writing on 2 October, was not pursued, and the ulcer is now 5 mm, deeper and at risk of perforation. Same-day referral, offered again today, was not accepted; I regard this as urgent.
Sable, with a body condition score of 2 out of 9 throughout, had recently whelped when first seen and now appears pregnant again, not yet confirmed by ultrasound.

The 18 September review was missed, and financial assistance offered on 2 and 30 October was not taken up. I am not stating that an offence has been committed, and I have not visited the address. The keeper knows of this letter.

commentary.opening: The first paragraph states the purpose, a report for the inspectorate to consider, and immediately limits it to what the vet has examined, which sets the factual basis of the letter.
commentary.selection: For each dog the measured findings, the advice given and the lack of progress are kept, because these are the substance of the concern; Willow's eye is flagged as urgent because it is at risk of perforation. Detailed skin, ear and dental findings, the neutering discussion and the enclosure list are left out as covered by the enclosed records.
commentary.organisation: Purpose, one paragraph per dog in order of concern, then non-attendance, refused help and the limits of the report.
commentary.tone: Formal, neutral and evidential: findings are stated without any judgement of the keeper's intent, and 'Yours faithfully' suits an unnamed recipient.

letters.re: Re: Hemlock, British Shorthair, male neutered, aged 4 years 9 months, urethral obstruction
body: Thank you for referring Hemlock, who was discharged today after urethral obstruction caused by feline idiopathic cystitis. I would be grateful if you would recheck him 48 hours from discharge and repeat renal parameters and potassium at 7 days.

He was admitted on 3 February 2025 with potassium 8.6 mmol/L, creatinine 588 micromol/L and a bradyarrhythmia. After stabilisation, a urethral plug was retropulsed and a catheter maintained for 48 hours. Creatinine was 121 micromol/L at discharge, and he has urinated normally since catheter removal. Culture was negative and no calculi were seen.

He is discharged on prazosin 0.5 mg twice daily for 14 days, meloxicam 0.05 mg/kg once daily for 5 days with food, and buprenorphine 0.02 mg/kg three times daily for 3 days. Given his recent kidney injury, please stop meloxicam if he is not eating or drinking normally. No antibiotic was dispensed.

To reduce recurrence, please begin a structured weight plan at the 7-day recheck, alongside a mainly wet diet, more water and litter provision, and exploration of tension with another cat. Mr Osei-Bramwell knows that straining, vomiting or lethargy require same-day attention.

letters.re: Re: Bramble, Standard Poodle, female neutered, aged 4 years 3 months, suspected hypoadrenocorticism
body: I would be grateful if you would see Bramble, ideally tomorrow, 17 March, to confirm or exclude hypoadrenocorticism, my working diagnosis, by ACTH stimulation testing, and to guide long-term management if it is confirmed.

She presented collapsed on 14 March after a three-month history of waxing and waning vomiting and diarrhoea, weight loss of 3.7 kg and increased thirst. Despite hypovolaemic shock she was bradycardic at 56 beats per minute. Sodium was 128 mmol/L and potassium 7.9 mmol/L, a ratio of 16.2, with hypoglycaemia and no stress leucogram.

She received 0.9 per cent sodium chloride, calcium gluconate, dextrose and maropitant. Dexamethasone 0.1 mg/kg intravenously, first given after a baseline cortisol sample, which is pending, has continued once daily, so her cover is continuous. It should continue until the test, which should be prompt, as dexamethasone suppresses the adrenal axis over time. By 16 March she was bright and eating, with sodium 138 mmol/L and potassium 5.4 mmol/L. She remains on intravenous fluids but is stable for travel.
If the diagnosis is excluded, I would value further investigation. Mrs Farnsworth-Adeyemi is insured, prefers a morning appointment and wishes to be present for any discussion of prognosis.

commentary.opening: The working diagnosis, the test needed to confirm it and the request to be seen tomorrow come first, because a dog with suspected hypoadrenocorticism must not wait and the specialist's first action is the ACTH stimulation test.
commentary.selection: The history, the bradycardia in shock, the key electrolytes and ratio, the continuous dexamethasone cover and why the test must be prompt, and the response to treatment are kept. Liver enzymes, protein values, the full ECG description and the differentials if excluded are left out as enclosed or for the specialist.
commentary.organisation: Request, then presentation and diagnostic findings, then treatment and current status, then the alternative pathway and owner arrangements.
commentary.tone: Collegial and concise, with a clear clinical argument for the working diagnosis.

letters.re: Re: Wolseley, Labrador Retriever, male neutered, aged 6 years 8 months, right hindlimb lameness
body: I would be grateful if you would assess Wolseley for surgical stabilisation of the right stifle, with your view on technique and on the meniscus.

He became acutely lame on 2 May after turning sharply. Despite four weeks of strict rest and meloxicam 0.1 mg/kg once daily, which continues, he has a grade 3 out of 5 right hindlimb lameness, a positive sit test and 5 cm of thigh muscle atrophy. Under sedation, cranial drawer and tibial compression were positive, with a meniscal click on two of three attempts. Radiographs show marked effusion and periarticular new bone.

The left stifle has a mild medial buttress and mild new bone, and he had a milder left hindlimb episode fourteen months ago, so I would value your opinion on it. He weighs 41.2 kg with a body condition score of 8 out of 9, and weight loss should form part of any plan.

We would deliver post-operative rehabilitation here and would welcome your guidance. Mr Nkemelu-Harrowgate is insured and understands that recovery takes about three months. He lives in a first-floor flat with fourteen steps and no lift, which should be considered at discharge, and prefers telephone contact.

commentary.organisation: Request, then right stifle evidence, then the left stifle and weight, then rehabilitation and practical discharge planning.
commentary.tone: Collegial and concise, anticipating the practical issues the surgeon will need for discharge.

letters.re: Re: Hettie, Boxer, female neutered, aged 8 years 1 month, cutaneous mast cell tumour
body: I am writing to refer Hettie for full staging, grading, a treatment plan and an honest prognosis for a cutaneous mast cell tumour on her right thigh.

The mass, first noticed in February 2025, has waxed and waned. On 21 June it measured 3.2 cm by 2.8 cm, poorly demarcated at its deep margin, and Darier's sign was positive on gentle examination; it has since been handled minimally. The 2 June aspirate confirmed a mast cell tumour. Today I found a new 8 mm mass on the right flank, left unaspirated for you, and enlarged right popliteal and inguinal nodes; the popliteal aspirate result will follow.
Haematology, biochemistry and thoracic radiographs were unremarkable, with no systemic signs, but abdominal ultrasound has not been performed.

She has received chlorphenamine 0.5 mg/kg twice daily and omeprazole 1 mg/kg twice daily since 2 June. No corticosteroid has been given, and I have not attempted excision, as adequate margins were unachievable.

I would be grateful for abdominal ultrasound with liver and spleen aspirates, biopsy grading and c-KIT assessment. Her owner wants everything reasonable but asks to be told plainly when treatment would benefit her rather than Hettie. About half her annual insurance limit remains.

commentary.opening: The letter opens with exactly what the oncologist is asked to do — stage, grade, plan and give an honest prognosis — so the purpose is clear before any clinical detail.
commentary.selection: The cytology diagnosis, size and character of the mass, the new second mass, the enlarged nodes and the staging done so far are kept, because they shape staging and surgery. Normal individual blood values, vital signs and the household are left out as not changing the specialist's plan.
commentary.organisation: Purpose, then history and examination findings, then staging results, then treatment given and withheld, and finally the specific requests and the owner's wishes.
commentary.tone: Collegial and precise between veterinary surgeons, with a respectful note conveying the owner's request for plain honesty.

letters.re: Re: Ottoline, Great Dane, female neutered, aged 7 years 5 months, gastric dilatation-volvulus
body: Thank you for referring Ottoline, owned by Mr Ignatius Whitcombe-Adesanya, who was discharged today after surgery for gastric dilatation-volvulus. I would be grateful if you could take over her aftercare, including wound checks at 3 days and 10 days, as her owner requested.

On 12 September, a 180-degree volvulus was derotated. The stomach and spleen regained perfusion, so no resection or splenectomy was needed, and a right-sided incisional gastropexy was performed. Post-operative ventricular tachycardia was controlled with lidocaine and has not recurred over 48 hours. There are no skin sutures.

She is discharged on paracetamol 10 mg/kg three times daily for five days, gabapentin 10 mg/kg three times daily for seven days, omeprazole 1 mg/kg once daily for fourteen days, and maropitant 2 mg/kg once daily for three days if required. Antibiotics are not indicated, despite the owner's two requests.

Please ensure strict lead exercise for fourteen days, small meals four times daily, and, permanently, no exercise for one hour before and two hours after meals. Please repeat haematology, biochemistry and an ECG at 14 days, or the ECG sooner if collapse, weakness or exercise intolerance occurs.
The prognosis is good; the owner has written emergency signs.
signoff: Veterinary Surgeon, Emergency and Critical Care

letters.re: Re: Barnaby, Cavalier King Charles Spaniel, male entire, aged 9 years 2 months, suspected congestive heart failure
body: I am writing to refer Barnaby for echocardiography to confirm suspected myxomatous mitral valve disease with stage C congestive heart failure, pulmonary hypertension assessment, and a long-term plan.

His left apical systolic murmur, grade 2 out of 6 since 2021, reached grade 4 in February and is now grade 5 with a thrill. He has a cough of over six weeks, reduced exercise tolerance and two night-time episodes of respiratory distress. Home sleeping respiratory rates were 34 to 42.

Today he had caudodorsal crackles and a resting respiratory rate of 44. Radiographs showed a vertebral heart score of 11.9, marked left atrial enlargement with bronchial compression, and cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Bloods and blood pressure were normal.

I started furosemide 2 mg/kg twice daily, pimobendan 0.25 mg/kg twice daily and benazepril 0.25 mg/kg once daily, but not spironolactone, on which I would value your view. I will recheck him on 22 August, with renal values and potassium on 26 August.

His owner has written advice to seek emergency care if his breathing becomes laboured. She is 78, uninsured, and asks that costs be discussed in advance at each stage. She wants honesty about how long he has.

commentary.selection: Murmur progression, signs of failure, the sleeping respiratory rates, radiographic findings, the medication started, the early recheck with renal values, and the emergency advice to the owner are kept, because a dog in active failure is at home on new diuretic treatment. Dental disease, vaccination, prostatic history, weight loss and individual laboratory values are left out as not relevant to the cardiac question or enclosed.
commentary.organisation: Request, then history and progression, then today's examination and radiographs, then treatment and its monitoring, and finally the owner's emergency advice and circumstances.
commentary.tone: Professional and concise for a specialist, with a respectful, non-judgemental note about cost and the owner's wish for honesty.

letters.re: Re: Persimmon, American Cocker Spaniel, female neutered, aged 6 years 11 months, acute painful right eye
body: Further to my call with your duty ophthalmologist at 08:50, I am referring Persimmon for urgent assessment of suspected acute primary angle-closure glaucoma of the right eye and protection of the left eye. They expect to arrive within forty minutes.

Signs were noticed at 06:30, but she seemed unwell yesterday evening, so they may have been present for over twelve hours. The right intraocular pressure was 62 mmHg, against 19 mmHg on the left, with corneal oedema, a fixed dilated pupil, and absent menace and dazzle responses. Fluorescein was negative. Lens luxation, uveitis, neoplasia and hyphaema cannot be excluded.

She received dorzolamide 2 per cent to the right eye at 08:35 and methadone 0.2 mg/kg intramuscularly at 08:40. The pressure was 54 mmHg at 08:55, and mannitol 1 g/kg intravenously was started at 09:10; water has been withheld since. Latanoprost, corticosteroids, mydriatics and atropine have not been given. Blood results will be telephoned to you; please check them for renal or cardiac disease, given the mannitol.

The left eye appears normal, but gonioscopy was not possible and no prophylaxis has been started; please advise on arrival. Mr Trelawny-Obiora understands that the right eye may be blind and enucleation is possible.

commentary.opening: An emergency letter links to the phone call already made and states the request and arrival time in the first paragraph, because the reader must be ready for the patient.
commentary.selection: Pressures, vision tests, the possibly longer duration, treatment with exact times, the bloods to check after mannitol and what was deliberately withheld are kept, as the ophthalmologist needs them to continue treatment safely. Normal systemic findings, vaccination and travel history are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request and arrival, then onset and examination, then a timed treatment record, then the left eye and the owner's understanding.
commentary.tone: Urgent but measured and factual, as between veterinary surgeons handling an emergency.

letters.re: Re: Clementine, West Highland White Terrier, female neutered, aged 3 years 7 months, chronic pruritus
body: I am writing to refer Clementine, owned by Mrs Beatrix Nwankwo-Ellingham, principally for allergy testing and your view on allergen-specific immunotherapy. I would also value a supervised repeat food trial, ear culture with otoscopic assessment, and a long-term plan this practice can maintain.

Pruritus began at 11 months, initially seasonal, but has been continuous since November 2024. It affects the face, pinnae, axillae, ventral abdomen and feet, sparing the dorsum and tail head. She has had five episodes of bilateral otitis externa and recurrent Malassezia and bacterial skin infections.

Ectoparasites and dermatophytes have been excluded, with year-round isoxazoline flea control. A strict ten-week hydrolysed diet trial was equivocal, and concurrent medication was not recorded. Oclacitinib, now 0.5 mg/kg once daily, initially worked well but has waned. Prednisolone caused polyuria, polydipsia and behavioural change, which the owner will not accept again.
Ear cytology in May 2025 showed rods for the first time, and I have not seen the right tympanic membrane on two visits, so I have avoided ototoxic topical products.
Her insurance excludes skin disease. She is very compliant, but night-time scratching is affecting her sleep, and she needs to know whether this is manageable long term.

commentary.selection: The pattern and course of the pruritus, what has been excluded, the diet trial result and why it is weak, the drug responses and the ototoxicity caution are kept because they justify allergy testing and protect the ear. Individual scrape dates, scores, shampoo details and the untried drugs are left out as in the enclosed records or for the specialist.
commentary.organisation: Requests, then history and distribution, then work-up and treatment response, then the ear concern, and finally the owner's position.
commentary.tone: Collegial and analytical for a specialist, acknowledging the owner's exhaustion without emotional language.

letters.re: Re: Wendell, Miniature Dachshund, male entire, aged 5 years 4 months, acute non-ambulatory paraparesis
body: Further to my call to your duty neurologist at 16:55, I am referring Wendell, owned by Miss Cordelia Farquharson-Igwe, for urgent imaging and probable surgery for suspected acute Hansen type I intervertebral disc extrusion. He should arrive by 17:50.

He yelped jumping from the sofa at approximately 09:00 today and was dragging both hindlimbs by 12:30. At 16:30 he had non-ambulatory paraparesis with weak voluntary movement, absent proprioception, normal to increased pelvic limb reflexes and a cutaneous trunci cut-off at L2. There was marked pain over T13 to L1, localising the lesion to T3 to L3.
Crucially, deep pain perception was present in both pelvic limbs and the tail at 16:35 and again at 16:50. His distended bladder was expressed at 16:45.
He received methadone 0.3 mg/kg intramuscularly at 16:40 and Hartmann's at maintenance rate. No corticosteroid or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory has been given, and he is on strict cage rest.

His owner is insured to £7,000 and understands that MRI and surgery are likely and nursing will be prolonged. She lives alone and works full-time, so post-operative care needs honest discussion. She will telephone you immediately if he stops moving his hindlimbs or worsens during the journey.

letters.re: Re: Saffron, Domestic Shorthair, female neutered, aged 11 years 6 months, diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease
body: I am writing to transfer the care of Saffron, owned by Mr Ptolemy Wainwright-Osagie, who has registered with you. I would be grateful if you could continue her diabetic protocol unchanged unless a home curve indicates otherwise, and confirm at her first appointment that her care will not start again from scratch.

Diabetes was diagnosed on 14 August 2023. After weight loss from 5.9 kg to 4.4 kg, she now receives porcine lente insulin, 40 IU/mL, 1 unit subcutaneously every 12 hours with U-40 syringes, at 07:30 and 19:30, always immediately after food. She eats a low-carbohydrate wet diet, with no dry food or treats. On 22 March 2025 her curve nadir was 6.1 mmol/L, and fructosamine was 342 micromol/L.

She has had two hypoglycaemic episodes after missed meals. Please consider remission, and reduce the dose if pre-insulin glucose is consistently below 8 mmol/L. Stress makes in-clinic glucose falsely high, so please rely on his home meter data.

She also has IRIS stage 2 chronic kidney disease and untreated systolic blood pressure of 148 mmHg. Renal diets are higher in carbohydrate, so any change needs close glucose and phosphate monitoring. Total T4 has not been measured.

commentary.opening: The opening states the transfer and the two things the new practice is asked to do: keep the protocol unchanged and reassure the owner at the first visit.
commentary.selection: The exact insulin protocol with its U-40 strength and syringes, feeding, recent curve and fructosamine, the hypoglycaemia history, the remission warning, the stress hyperglycaemia and the home meter are kept, because a new practice could otherwise change the dose in error. The carbohydrate effect of a renal diet and the unmeasured T4 are added for the kidney and age question. Diagnostic values from 2023, the dose history, the sampling method and the monitoring timetable are left out as in the enclosures.
commentary.organisation: Purpose and request, then the current diabetic protocol, then cautions, and finally the concurrent kidney disease.
commentary.tone: Collegial and practical, as one practice handing over to another, with clear but courteous instructions.

letters.re: Re: 'Smokey', 9 years, home care for newly diagnosed diabetes
body: This letter explains Smokey's home care now that he has diabetes. Never give his insulin if he is unwell, vomiting or has not eaten, because a missed dose is far safer than one given to a cat that has not eaten.

Give 1 unit of insulin under the skin twice daily, at 8 am and 8 pm, after his meal. Store insulin in the fridge, check that it is clear before each dose, do not shake it, and use a new needle every time. Never change the dose without our advice, and log each dose, the time, his appetite and anything unusual.

Over seven days, change him gradually to the diabetic diet. Feed weighed portions twice daily at injection times, with no free feeding and no treats. Weight loss must be slow, as rapid loss can damage his liver.
If he becomes wobbly, weak, confused, twitchy or unresponsive, his blood sugar may be too low. Rub honey or glucose syrup on his gums and telephone us immediately.
Your husband should first give one injection here under supervision. A nurse will ring you in three days, and we will check his blood glucose and weight in 7 to 10 days.

commentary.opening: The letter opens by stating its purpose and then gives the single most important rule at once, because a dose given to a cat that has not eaten is the main danger at home.
commentary.selection: Only what the owner must do is kept: the dose and times, insulin handling, the log, the diet, hypoglycaemia signs and first aid, the supervised injection for her husband, and follow-up. Test results, examination findings, the cascade consent she has already given, old illnesses and social details such as the book club, Cornwall and parking are left out because she does not need them to act.
commentary.organisation: The safety rule, then the daily injection routine, then feeding, then warning signs and what to do, then the back-up injector and follow-up.
commentary.tone: Warm, plain English for an owner, with clear instructions and no unexplained medical terms.

letters.re: Re: 'Misty', 13-year-old female spayed Domestic Shorthair, chronic kidney disease
body: I am handing Misty back to your care for long-term monitoring of newly diagnosed chronic kidney disease. Her first recheck is provisionally booked with you for 11 September 2026.

She was admitted on 25 August 2026 with polyuria, polydipsia, reduced appetite, lethargy and vomiting. She was 6 to 8 per cent dehydrated, with small irregular kidneys and systolic blood pressure of 178 mmHg. Creatinine was 320 micromol/L, SDMA 28 micrograms/dL, phosphate 2.1 mmol/L and UPC 0.6, so she is IRIS Stage 3, hypertensive and proteinuric.
She received intravenous fluids for 48 hours, maropitant, and amlodipine from day two. She is now rehydrated, eating the wet renal diet voluntarily, with blood pressure of 150 mmHg.

Please continue amlodipine 0.625 mg every 24 hours and the renal diet exclusively. Please check creatinine, phosphate, potassium and blood pressure then, and every three months. Please repeat the UPC and start telmisartan or benazepril if proteinuria persists once she is stable, consider a phosphate binder if phosphate stays above target, and potassium supplementation if potassium falls below the reference range.
The owners will contact you if vomiting recurs, she stops eating for more than 24 hours, or she seems suddenly blind or disorientated.

commentary.opening: The first paragraph tells Dr Khan what is being handed over and when he will next see the cat, which is the action he must take.
commentary.selection: The staging values, blood pressure, treatment in hospital and every point of the ongoing plan, including potassium supplementation if potassium falls, are kept because the regular vet will manage them. Old dental and flea history, the house move, insurance, the daughter, the grandson and the heated pad are left out as irrelevant to monitoring.
commentary.organisation: Purpose and booking, then diagnosis and staging, then the hospital course and discharge status, then the monitoring plan, then the warning signs the owners know.
commentary.tone: Concise and collegial, vet to vet, using standard staging terms without explanation.

letters.re: Re: 'Diesel', Bernese Mountain Dog, 14 months, left elbow arthroscopy
body: Diesel was discharged today after left elbow arthroscopy. Please remove his sutures on 6 September 2026 and support his rehabilitation and weight loss.

The fragmented medial coronoid process seen on CT was removed. Medial compartment cartilage was modified Outerbridge grade 2, with synovitis; the lateral compartment and anconeal process were normal. There were no complications. At discharge he was weight-bearing, mildly lame and had a low pain score.

He is on meloxicam 0.1 mg/kg once daily for 10 days with food. The owners know to give no human pain relief, especially ibuprofen or aspirin, and to stop meloxicam and contact a vet if he vomits, has diarrhoea or stops eating.

He needs strict lead-only exercise for two weeks, five to ten minutes three times daily, with no stairs, jumping, play or slippery floors, and a collar if he licks. From week three, exercise increases gradually alongside physiotherapy and hydrotherapy.

Losing approximately 4 kg, to body condition score 4 to 5 out of 9, is the most effective long-term intervention, so nurse weigh-ins every two to three weeks would be helpful. We will recheck him here around 8 October 2026. Osteoarthritis is expected, and the breeder should be informed.

commentary.opening: The letter thanks the referring vet, states that the dog is home, and asks at once for the two things the clinic must do: suture removal on a fixed date and support with rehabilitation and weight.
commentary.selection: Surgical findings, medication, the warning against human pain relief, what to do if meloxicam upsets him, exercise restriction, the rehabilitation start, weight target and recheck are kept. The swallowed sock, diarrhoea, agility history, insurance, the son's driving test, groomer, parking and holiday are left out as irrelevant.
commentary.organisation: Request, then the procedure, then medication, then home exercise and rehabilitation, then long-term weight management and follow-up.
commentary.tone: Professional and concise, vet to vet, with specific clinical terms the reader will understand.

letters.re: Re: 'Nala', Labrador Retriever, 7 years, ovariohysterectomy for pyometra
body: Nala was discharged today after emergency ovariohysterectomy for open pyometra. Please see her for her suture check on 29 August and suture removal on 3 September, both booked at your practice.

She was admitted on 24 August 2026 with lethargy, anorexia, polydipsia and purulent vulval discharge. She had a marked leucocytosis with a left shift and mild azotaemia, creatinine 145 micromol/L, which resolved with fluids. Ultrasound confirmed a distended, fluid-filled uterus, which was removed intact that evening without spillage.
On day two, her white cell count was falling and her creatinine was normal. She is eating, urinating normally, and the wound is clean and dry.

She is discharged on amoxicillin-clavulanate 12.5 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days and meloxicam 0.1 mg/kg once daily for 5 days, both with food. Buprenorphine was not continued. Meloxicam should stop if she eats or drinks poorly or vomits.

She needs lead exercise only and a buster collar until suture removal, with no bathing or swimming. Please recheck her renal values in 2 weeks to confirm the azotaemia has fully resolved. Mrs Mitchell knows to contact the clinic immediately if Nala becomes dull, stops eating, vomits, or if the wound opens.

commentary.opening: The opening gives the reason for the letter and asks the primary vet for the two booked appointments, with their dates, so the request is clear at once.
commentary.selection: The diagnosis, azotaemia and its follow-up, the surgery, discharge medication with the rule for stopping meloxicam, home restrictions and warning signs are kept. The lipoma, ear infection, breeding history, children, cat, dog show and beach visits are left out as they do not affect her care.
commentary.organisation: Request, then admission findings and surgery, then progress, then medication, then home care, follow-up tests and red flags.
commentary.tone: Professional and factual, vet to vet, with standard clinical terms.

letters.re: Re: 'Bruno', Great Dane, 5 years, 62 kg, gastric dilatation-volvulus
body: I am transferring Bruno for immediate surgery for confirmed gastric dilatation-volvulus: derotation, assessment of gastric and splenic viability, and gastropexy. He leaves at 21.55 with a registered veterinary nurse and should be with you within 25 minutes.

He presented at 21.15 with unproductive retching, abdominal distension and restlessness after a large meal followed by exercise. He was tachycardic at 160 beats per minute, with weak femoral pulses, pale mucous membranes, capillary refill time 3 seconds and a tympanic abdomen. A right lateral radiograph, emailed at 21.45, confirms volvulus. Lactate was 6.2 mmol/L before fluids; please recheck it on arrival.

Two 16 gauge cephalic catheters are in place. He received a 20 mL/kg Hartmann's bolus, with a second running since 21.40, and methadone 0.2 mg/kg intravenously at 21.30. Orogastric decompression was only partial, so right flank trocarisation was performed, reducing distension. After the first bolus his heart rate fell to 140 beats per minute. The ECG shows occasional ventricular premature complexes, not currently needing treatment but requiring continued monitoring.
Mr Reid has consented to surgery and asks to be telephoned afterwards, whatever the time. Pre-fluid blood samples travel with Bruno. Please telephone us on arrival.

commentary.opening: In an emergency transfer the first paragraph must say what is needed and when the dog will arrive, so the surgeon can prepare theatre straight away.
commentary.selection: Presenting signs, shock parameters, radiograph result, lactate, catheters, fluids, analgesia, decompression and the arrhythmia are kept because the surgeon acts on them. Old dewclaw and lick granuloma history, the show career, nervousness, the lorry shift, parking and insurance are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request and arrival time, then presentation and diagnostics, then stabilisation given and response, then consent and practical handover.
commentary.tone: Brief, urgent and precise, vet to vet, with times given so the timeline is clear.

letters.re: Re: 'Biscuit', domestic shorthair cat, 13 years, uncontrolled hyperthyroidism
body: I would be grateful if you could assess Biscuit for radioiodine therapy, including pre-treatment renal and cardiac assessment, as her hyperthyroidism is no longer controlled medically.

She was diagnosed eleven months ago with a total T4 of 78 nmol/L. Despite methimazole, increased to 5 mg twice daily, her total T4 remains 65 nmol/L. Tableting has become very difficult, with several missed doses weekly, and Mrs Fenwick cannot continue twice-daily tableting. Biscuit has lost weight from 4.2 kg to 3.4 kg despite polyphagia, with vomiting about twice weekly.

Heart rate is 220 beats per minute, with an unchanged grade II out of VI systolic murmur, so echocardiography is suggested. A left thyroid goitre is palpable. Creatinine is 132 micromol/L, upper end of normal, but hyperthyroidism lowers creatinine, so masked kidney disease is possible; please include SDMA pre-treatment. I would value your view on whether a methimazole trial is needed before treatment, given the compliance problem.

Systolic blood pressure is 168 mmHg despite amlodipine 0.625 mg once daily, started two weeks ago, and I would welcome your view on 1.25 mg once daily. Methimazole will continue as best Mrs Fenwick can manage until she hears from you. All reports are attached.

commentary.opening: The request comes first: assessment for radioiodine with the pre-treatment work-up, and the reason, failed medical control, in the same sentence.
commentary.selection: The T4 trend, compliance problem, weight loss, cardiac findings, borderline renal value, blood pressure and the two questions for the specialist are kept. Dental history, the choir, charity shop, redecorating and transport arrangements are left out as irrelevant to the clinical decision.
commentary.organisation: Request, then history and reason for failure, then cardiac and renal concerns with the first question, then blood pressure, the second question and interim treatment.
commentary.tone: Collegial and courteous to a specialist, with questions phrased as requests for her view.

letters.re: Re: 'Bramble', Labrador Retriever, 4 years, suspected right cranial cruciate ligament rupture
body: I would be grateful if you could assess Bramble for surgical stabilisation of a suspected right cranial cruciate ligament rupture. Tibial plateau levelling osteotomy has been discussed with the owners as the likely option.

He has a three-week history of progressive right hindlimb lameness, which worsened acutely after running four days ago, and he is now intermittently non-weight-bearing. He has right stifle effusion, a palpable medial buttress, positive cranial drawer and tibial thrust, pain on extension and 2 cm of thigh muscle atrophy. No meniscal click was detected conscious. Sedated examination confirmed a cranial drawer of approximately 8 mm. Radiographs show effusion and mild trochlear osteophytosis without fracture, and the tibial plateau angle is 27 degrees. Routine bloods were unremarkable.
The left stifle has mild effusion without drawer, suggesting possible early contralateral disease. The owners have been counselled that it may need surgery within a year.

He weighs 38 kg and has started a weight-loss diet with a target of 33 kg. Meloxicam 0.1 mg/kg by mouth every 24 hours, with a partial response, and strict lead-only rest will continue meanwhile. He has no known drug reactions. Radiographs and blood results are attached.

commentary.opening: The referral states its purpose in the first sentence and names the likely procedure, so the specialist knows what has already been discussed with the owners.
commentary.selection: History, key orthopaedic signs, sedated drawer, radiographic findings, tibial plateau angle, the contralateral stifle, current treatment and readiness for surgery are kept. Ear infection, vaccination dates, the cat, the football team, camping and parking are left out.
commentary.organisation: Request, then history and findings, then the contralateral concern given its own paragraph for emphasis, then weight, current treatment and practical readiness.
commentary.tone: Collegial and precise, using orthopaedic terms a specialist expects.

letters.re: Re: 'Sasha', Rottweiler, 8 years, suspected osteosarcoma of the right distal radius
body: I would be grateful if you could see Sasha promptly for confirmation and full staging of a suspected osteosarcoma of the right distal radius, and to discuss forelimb amputation with adjuvant carboplatin. Pathological fracture is a real and imminent risk.

She has a six-week history of progressive right forelimb lameness, now non-weight-bearing, which responded partially to meloxicam before deteriorating. There is a firm, painful distal radial swelling. Radiographs show an aggressive mixed lytic and proliferative lesion with cortical destruction, a long zone of transition and a thin cortex, but no fracture. Three-view thoracic radiographs show no overt metastasis. Haematology and biochemistry are unremarkable, with normal alkaline phosphatase, and her lymph nodes are normal.

She receives meloxicam 0.1 mg/kg once daily and gabapentin 10 mg/kg three times daily, and her pain at rest has improved. No paracetamol-containing product is used. Exercise is strictly restricted, with a short lead, no jumping and a ramp for the car.

Mr Clarke understands the likely diagnosis and that micrometastasis is probable. He is considering amputation, and her other joints are clinically normal. Please also present palliative options, including radiotherapy and bisphosphonates, as he may not choose surgery. Results are attached.

letters.re: Re: Tilly, Cocker Spaniel, female neutered, 7 years, bilateral cataracts
body: I am writing to refer Tilly, a neutered female Cocker Spaniel, for electroretinography and ocular ultrasound to assess retinal function and exclude retinal detachment or lens capsule rupture, followed by assessment of her suitability for phacoemulsification.

She has had progressive vision loss over three months, particularly in dim light, with cloudiness in both eyes noticed about six weeks ago. Diabetes has been excluded, and haematology and biochemistry are normal. There is no history of ocular trauma or eye disease.

Today she has bilateral immature to mature cataracts, more advanced on the left, where the fundus cannot be visualised. The menace response is reduced bilaterally and absent on the left, but dazzle and pupillary light reflexes are present in both eyes. There is no uveitis or aqueous flare. Intraocular pressures are left 16 and right 18 mmHg, and Schirmer and fluorescein tests are normal.
She receives topical ketorolac twice daily to prevent lens-induced uveitis, and this should continue until you see her.

Mr and Mrs Hartley are keen to restore her vision if retinal function is confirmed and can manage postoperative care. As the lenses are maturing, I would be grateful for an early appointment. Findings are attached.

letters.re: Re: Rolo, French Bulldog, male neutered, 4 years, chronic atopic dermatitis
body: I am writing to refer Rolo, a neutered male French Bulldog, for intradermal or serological allergy testing, consideration of allergen-specific immunotherapy and video-otoscopy, as his ear canal stenosis is progressing.

His pruritus began at 18 months, initially seasonal and now year-round, affecting the face, paws, axillae and ventral abdomen. His owner scores it 7 out of 10 on a bad week, and sleep is disturbed. He has needed five courses of treatment for ear infections in two years, and antibiotics and steroids gave only partial responses with prompt relapse.

He has axillary and interdigital erythema and lichenification, and bilateral otitis externa with stenotic vertical canals, worse on the left. Cytology shows Malassezia and cocci in the ears and skin. Ectoparasites and dermatophytes have been excluded, and a strict eight-week hydrolysed diet trial gave limited improvement, making food allergy unlikely.

He currently receives oclacitinib 0.5 mg/kg once daily, with antiseptic shampoo and ear cleaner twice weekly. These should continue until you advise, but oclacitinib will need withdrawing before intradermal testing, and I would appreciate your guidance on timing.
Ms Bennett wants steroid-sparing long-term control and can give injections at home. Cytology reports and the diet diary are enclosed.

commentary.selection: Onset and course, the failed treatments, ear stenosis, cytology, the excluded differentials and the diet trial are kept because they support the atopy diagnosis. Old injuries, the sock, daycare, flooring, the partner's hay fever and waiting-room questions are left out as irrelevant to the dermatologist.

commentary.tone: Professional and precise, vet to specialist, with a direct request for advice on drug withdrawal.

letters.re: Re: Clover, Netherland Dwarf rabbit, female neutered, 3 years, molar malocclusion
body: I am writing to refer Clover, a neutered female Netherland Dwarf rabbit, for skull imaging, preferably CT, and dental burring under general anaesthesia for acquired molar malocclusion.

Over two weeks she has had a reduced appetite, dropping of food, weight loss and a watery left eye. She now weighs 1.1 kg, compared with 1.35 kg in February, and her body condition score is 2 out of 5. Her diet has been mainly pellets and a muesli mix with little hay.

Otoscopic examination showed sharp lower cheek-teeth spurs lacerating the left lateral tongue; incisors are normal. She has moist dermatitis from drooling and palpable irregularity of the ventral mandible. The nasolacrimal duct is patent but was difficult to flush, so root elongation is suspected. Faecal output and gut sounds are reduced.
She is being syringe-fed a critical care formula, 50 mL/kg daily in six feeds, with meloxicam 0.5 mg/kg once daily, a prokinetic and subcutaneous fluids, and is taking feeds willingly.

Dietary correction has begun. Mrs Price understands that this is likely to be lifelong and recurring. Her bonded companion is being kept with her for comfort. Her weight record is attached; I would appreciate early assessment.

commentary.opening: The opening sentence names the imaging, the procedure and the need for anaesthesia, so the specialist can plan the admission straight away.
commentary.selection: Weight loss with both weights, the oral findings, signs of root elongation, gut slowdown and current supportive treatment are kept. Nails, the bite wound, the guinea pig, holidays, carrots and carrier questions are left out because they do not affect the dental referral.
commentary.organisation: Request, presenting signs and diet, examination findings, current support, then the owner's understanding and practical points for the stay.
commentary.tone: Clear and clinical between colleagues, with exact doses so the specialist can continue care without a phone call.

letters.re: Re: Comet, Warmblood gelding, 12 years, recurrent colic
body: I am writing to refer Comet, a Warmblood gelding of approximately 560 kg, urgently for surgical assessment and possible exploratory laparotomy. He is loading now, and the journey takes approximately 50 minutes.

This is his third colic episode in 36 hours, with pain recurring within two hours of each treatment. His forage changed abruptly from haylage to hay ten days ago. He has had two previous mild spasmodic colics and no abdominal surgery.

His heart rate has risen from 48 to 64 beats per minute, with congested mucous membranes, a capillary refill time of 3 seconds, reduced gut sounds and mild abdominal distension. Rectal examination found a gas-distended large colon suggesting displacement. Nasogastric intubation produced approximately 4 litres of net reflux; packed cell volume is 46 per cent. Peritoneal fluid has mildly elevated protein with a normal lactate, but this can change quickly.

He has received intravenous flunixin, which may mask deterioration; the time is on the referral form. Buscopan was given at the second visit. Intravenous fluids run via a left jugular catheter, and the nasogastric tube remains in place.
Ms Doyle has consented to surgery; insurance is in place. His passport and our notes travel with him.

commentary.selection: The three drivers of referral (rising heart rate, reflux, recurrent pain), rectal and peritoneal findings and every drug given are kept. Hoof abscess, farrier, competition, parking, bedding and yard detail are left out as irrelevant to an emergency surgical decision.
commentary.organisation: Request and timing, history of the episode, clinical and diagnostic findings, treatment with the flunixin warning, then consent and documents.
commentary.tone: Brief, urgent and factual, written for a surgeon who may read it on arrival.

letters.re: Re: Pippa, Miniature Schnauzer, female neutered, 10 years, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus
body: I am writing to refer Pippa, a neutered female Miniature Schnauzer, for ACTH stimulation or low-dose dexamethasone suppression testing for suspected hyperadrenocorticism, and for a review of her poorly controlled diabetes mellitus.

She was diagnosed diabetic eight months ago. Despite increases in caninsulin from 0.5 to 1.1 IU/kg twice daily, she has persistent polyuria, polydipsia and polyphagia. Over four months she has also developed a pot-bellied appearance and a thinning coat. She has had no steroids in the past year and no pancreatitis, although triglycerides are mildly elevated.

On examination, she had symmetrical truncal alopecia, thin skin, hepatomegaly and hindlimb muscle wastage. Her glucose curve remained above 18 mmol/L throughout, fructosamine is elevated and alkaline phosphatase is moderately raised at 620 U/L. There are no urinary ketones, and urine culture was negative.

She currently receives caninsulin 1.1 IU/kg twice daily with a high-fibre diet. Injection technique and storage have been checked, and a fresh vial made no difference. Trilostane has deliberately not been started pending confirmation, and her insulin dose will need adjusting once adrenal disease is controlled.
Mr Wells is committed to her care and is happy for her to stay in hospital for testing. Results are attached.

commentary.organisation: Request, history and failed insulin escalation, examination and results, current treatment and the decision not to start trilostane, then the owner's commitment.
commentary.tone: Formal and precise, vet to specialist, presenting evidence rather than asserting the diagnosis.

letters.re: Re: Hugo, Springer Spaniel, male entire, 6 years, suspected immune-mediated haemolytic anaemia
body: I am writing to refer Hugo, an entire male Springer Spaniel of 19.4 kg, urgently for blood typing and packed red cell transfusion, and for immunosuppressive management of suspected primary immune-mediated haemolytic anaemia. His packed cell volume is falling and he is symptomatic at rest.
Over 48 hours he has developed lethargy, pale gums, reluctance to exercise and one collapse. There is no toxin access, travel abroad or recent medication; he was vaccinated four months ago.

He has pale to icteric mucous membranes, a heart rate of 170 beats per minute, pulses that were bounding and are now weak, splenomegaly, a respiratory rate of 44 and a temperature of 39.4 degrees Celsius. Packed cell volume is 14 per cent and regenerative, with spherocytosis and persistent saline agglutination. Platelets are normal, and imaging and vector-borne disease tests found no trigger.

This morning he started prednisolone 2 mg/kg per day, clopidogrel for thromboprophylaxis, a gastroprotectant and intravenous crystalloids. Second-line immunosuppression may be needed if he does not respond within the first few days.
Mr Raines understands the guarded prognosis and costs, wishes to proceed, and is travelling with Hugo and our records now. He would appreciate a daily telephone update.

commentary.opening: The urgent transfusion request and the reason (falling PCV, symptomatic at rest) appear in the first paragraph, so the hospital can prepare blood products before arrival.
commentary.selection: The deterioration, the diagnostic evidence for IMHA, the exclusion of triggers and every drug started are kept. Gundog work, the shoot captain, the toy, parking and the previous dog are left out as irrelevant to emergency care.
commentary.organisation: Request and urgency, history and negatives, examination and results, treatment started with the next step, then owner consent and communication.
commentary.tone: Urgent but measured, vet to specialist, with precise values so treatment can continue without delay.

letters.re: Re: Mochi, Maine Coon, male neutered, 6 years, arterial thromboembolism
body: I am writing to refer Mochi, a neutered male Maine Coon, urgently for full echocardiography, thromboprophylaxis planning and heart failure management after suspected arterial thromboembolism this morning.
His owner found him dragging both hindlimbs and crying at 08.30. He had no previous cardiac diagnosis, although he had been mildly lethargic for some weeks.

On presentation at 09.40, both hindlimbs were cold, with absent femoral pulses, cyanotic nail beds and firm, painful gastrocnemius muscles. Motor function is absent in both hindlimbs, and deep pain sensation is reduced but present on the right. He has a gallop rhythm, a respiratory rate of 48 per minute and a rectal temperature of 36.2 degrees Celsius. NT-proBNP is markedly elevated, and point-of-care echocardiography shows a left atrium to aorta ratio of 2.2 and a thickened left ventricular wall, with mild pleural effusion on ultrasound. Potassium is 4.2 mmol/L and must be rechecked, as reperfusion can cause a dangerous rise.
He has received intravenous methadone, clopidogrel 18.75 mg once daily, low-dose furosemide and passive warming.
Ms Lee understands the guarded prognosis and the risk of recurrence. She wishes to attempt treatment and reassess at 48 hours. Our records are being sent electronically.

commentary.selection: Onset time, limb findings with neurological status, cardiac and thoracic findings, the potassium warning and all drugs given are kept. Littermate behaviour, the cat tree, blanket, visiting and travel time are left out as irrelevant to emergency management.
commentary.organisation: Request, onset, examination and diagnostics ending with the potassium warning, treatment, then the owner's decision and the 48-hour review.
commentary.tone: Urgent and factual, vet to specialist, with prognostic facts stated plainly.
